title: 10 Tips for Writing Good User Stories (2016)
author: Roman Pichler
summary:
The most opinionated of the bunch and probably the most useful one to internalize. Pichler's whole stance is that user stories are a *conversation tool*, not a spec — treat them as documentation and you've already lost the point.

**Core principles:**

- **Users come first.** No user research = no user stories. Otherwise you're writing fiction based on assumptions.
- **Use personas as the source.** Personas hold the goals; goals reveal which stories to write.
- **Stories are collaborative.** Product owner + team writing them together. If you can't involve the team, use a more formal method (like use cases) instead.
- **Keep them simple.** Template: *As [persona], I want [what], so that [why]*. Use active voice. Don't force the template when it doesn't fit.
- **Start with epics** (big, sketchy, coarse-grained). Break them down over time as you learn from feedback and prototypes.
- **Refine until Ready:** clear, feasible, testable, fits in a sprint, shared understanding across the team.
- **Add 3–5 acceptance criteria** to detailed stories so "done" is verifiable.
- **Paper cards work.** Cheap, tactile, easy to group on a wall. Even if you also track them digitally.
- **Keep them visible.** Don't bury them in a licensed tool nobody opens. Wall > network drive.
- **Don't rely on stories alone.** They can't capture user journeys, visual design, or technical architecture — pair them with story maps, workflow diagrams, sketches, mockups, or UML for technical needs.

Stories are collaborative — Product owner + team writing them together

title: User Stories With Examples and a Template
author: Atlassian
summary:
A cleaner, more digestible intro than Pichler but less opinionated. Worth remembering for a few things:

- **A user story is the smallest unit of work in Agile** — an end goal from the user's perspective, not a feature.
- **"Customers" can be internal.** Colleagues who depend on your team count.
- **The 3 C's:** Card (written description), Conversation (discussion that clarifies details), Confirmation (acceptance criteria defining "done").
- **Why bother with stories vs. just tasks?** Stories keep focus on the user, enable collaboration, drive creative solutions, create momentum through small wins.
- **Template unpacked:**
 - *As [persona]* → not just a job title, the actual person with empathy behind them
 - *Wants to* → intent, not features. If you're describing UI, you've missed the point.
 - *So that* → the bigger-picture benefit

title: Epics, Stories, and Initiatives
author: Atlassian
summary:
Simple hierarchy that keeps getting muddled in real teams:

| Level | What it is | Timeframe |
|---|---|---|
| **Story** | Short, user-focused, fits in one sprint | 1–2 weeks |
| **Epic** | Group of related stories driving toward a larger goal | Weeks to a quarter |
| **Initiative** | Collection of epics driving toward a broader business goal | Multiple quarters to a year |

**Useful mental model:** if you're talking to a developer, speak in stories. To an eng lead, epics. To leadership, initiatives.

**Not every story needs an epic.** A small bug fix or UI tweak can stand alone. Force everything into an epic and you make the backlog messier, not cleaner.
still_relevant: Yes. Naming varies by company (initiatives vs. themes vs. PC tickets vs. OKRs), but the layered structure is universal.

title: Replacing the User Story With the Job Story (2013)
author: Alan Klement
summary:
**Note:** The original was blocked, so this is reconstructed from Klement's summaries and secondary sources.

Klement's argument: user stories bake in too many assumptions and ignore *why* people act. "As a [user], I want X, so that Y" locks you into a persona and a solution before you understand the situation.

**The job story format instead:**
> **When** [situation], **I want to** [motivation], **so I can** [expected outcome].

The shift is from "who" to "situation." Same person behaves differently depending on context — a job story captures the trigger and context, which often matters more than demographics.

**Example contrast:**
- User story: *As a commuter, I want to listen to podcasts so I can stay entertained.*
- Job story: *When I'm stuck in traffic on my morning commute, I want something that keeps me engaged without needing my hands, so I don't feel like I'm wasting the time.*

The job story leaves the *solution* open (podcast? audiobook? call a friend?). The user story pre-decides it.
still_relevant: Very. JTBD has become a legit alternative framework, especially in product design and discovery. Not a replacement for user stories in all cases, but a good tool for early problem framing when you don't want to jump to solutions.

title: User Stories
author: Mountain Goat Software (Mike Cohn)
summary:
Cohn is one of the people who popularized user stories in the first place, so his framing is the source most others build on. Big overlaps with Pichler and Atlassian, but a few additions worth keeping:

**What makes a *good* story (the 4 qualities):**
1. **Clear value** — someone cares whether it gets done, and you can say who and why
2. **Small enough to finish** in one sprint (otherwise "almost done" forever)
3. **Testable** — you can tell when it's done, even if all criteria aren't spelled out yet
4. **Leaves room for conversation** — doesn't over-prescribe the solution

**"Just enough detail" principle.** Stories near the top of the backlog need clarity because you'll work on them soon. Stories lower down can stay vague — priorities and users may change before you get there. Adding detail too early = wasted work.

**Common mistakes worth flagging:**
- Treating the written story as *the* requirement (it's a reminder to have a conversation)
- Writing stories too large — hides complexity, kills feedback
- Splitting into tasks instead of smaller outcomes (a task is *how*; a story is *what for*)
- Writing everything from the product owner's perspective (they're usually not the user)
- Adding detail too soon
- Using the template robotically without thinking

**Pre-sprint checklist:**
- Who benefits?
- What outcome does this support?
- Why now?
- Small enough to finish?
- Not split by technical layer only (frontend/backend halves aren't real stories)?
- Room for conversation?
- Clear "done"?
still_relevant: Extremely. This is probably the most complete and current writeup of the five.

title: User Experience Design (the UX Honeycomb)
author: Peter Morville
summary:
Morville's original article introducing the seven facets of UX. Even 20+ years on, this is probably the single cleanest framework for talking about UX quality.

**The seven facets:**

- **Useful** — Does it actually solve a real problem? Don't just execute the brief; ask whether the thing is worth building.
- **Usable** — Ease of use. Necessary but not sufficient (his line, and it's a good one).
- **Desirable** — Emotional pull, brand, identity, aesthetic power. Efficiency isn't the whole story.
- **Findable** — People can locate what they need, both across the site and within it.
- **Accessible** — Designed for people with disabilities. Framed as ethical and increasingly legal (accurate: EAA came into force 2025, WCAG is the global baseline).
- **Credible** — Design elements that make users trust what you're telling them.
- **Valuable** — Delivers value to the business/sponsor, not just the user.

**Why the model still matters:**
1. Forces prioritization. "Is desirability or accessibility more important for this project?" is a real conversation you have to have.
2. Modular. You can attack one facet at a time (e.g., a credibility-focused redesign) instead of always ripping everything up.
3. Each facet becomes a lens. Focusing on findability, for example, pulls you into SEO and IA in ways you wouldn't otherwise go.

title: UX Without User Research Is Not UX (2014)
author: Hoa Loranger (NN/g)
summary:
The thesis is right there in the title. NN/g's argument: having a UX title, department, or process means nothing if you're not talking to actual users. The best line: **UX − U = X** (where X means "don't do it").

**Key points:**

- **UX is everyone's job.** Product, dev, marketing, content, support, graphic design, IxD — all responsible for user outcomes. A UX department alone can't save a company that isn't user-centered.
- **Agile makes this harder.** Fast release cycles push teams to skip research; Scrum doesn't include UX as a core role. Result: teams ship without knowing whether the thing works. "It doesn't matter how many products we release. If they're junk, we're simply shipping a lot more of it."
- **Common methodology mistakes:**
 - **Asking the wrong people** — stakeholders and colleagues aren't real users
 - **Leading the witness** — biased questions from inexperienced facilitators
 - **Wrong method for the question** — surveys ≠ usability tests ≠ A/B tests. Applying the wrong one gives you confidently wrong answers.
- **User research doubles as team-building.** Nothing kills internal debates faster than "let's test it." Data ends arguments that opinions can't.
- **Test sketches and wireframes, not code.** You don't need a built product to test a concept. Waiting until launch to test is the waterfall trap dressed up as Lean.

title: UI vs. UX (2018)
author: UserTesting
summary:
The perennial "explain this to a hiring manager" question. Best analogies from the article:

- **Ken Norton (ex-Google):** "UI is the table, chair, plate, glass, and utensils. UX is everything from the food, to the service, parking, lighting and music."
- **Craig Morrison:** UI and UX aren't comparable — UI is a *component* of UX, not a parallel discipline. Like asking the difference between "a car and the color it's painted."
- **Jason Ogle:** "UI is the bridge that gets us where we want to go. UX is the feeling we get when we arrive."
- **Scott Jenson (Google):** "The UI copes with constraints; the UX challenges them."

**Core definitions:**
- **UI** = the visual/interactive layer users touch (screens, buttons, icons, sound, gestures)
- **UX** = the full experience of using a product or service, on-screen and off, before, during, after

title: Interviewing Users (2010)
author: Jakob Nielsen (NN/g)
summary:
Nielsen's core stance: interviews are useful, but only for the narrow set of questions they can actually answer. Misusing them = confidently wrong data.

**What interviews CAN'T tell you:**
- What users did in the past (memory is fallible; people invent logical-sounding stories to rationalize what they half-remember)
- What users would do with a future feature (users are not designers — they can't envision what doesn't exist)
- Specific design decisions (button color, radio vs. dropdown, IA placement, help copy) — these need behavioral testing, not opinions
- Whether a feature is "useful" — famously, if you ask people to rate feature usefulness, they'll rate fake features positively too

**The timeline principle:** valid data only comes from the *present moment*. Anything about the past = misremembered. Anything about the future = speculation.

**What interviews CAN do well:**
- **General attitudes** and mental models around a problem
- **Brand impressions** built up over long-term use (this is what you can't observe in a session)
- **Critical incident technique** — ask about specific extreme cases (things that went really wrong or really well). These vivid moments give you actionable detail. Much better than asking "how do you usually do X?" which gets you an idealized fiction.

**Beware the query effect:** ask about anything and people will fabricate opinions. If you ask about visual design, they'll comment on colors even if they don't care. But if colors come up *unprompted* during actual use — that's a real signal.

**Triangulation is the answer.** Combine interviews with observation, testing, analytics. No single method is enough.

Brand impressions — built up over long-term use (this is what you can't observe in a session)
Critical incident technique — ask about specific extreme cases (things that went really wrong or really well)
still_relevant: Timeless. The Microsoft Office 2007 example (users "requested" features that already existed = discoverability problem, not missing features) is still the cleanest way to explain why you can't just ask users what they want.

title: UX Research Methods (2015)
author: Jackie Tanner (Prototypr)
summary:
Long article, but the format is basically: method name → what it is → pros → cons. Below is the summarized cheat sheet, since that's what makes this useful long-term.

**Evaluative / Testing methods:**

| Method | Best for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| **Heuristic Evaluation** | Cheap first pass; identifies obvious usability issues | "Expert" is subjective — different evaluators find different things |
| **Moderated Usability Test** | Complex interfaces; deep insights; 3–5 users is enough | Cost adds up (~$50/test at commercial platforms); needs good moderator |
| **Unmoderated Usability Test** | Cheaper, natural behavior, quantitative metrics | No follow-up; test setup has to be bulletproof |
| **A/B / Multivariate Testing** | Choosing between concrete alternatives with clear KPI | No behavioral insight — just tells you which won |

**Generative / Discovery methods:**

| Method | Best for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| **Individual Interviews** | High-level attitudes and mental models | Say ≠ do; leading questions bias answers |
| **Focus Groups** | Direct user access; conversation | Expensive, groupthink, say ≠ do (again) |
| **Contextual Inquiry / Field Studies** | Seeing actual use in real environment — often the best method | Qualitative, travel cost, workplace access can be a barrier |
| **Diary Studies** | Longitudinal insight into thoughts during real use | Recruiting and monitoring is hard |
| **Surveys** | Fast, cheap, remote, quantifiable | Say ≠ do; response bias; question wording matters a lot |
| **Card Sorting** | Structuring IA and navigation | Recruiting is the main friction |

**Communication / Craft:**

| Method | Best for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| **Personas** | Keep team user-focused during design | Not real people; can drift into fiction if not grounded in data |
| **Wireframes** | Communicating layout early and cheaply | — (basically always worth doing) |
| **Rapid / Paper Prototyping** | Testing interactions before building | Complex prototypes take time; can confuse users if unclear |
| **Parallel Design** | Converging on best solution from many minds | Time-consuming; needs multiple designers |
| **Competitive Analysis** | Baseline for industry norms and best practices | Time-consuming; can lead to copying instead of thinking |

**Analytics:**
- **Clickstream analysis** — quantitative behavior, no *why*
- **Customer feedback** — free, but subjective

**Lean UX vs. Agile UX** (from the last section):
- **Lean UX** — MVP + build/measure/learn loops. Data-driven iteration on the smallest thing that could work.
- **Agile UX** — Dynamic dev process that accommodates change mid-project (vs. Waterfall's frozen requirements).
- They integrate. Lean is the philosophy, Agile is the framework, and both replace Waterfall.

title: 10 Design Thinking Frameworks
author: IxDF
summary:
The value of this article isn't the frameworks themselves — it's realizing they're **all the same thing wearing different jackets**. Every design thinking process has:

- **Empathy** with users
- **Reframing** the problem
- **Divergent thinking** (generate ideas, no judgment)
- **Convergent thinking** (narrow, combine, refine)
- **Prototype and test**
- **Iterate**

**The ten frameworks, compressed:**

| Framework | Stages |
|---|---|
| **d.school (Stanford) — 5-stage** | Empathize → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test |
| **Herbert Simon (1969)** | Define → Research → Ideate → Prototype → Choose → Implement → Learn |
| **AIGA — Head, Heart, Hand** | Solve (head) + Empathize (heart) + Create (hand) |
| **IDEO DeepDive™** | Understand → Observe → Visualize → Evaluate → Implement |
| **IDEO 3-stage** | Inspiration → Ideation → Implementation |
| **IDEO Human-Centered Design Toolkit** | Hear → Create → Deliver |
| **Design Council — Double Diamond** | Discover → Define → Develop → Deliver (2 diamonds of diverge/converge) |
| **Frog — Collective Action Toolkit (CAT)** | Clarify → Build → Seek → Imagine → Make → Plan |
| **Liedtka & Ogilvie — Designing for Growth** | What is? → What if? → What wows? → What works? |
| **LUMA Institute** | Looking → Understanding → Making |

**What actually matters:**
- Pick one framework that fits your organization and stick with it enough to internalize it
- Don't confuse the stages with linear steps — every good framework is iterative and non-linear
- The Double Diamond is probably the most useful shared vocabulary for cross-functional teams (business, dev, design all recognize it)
key_points: Empathy — with users
Reframing — the problem
Divergent thinking — (generate ideas, no judgment)
Convergent thinking — (narrow, combine, refine)
Prototype and test
Iterate
still_relevant: Yes for vocabulary and shared language, though "design thinking" as a branded discipline has taken a beating in the last few years (IDEO's own struggles, critiques from Natasha Jen and others about it becoming a corporate ritual). The *principles* remain sound; the *cargo-culting* is what got criticized.

title: Challenges of Enterprise User Research (2018)
author: Anusha Bollimuntha (UX Collective)
summary:
This is the article most people should read before taking their first enterprise/B2B role. The rules are genuinely different from consumer UX.

**The core challenges:**

1. **Domain expertise is required.** You can't fake understanding of payroll workflows, financial systems, or logistics pipelines. Expect to specialize in a domain — or move between adjacent ones — because the learning curve is steep. Upside: you're surrounded by long-tenured experts, use them.

2. **Clients ≠ users.** In consumer UX, the buyer and user are usually the same person. In enterprise, someone in procurement or IT buys the tool, and someone completely different has to use it. Users often didn't choose the software and can't opt out. Reimann's quote in the piece: *"Most users of enterprise applications don't have a choice about using them."* Which means expectations are high and frustration builds fast.

3. **Business segments behave differently.** Large orgs have specialized roles; medium orgs have people wearing 2–3 hats; small orgs have one person doing everything. Same product, three completely different usage patterns. Design for one and you break the others.

4. **Multiple personas, single workflow.** Enterprise workflows chain across roles — a payroll practitioner starts something, a manager approves, an accountant finalizes. You have to research the *handoffs* between roles, not just each role in isolation. Communication patterns between teams are often where the real pain lives.

5. **Legacy system loyalty is real.** People have optimized their workflow around a mainframe for 15 years. Any change to their tools = a productivity hit while they relearn. Users will resist redesigns even when the new thing is objectively better. Understand the current behavior before proposing changes.

6. **Delight isn't the goal — reducing pain is.** Consumer UX chases delight. Enterprise UX succeeds when it removes friction. Users are often venting when you interview them; that's data. Listen to what they say, but focus on observing what they actually do.

7. **Validation matters more.** Multi-stakeholder projects, political dynamics, legacy constraints. You have to triangulate what different groups tell you and figure out what's true vs. what's opinion vs. what's territory.
still_relevant: Extremely, especially for anyone considering B2B/SaaS roles. This article ages well because enterprise UX moves slowly by definition.

title: Scrum Ceremonies
author: Visual Paradigm
summary:
Basic ceremony reference. Not deep, but useful when you need to explain to yourself or someone else what happens when in a Scrum team.

**The four core ceremonies:**

| Ceremony | When | Purpose | Typical length |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Backlog Refinement** | Ongoing | Add detail, estimates, ordering to backlog items | Ongoing / occasional session |
| **Sprint Planning** | Start of sprint | Decide what to build this sprint and how | A few hours |
| **Daily Scrum / Standup** | Every day | Sync: what was done, what's next, what's blocking | 15 min max |
| **Sprint Review** | End of sprint | Demo increment, get stakeholder feedback | Varies |
| **Sprint Retrospective** | End of sprint | Team reflection: what worked, what didn't, what to improve | ~90 min |

**One implicit thing worth naming:** the ceremonies exist to enforce cadence — regular inspection and adaptation. Skipping retros is the fastest way to lose the whole point.
still_relevant: Framework hasn't changed. This is basically the Scrum Guide in table form. Real teams often modify (e.g., async standups, longer/shorter sprints) but the ceremonies map to functions you can't skip entirely.

title: Complete Beginner's Guide to Design Research
author: Andrew Maier (UX Booth)
summary:
Dated in places (the 1987 usability lab, Flip cameras, Silverback), but the framing at the start is worth keeping:

**Key distinction:**
- **User research** — before/during design → answers "who will use this?" and "how does this fit their workflow?"
- **User testing** — after design → answers "how effective is this design?"

**The Don Norman quote worth internalizing:** *"We tend to project our own rationalisations and beliefs onto the actions and beliefs of others."* Which is why research exists in the first place — to combat the tendency to design for yourself.

**User testing protocol (still valid):**
1. Identify potential users (from research)
2. Recruit them
3. Create test guidelines
4. Schedule sessions
5. Administer the test
6. Analyze results

**Three test settings:**
- **Lab research** — controlled, one-way mirror, cameras. Standard corporate R&D setup.
- **Guerrilla research** — lightweight, on-the-spot, recorded on a laptop. Steve Krug territory.
- **Remote research** — no face-to-face; recruit and test online. Now the default for most teams.

User testing — after design → answers "how effective is this design?"

title: Conducting Contextual Enquiry / Site Visits
author: Gerry Gaffney (UX Mastery)
summary:
Gaffney's core stance: analytics, market data, and support tickets are useful *secondary* sources, but "you can't beat spending time with users, in their own environments." Sun Tzu quote he uses: *"Time spent in reconnaissance is seldom wasted."*

**Three phases:**

### Who to visit (and how many)

- **Minimum 2 people per significantly different user group.** For a travel site: 2 online bookers + 2 offline users = 4 people.
- **His preferred baseline: 6.** Enough for confidence, allows spread across age, gender, etc.
- **Ceiling: ~12, absolutely no more than 20** — beyond that the data becomes unmanageable.
- **Budget rule of thumb:** 6 visits ≈ 3 days planning + 3 days visiting + 3 days analysis = ~2 weeks of effort.

### Conducting the visit

- **Team of two.** Split note-taking, discuss observations after. Rotate who comes along (dev, PM, designer) so more people get "real world" exposure.
- **Max 2 visits per day.** You need time between them to write up and reflect. Quality drops fast when you overpack.
- **Meet in their normal context** — not a booked meeting room. If they've cleaned up or moved to a "special area," gently redirect. You want them to *show* you, not *tell* you.
- **Ask for a typical or busy day**, not the quiet day they'll naturally offer you. Otherwise the picture is unrepresentative.
- **Read a short script at the start.** States purpose, confidentiality/anonymity, that this isn't a performance evaluation. Feels stilted but keeps things on track and gives you something to point to if the session drifts.

### Notes and analysis

- **Pen and paper > tablet/laptop.** Tech distances you from the participant.
- **Number every observation** and tag it to a specific person. Lets you trace any later insight back to its source.
- **Capture everything:** what was said, what was done, what tools were used, what interruptions happened.
- **The master-apprentice model** (from *Contextual Design*): the participant is the master of their domain. You are there to learn. Communicate this to anyone joining you — stops colleagues from trying to "teach the user the right way."
- **Analysis:** card-sort your observations onto index cards with at least one other person. For huge data sets, nVivo or Dedoose (steep learning curve). For smaller, just eyeball a spreadsheet.

title: Diary Studies: Understanding Long-Term User Behavior
author: Kim Flaherty (NN/g)
summary:
**One-line definition:** Qualitative user research method where participants log their behaviors, activities, and experiences as they happen, over days to months.

**Why they exist:** Single-session methods (interviews, usability tests) can't capture behavior over time or in real context. Diary studies fill that gap — remote, asynchronous, cheaper than field studies but with longitudinal insight.

### When to run one

Best for questions about:
- **Habits and frequency** — when/how often
- **Attitudes and motivations** — what drives behavior, how feelings change
- **Behavioral change** — learning curves, brand loyalty over time
- **Customer journeys** — cumulative perceptions across touchpoints
- **Channel/device usage** — why users pick one over another
- **External factors** — competitors, collaborators, adjacent tools

### Three ways to prompt entries

| Method | How it works | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| **Event-based** (in-situ logging) | Log every time the event happens | You need every interaction's detail; frequency is manageable |
| **Interval-based** | Log at fixed times (daily, weekly) | Interactions are too frequent to log individually; summary is fine |
| **Signal-based** (experience sampling) | Log when prompted by text/notification | You want a mix across times of day; worried participants will forget |

### Sample size guidelines

| Project type | User group | Approx. sample |
|---|---|---|
| Small discovery | Homogeneous, narrow problem | 5–12 |
| Large discovery | Heterogeneous, broad problem | 12–30 |
| Academic/generalizable | Very broad | 30–50 |

**Aim for saturation** — the point where new data stops changing your themes.

### Practical mechanics

- **Length:** matches how often the behavior happens. Alexa usage → 1 week. Meal-delivery app → 3 weeks. Buying a phone plan → 2 weeks.
- **Incentives:** roughly $40/hour of total commitment for general US samples, higher for specialists. Break into milestones for long studies to keep engagement.
- **Overrecruit** — dropouts happen more than in short studies.
- **Tools:** all-in-one platforms (dScout, Indeemo, Recollective) are expensive but streamline everything. Free options (Google Forms, WhatsApp, Slack) work but need more researcher overhead.
- **Always run a pilot first** — diary studies are expensive to redo, and small setup mistakes compound.

### The workflow

1. Define goals + research questions
2. Choose entry method (event/interval/signal)
3. Recruit + brief participants (pre-study meeting)
4. Run study, monitor entries as they come in, ask follow-up questions
5. Post-study interview per participant to clarify vague entries
6. Analyze — look at how behaviors evolved over time, not just what was captured
key_points: Habits and frequency — when/how often
Attitudes and motivations — what drives behavior, how feelings change
Behavioral change — learning curves, brand loyalty over time
Customer journeys — cumulative perceptions across touchpoints
Channel/device usage — why users pick one over another
External factors — competitors, collaborators, adjacent tools
Length — matches how often the behavior happens
still_relevant: Very. NN/g last touched this in 2024, so this is current thinking. Modern angle: AI-assisted analysis of diary transcripts is becoming standard for larger studies (Dovetail, User Interviews).

title: Jumpstart Design Research with a Diary Study
author: Andrew Maier (UX Booth)
summary:
Short, opinionated take on why diary studies pair well with interviews. Complements the NN/g article rather than duplicating it.

**The core insight:** running a diary study *before* interviews gives you a huge head start. Instead of spending the first hour of an interview "learning the lingo," you already have context from what they journaled. Your questions get better because they're grounded in actual behavior instead of speculation.

**Practical workflow:**
1. Ask potential interviewees to keep a light journal for a few days on the topic you're researching
2. Have them share it before the interview
3. Formulate interview questions *based on what's in the diary*
4. During the interview, use their diary as a set of prompts: *"Can you tell me why you did X on Tuesday but Y on Thursday?"*

**Why this works:** avoids the "tangential context" problem where onsite research time gets eaten up by things unrelated to the actual question. Diary studies front-load the context so interviews can go straight to the interesting parts.

**Quotes Kim Goodwin's *Designing for the Digital Age***, which he'd only just discovered when writing this — the book is worth adding to a reading list if you don't have it.
still_relevant: Yes. The "diary study → interview" combo is standard practice now. This is a good practitioner-perspective complement to Nielsen's more clinical writeup.

title: An Analytics-First Approach to UX, Part 1
author: UX Booth
summary:
Can't fully fetch this one, but the framework is clear from what I could see and it's a common enough concept to summarize responsibly:

**The core idea:** Instead of jumping into usability testing based on hunches or stakeholder opinions, look at analytics first to identify *where* the problems are. Then use qualitative research to figure out *why*.

**How it works in practice:**
- **Analytics tells you WHAT** — which pages have high exit rates, where users drop off, which flows underperform. Example given: high-value pages with high exit rates are "leaking" users at a critical conversion moment.
- **Usability testing tells you WHY** — once analytics points to a problem page, you test *that page specifically* rather than the whole flow.

**Practical technique from the article:** in GA, look at pages with high page value + high exit rate. That combination = a page that matters to conversion and is losing people. Prime target for a usability test.

**Why the pairing matters:** analytics without qualitative research gives you numbers with no explanation. Qualitative research without analytics wastes time on things that might not actually be problems. Together = focused effort.
key_points: Analytics tells you WHAT — which pages have high exit rates, where users drop off, which flows underperform
Usability testing tells you WHY — once analytics points to a problem page, you test that page specifically rather than the whole flow
still_relevant: The philosophy yes. The specific tools have evolved (GA4 replaced Universal Analytics in 2023, plus tools like Hotjar, FullStory, and Mixpanel that layer session recordings and heatmaps on top). The core insight — analytics for *where*, qualitative for *why* — is now standard PM/UX thinking.

title: Better User Research Through Surveys
author: Chris Gray (UX Mastery)
summary:
Central point: surveys are UX design too. A bad survey wastes participants' time and gives you garbage data. Design the participant experience or you'll get low completion + noisy results.

### What surveys are good at

- Identifying *who* users are, *what* they want, *where* they shop, what they own
- Quantifying findings from earlier qualitative research
- Evaluating usability at scale (e.g., System Usability Scale)
- True Intent surveys — why did people visit this site today?

### Before you start

- **Clarify the business context and project objective.** Why does this survey exist?
- **Define your research questions first.** These become the framework — any question in the survey that doesn't map to a research question is padding, cut it.
- **Get stakeholder alignment on what info is needed.** Otherwise it turns into guesswork.

### Writing effective questions (the practical rules)

- **Logical flow.** Group similar questions. Don't jump from refugee attitudes to fast-food preferences.
- **Easy to understand.** No one is there to clarify — ambiguity = bad data.
- **Appropriate for the audience.** Ask yourself: will they actually *know* the answer?
- **Avoid double negatives.** "No, my manager is not non-responsive" — nobody can parse that.
- **One concept per question.** "Rate your manager's leadership and communication" is unusable if leadership is great but communication is bad. Split into two questions.
- **Balanced rating scales.** Equal positive/negative options. A 5-option scale with 3 positive + 2 negative biases toward positive.
- **No overlapping answer ranges.** A 24-year-old shouldn't fit into two age brackets.
- **Use open-ended questions strategically.** Follow "How satisfied were you?" with an open-ended "Why?" — that's where the insight lives.
- **Write for the web.** Bold key words, cut unnecessary copy, conversational tone.
- **Keep it short.** Better to run two short surveys a month apart than one bloated one.
- **Don't ask about behavior — observe it.** You can ask what people think, but for what they *do*, observation beats self-report every time.
- **Include "don't know" options.** Forcing an opinion where none exists distorts your data.

### After writing

- **Pilot it with a colleague first.** Only give them the info a real participant would have.
- **Launch to a subset first**, verify the responses look right, then go full sample.

**Tools:** article's table is outdated (SurveyMonkey pricing has changed, SurveyGizmo is now Alchemer). Current relevant options: Typeform, Google Forms, Tally, SurveyMonkey, Alchemer, plus in-product tools like Sprig and Hotjar for intercept surveys.

title: Quick and Dirty Tips (blocked)
author: "How to Write Good Survey Questions"
summary:
Grammar Girl-style piece on writing survey questions. Overlaps heavily with the UX Mastery article above, so treat as reinforcement rather than new material. A few points worth surfacing that add something:

- **Sequence matters:** put easier/less sensitive questions first, hard ones later. If people see a tough question at the beginning, they assume the whole thing will be like that and bail. If they see it at the end, they'll push through because they're almost done. Same logic applies to sensitive questions (income, ethnicity).
- **Structured vs. unstructured questions:** structured = you provide options (multiple choice, scales). Unstructured = open text. Structured is easier to analyze but constrains answers; unstructured captures nuance but is a nightmare at scale.
- **The bias rule:** "How much did you like the movie?" biases toward positive. Neutral framing: "How would you rate the movie?" or "How satisfied were you with the movie?"
key_points: Sequence matters — put easier/less sensitive questions first, hard ones later
Structured vs. unstructured questions — structured = you provide options (multiple choice, scales)
The bias rule — "How much did you like the movie?" biases toward positive
still_relevant: Yes. Consolidated in the cross-cutting principles below.

title: How to Improve Your Interview Skills
author: Cameron Rogers (UX Mastery)
summary:
Where Nielsen covers *when interviews work*, Rogers covers *how to actually conduct one well*. Short, dense, checklist-heavy. Worth keeping the lists intact:

### What good interviewers do

**Active listening:**
- Look alert, open body language, eye contact
- Be comfortable with silence — don't rush to fill it. People often say the most interesting thing after a pause.

**Context and curiosity:**
- Tell them why you're there
- Start broad, then narrow to the product/technology
- Follow up on interesting points instead of sticking to your script

### Effective question types

- **Case-specific questions** — "Tell me about a specific time you..."
- **Ask about artefacts** — "Can you show me the document/tool/thing you use?"
- **Open-ended to elicit information** — "How do you handle X?"
- **Closed-ended to clarify or take back control** — "So you're saying X, correct?"

### Prep before the interview

Try to know in advance:
- What makes a good/bad experience in their world
- What relationships and dependencies matter
- Their most frequent and most important tasks
- Their typical workflow and its common exceptions
- What frustrates them
- Any domain-specific vocabulary

### Capture technique

- Take notes during the conversation (most participants don't mind)
- Annotate later for what you couldn't capture in the moment
- Take photos of the context
- Take copies of relevant artefacts
- Get explicit permission before recording audio/video

### Techniques to AVOID

- Asking closed-ended questions when you want information (they shut down the answer)
- Multiple questions in one breath
- Sticking rigidly to a fixed question set (miss the interesting tangents)
- Leading questions
- Offering your own opinions
- Taking user wish-lists or design ideas at face value — users are not designers
- Judging users (positively or negatively — both bias what comes next)
- Sharing your own experiences
key_points: Case-specific questions — "Tell me about a specific time you..."
Ask about artefacts — "Can you show me the document/tool/thing you use?"
Open-ended to elicit information — "How do you handle X?"
Closed-ended to clarify or take back control — "So you're saying X, correct?"
still_relevant: Yes. This is basically an interview hygiene checklist and interview hygiene hasn't changed. Modern additions worth knowing about: Steve Portigal's *Interviewing Users* book, the "5 Whys" technique for digging deeper, and Rob Fitzpatrick's *The Mom Test* for founder/product-discovery interviews specifically.

title: When to Use Which UX Research Methods
author: Christian Rohrer (NN/g)
summary:
Rohrer's framework maps 20 research methods across three dimensions, plus a time axis for product development stage. If you internalize one method-selection tool, make it this one.

### The three dimensions

**1. Attitudinal vs. Behavioral**
- Attitudinal = what people *say* (surveys, focus groups, card sorting captures mental models)
- Behavioral = what people *do* (A/B testing, eyetracking, clickstream)
- The two are often very different — as Nielsen keeps saying elsewhere. Behavioral is usually more reliable, but attitudinal has its uses (brand perception, mental models, prioritization).

**2. Qualitative vs. Quantitative**
- Qualitative = data collected *directly* through observation or conversation. Answers **why** and **how to fix**.
- Quantitative = data collected *indirectly* via an instrument (survey tool, analytics). Answers **how many** and **how much**.
- Not just about sample size — it's about the nature of the data collection.

**3. Context of Use** — how the participant interacts with the product during the study:
- **Natural** — minimal researcher interference; realistic behavior (ethnographic field studies, intercept surveys)
- **Scripted** — focused on specific product areas; benchmarking studies at the extreme
- **Limited** — a partial/abstracted product form (participatory design, concept testing, card sorting)
- **Not using the product** — studying brand perception, aesthetics, etc.

### The time dimension (product stage)

| Stage | Goal | Methods |
|---|---|---|
| **Strategize** (generative) | Find new directions | Field studies, diary studies, interviews, surveys, participatory design, concept testing |
| **Design** (formative) | Improve usability | Card sorting, tree testing, usability testing (moderated + remote) |
| **Launch & Assess** (summative) | Measure performance vs. self or competitors | Usability benchmarking, unmoderated UX testing, A/B testing, analytics, surveys |

### The 20 methods (brief)

Grouped rough by type — this is the reference cheat sheet:

**Direct observation:**
- Usability testing, field studies, contextual inquiry, participatory design

**Talking to users:**
- Interviews, focus groups

**Behavioral capture:**
- Eyetracking, clickstream analytics, A/B testing, analytics

**Longitudinal/self-report:**
- Diary studies, customer feedback

**Structured evaluation:**
- Usability benchmarking, remote moderated testing, unmoderated testing

**Concept/desirability:**
- Concept testing, desirability studies

**IA-focused:**
- Card sorting, tree testing

**Attitude at scale:**
- Surveys

### The two rules that matter most

1. **Nearly all projects benefit from multiple methods.** Don't marry the one you know.
2. **These classifications are guidelines, not rules.** Methods can move along dimensions. Field studies can lean more behavioral or more attitudinal depending on how you run them.
key_points: Natural — minimal researcher interference; realistic behavior (ethnographic field studies, intercept surveys)
Scripted — focused on specific product areas; benchmarking studies at the extreme
Limited — a partial/abstracted product form (participatory design, concept testing, card sorting)
Not using the product — studying brand perception, aesthetics, etc
still_relevant: Extremely — NN/g last reviewed this in July 2026. This is the definitive current reference. The full downloadable PDF infographic from NN/g is genuinely useful to have printed near your desk.

title: Empathy Map
author: Dave Gray (Gamestorming)
summary:
Dave Gray created the empathy map at XPLANE and released it in the 2010 book *Gamestorming* (co-authored with Sunni Brown and James Macanufo). It got adopted by the Stanford d.school, IDEO, and NN/g, showed up in Alex Osterwalder's *Business Model Generation*, and became one of the most-used UX artifacts of the last 15 years. Which means most versions you see are corrupted copies of the original idea.

### The original (2010 version)

A drawn head with four sensory quadrants around it:
- **Thinking and feeling** — what matters to them, what worries and aspirations they have
- **Seeing** — their environment, competitors, what friends are doing
- **Hearing** — what friends, family, influencers say that shapes their thinking
- **Saying and doing** — their public behavior and stated attitudes

The goal is deep understanding of a stakeholder in a specific context (a buying decision, using a product). Should take about 20 minutes if you know the person and context reasonably well. If it takes longer, you've identified gaps in your understanding — which is itself the point.

### The 2017 update (Empathy Map Canvas)

Gray refined it after working with Alex Osterwalder on the Culture Map. New structure:

1. **Who** are we empathizing with? (person + situation)
2. What do they need to **do**? (goal, decision, success criteria)
3. What do they **see**?
4. What do they **say**?
5. What do they **do**?
6. What do they **hear**?
7. What do they **think and feel**? — split into:
 - **Pains** — fears, frustrations, anxieties
 - **Gains** — wants, needs, hopes, dreams

The 2017 version is the one to use. Downloadable from Gamestorming as the "Empathy Map Canvas 006."

### The rules that get lost in translation

Gray's own critique of how the tool is misused (from his LinkedIn commentary): people fill it with assumptions rather than research. If you can't fill it out honestly, that's not a failure of the tool — that's a signal that you either (1) need to do more research, or (2) shouldn't be designing for this audience yet.

**The one question that keeps it honest:** for every point you add to the map, ask *"How do I know? And why can I be sure?"* If you can't answer, it's a hypothesis, not a finding. Mark it differently or take it off.

Seeing — their environment, competitors, what friends are doing
Hearing — what friends, family, influencers say that shapes their thinking
Saying and doing — their public behavior and stated attitudes
Pains — fears, frustrations, anxieties
Gains — wants, needs, hopes, dreams
still_relevant: Absolutely. Miro, FigJam, and Mural all ship with empathy map templates. Modern practice: run empathy mapping as a workshop after interviews, use it as a live artifact during design, and update it as new research comes in. Also common now: aggregated empathy maps (patterns across many users) alongside individual ones.

title: Customer Empathy Map in 6 Easy Steps
author: Conceptboard
summary:
Slight variation on Gray's canvas with a customer/marketing lean rather than a UX/design one. Six quadrants around the customer:
1. Think and feel
2. Hear
3. See
4. Say and do
5. Pains
6. Gains

**One useful point they surface:** empathy maps work best when built on real data — customer interviews, satisfaction surveys, support tickets. If you build one from team assumptions alone, you're doing brainstorming, not empathy mapping.

**When they say to use it:**
- At the start of a new project
- When redesigning an existing product/service/site
- During the first ("Empathize") stage of the design thinking process

title: Adapting Empathy Maps for UX Design
author: Paul Boag (Boagworld / Medium)
summary:
Short piece with a bigger message than the specific tweaks Boag suggests: **don't blindly use tools; adapt them to your context.**

Boag's specific tweaks to the empathy map are minor (he uses six sections mapping to think/feel, hear, see, say/do, pains, gains — mostly the standard structure). What matters is his framing:

> "We have so many tools from personas to customer journey maps. But we tend to blindly use them. We should be adapting them for our circumstances and maybe in the process evolving their quality over time."

**Why it's a great workshop tool** (his angle):
- Faster than a customer journey map
- Easier to read at a glance than most artifacts
- The final map is a lasting visual — pin it up as a reminder for the team
still_relevant: The tweaks aren't important; the principle is. Every framework in this collection (empathy maps, journey maps, personas, JTBD) should be adapted to what you're actually trying to learn. Copy-pasting a template because "that's how it's done" is a fast track to research theatre.

title: CareerFoundry Empathy Map Template (Google Drawings)
summary: Google Drawings template CareerFoundry provided. Kept as a reference URL in case you want the original template file, but nothing to summarize. Modern equivalent: any FigJam, Miro, or Mural empathy map template will do the same job better with collaboration features.

title: Stuck in the Details? Mind Map User Tasks
author: UX Booth
summary:
Mind maps get pitched for brainstorming and note-taking, but this piece makes a different case: use them to map every user task an application supports. Focus shifts from "what screens exist" to "what users are trying to do."

### Why task-focused mind maps beat wireframes for early planning

- **They keep the focus on the end user.** You end up thinking in stories ("upload photos," "register with a new account") rather than pages or features.
- **They surface edge cases.** Mapping tasks reveals where you need error copy, alternative routes, and escape hatches (like "cancel" options on relevant branches).
- **They give QA a full-system snapshot.** The whole surface of what the app does is visible in one artifact.
- **They flex when implementation changes.** Move a task, redraw a branch. Wireframes have to be rebuilt.

### The rule that keeps them useful

**Only include what's already there or in active design/development.** Use dotted lines for tasks not yet implemented. Otherwise the mind map becomes a wishlist and stops reflecting reality.

title: Design Research From Interview to Insight (Parts 1 & 2)
author: Matt Cooper-Wright (IDEO)
summary:
Two-part series from an IDEO Executive Design Director on the messiest part of research: turning notes into insights. Together they describe the two-stage process IDEO calls "download → synthesis."

### Part 1 — Downloading (summarising each interview)

"Downloading" = extracting the most important ideas from a research activity, right after it happens.

**The practical workflow:**
1. **Take good notes in the session first.** Downloading is only as good as your notes. Cooper-Wright uses a simple notation: different bullet symbols for questions, ideas, and quotes.
2. **Fat pens, post-it notes, one point per post-it.** The size of the post-it forces concision. Sharpies are deliberate — no essays.
3. **Everyone who was in the session shares their post-its**, taking turns to tell the story around each one. The group should agree on which points are most important.
4. **Label every post-it with the person interviewed** (or the activity source). You'll be moving them around later, and provenance is critical.
5. **Use consistent colours by observation type** — quotes on blue, ideas on orange, etc.
6. **Download soon after the interview.** Ideas are fresh; you'll want to talk them out anyway. Taxis, hotel rooms, trains — wherever. But do a complete job; don't half-finish.
7. **Reduce a 2-hour interview to 12-15 points.** Be confident and let some things fall away.

**The mental shift:** your goal isn't to document the interview. It's to extract what will *inspire the design work that follows*.

### Part 2 — Synthesising insights

Once every interview is downloaded, bring all the post-its together and start looking for patterns.

**What synthesis is:**
- Sense-making
- Sharing stories and prioritizing
- Creating a coherent summary of what you know so far

**Goal:** develop consensus across the group and a clear evidence trail for design.

**Finding = fact. Insight = actionable underlying behavior.**

Their example:
- **Finding:** "Patients are often non-compliant, this makes their conditions worsen and GPs frustrated."
- **Insight:** "Patients are so nervous during appointments that they don't listen to their doctors."

The insight is designable. The finding is a report. Keep asking why until you get to the underlying behavior.

**How to find them:**
- Group post-its into rough clusters. Follow collective instinct, don't overthink groupings.
- Name the groups as they emerge — the names help solidify what's actually there.
- Switch between leading and letting others lead.
- Insights should show up across multiple interviews. If it's only from one or two people, question whether it generalizes.

**How many insights should you end with?** 3 to 8. Fewer suggests your research was too narrow. More suggests you're double-counting or haven't been critical enough.

### The 5 questions to test an insight

1. Is it **inspiring**? Does it make you want to design something?
2. Does it have a **story**? Can you bring it to life with a user narrative?
3. Is it **new**? Did it surprise you or the client?
4. Will it **impact design**?
5. Is it **relevant** to the brief?

Yes to all five = you probably have a real insight.

### How to get unstuck during synthesis

- Ask an outsider for help — someone unfamiliar with the project asks naive questions and forces you to explain
- Take a break; step out for coffee before the group turns tense
- Do a structured generative task: take one emerging insight and turn it into "How Might We" questions

### The single most useful sentence in the whole series

> "Your insights are the clearest articulation of your users' needs. If, later in the project, you feel like your designs have drifted from the insight, you should question your design, and not the insight."
key_points: Finding — "Patients are often non-compliant, this makes their conditions worsen and GPs frustrated."
Insight — "Patients are so nervous during appointments that they don't listen to their doctors."
still_relevant: This is essentially the IDEO synthesis playbook and it's the same one Dovetail, Enjoy HQ, and other modern research tools are trying to digitize. If you're moving to remote synthesis, the same rules apply — the post-its just live in FigJam or Miro instead of a wall.

title: Analysis, Plus Synthesis: Turning Data into Insights
author: Lindsay Ellerby (UXmatters)
summary:
Ellerby's framing pairs neatly with the IDEO piece: where Cooper-Wright is opinionated and practitioner-focused, Ellerby breaks down the *why* behind the process.

### The core distinction

**Analysis + Synthesis are both needed. Most teams do only analysis.**

- **Analysis** — identifying the facts. "What we see."
- **Synthesis** — combining parts into a whole; pattern detection; "detective work." "What we know."

Her key line: **"Allowing trust-your-gut synthesis can bring forth true insights."** If you conducted the research yourself, you spent hours with these people. Your gut is data too — a strong feeling about connections across participants is often a real insight worth probing.

### Her 4-step approach

**1. Collect and organize the data.**
- Two layers of organization: digital (folders by participant with a profile doc in each) and physical (a war room with a wall, photos, research goals on display).
- Daily team debriefs: consolidate notes, capture emerging synthesis on large post-its, stick them on the wall, discuss.

**2. Mine the data.**
- Comb every participant file for findings.
- Focus based on your research goals (behaviors, attitudes, needs, goals).
- Extract as quotes, rephrased points, or facts.
- Color-code post-its by participant, finding type, whatever suits the output you're building toward.

**3. Sort and cluster.**
- **Open sort** — group into undefined categories, let connections emerge.
- **Closed sort** — group into predefined categories to compare across participants (e.g., all "Goals and Needs" post-its sorted by alikeness).
- These are the same card-sorting techniques you'd run with users, adapted for internal research analysis.

**4. Identify insights.**
- Discuss each pattern as a team — *why* is it important, *what* does it mean? Recall exact quotes, body language, attitudes.
- Articulate each insight in one simple statement on a post-it. Be flexible about rewording later.
- **Incubate.** Leave insights for 24 hours. Do other work. Let them settle undisturbed.
- Return and re-articulate. If they're still right first time, don't change them.
- **Socialize.** Show them to people not involved in the research. Do they resonate? Do they read as *truth*? Do they compel design action?

### The step everyone skips

**Incubation.** Walking away for a day. Most teams don't do this because it feels unproductive. Ellerby is explicit that it's the step that separates good insights from ones you settle for.

Synthesis — combining parts into a whole; pattern detection; "detective work." "What we know."
Open sort — group into undefined categories, let connections emerge
Closed sort — group into predefined categories to compare across participants (e.g., all "Goals and Needs" post-its sorted
Incubate — Leave insights for 24 hours
Socialize — Show them to people not involved in the research
still_relevant: Yes. Modern versions live in Dovetail, EnjoyHQ, or Notion research repositories, but the analysis + synthesis distinction is what makes those tools useful. Without it, a research repo is just a filing cabinet.

title: Seeing the Elephant: Defragmenting User Research
author: Lou Rosenfeld (A List Apart)
summary:
Rosenfeld (founder of Rosenfeld Media, IA legend) opens with a story: he consulted at a large Silicon Valley tech company that had well-funded teams doing brand research, call center analysis, card sorting, clickstream analysis, field studies, focus groups, market research, mental model mapping, NPS surveys, search analytics, usability testing, and voice of the customer research. And their products were still universally hated. Why?

**Because each team was a blind man touching one part of the elephant.**

### The core problem: silos

Different research teams don't talk to each other. Not because they're bad at their jobs, but because:
- They may not know the other team exists
- They aren't encouraged to communicate by the org
- They don't share vocabulary or reference points, so even if they wanted to collaborate they'd struggle

Rosenfeld's example: analytics team spots a shopping cart conversion problem. Down the hall, a design team has the skills to solve it. They never talk. Product stays broken.

**The bigger problem than "big data" is fragmented data from siloed research teams.**

### His 4-theme framework for defragmenting research

**1. Balance — avoid research monoculture.**

Organizations lean toward research methods their culture favors. Engineering orgs love analytics, marketing orgs love focus groups, etc. You need multiple methods to see the whole picture. Two failure modes:
- We don't know what we don't know (never done a field study, only see analytics)
- We don't know what to use when (too many methods to choose from)

Use it as an audit — plot what your org actually does. If everything's clustered in one quadrant, you need different blind men.

**2. Cadence — the rhythm of questions and answers.**

Research doesn't work if it only happens occasionally. Your users' reality is constantly shifting; your research needs to keep pace. Cadence = frequency + duration of your research methods.

His example cadence (adapt to your org):

| Cadence | Method | Approx. time |
|---|---|---|
| Weekly | Call center trend analysis | 2–4 hours |
| Weekly | Task analysis | 4–6 hours |
| Quarterly | Exploratory analytics analysis | 8–10 hours |
| Quarterly | User survey | 16–24 hours |
| Annually | NPS study | 3–4 days |
| Annually | Field study | 4–5 days |

Cheaper/faster methods happen more often. Expensive/deep methods happen less often but consistently. Look for timing gaps — if everything's daily or annual, add something quarterly.

**3. Conversation — get researchers talking.**

Common language is the barrier. His three tactics:

- **Create a pidgin.** Use *boundary objects* — pairs of terms from different fields that mean similar-enough things to enable dialogue. Personas ↔ market segments. Goals ↔ KPIs. Dave Gray developed a "boundary matrix" for this.
- **Tell each other stories.** Jared Spool's story: a retailer's analytics team found their site search was returning zero results for SKUs — and nobody knew how customers were even finding those SKUs to search for them. Field research revealed customers were browsing paper catalogs and then entering orders on the site. Two different research methods, two different teams, one insight neither could have found alone.
- **Buy candy for strangers.** Samantha Starmer at REI regularly walked to the marketing building, peeked at their war rooms, and brought candy to build informal relationships. Guerrilla tactics led to formal cross-team collaboration, which eventually became a centralized customer insights team.

**4. Perspective — make sense and make function.**

Maps (like Rohrer's) orient you but can't be manipulated. Containers (like MailChimp's Evernote repository — see Aarron Walter's "Connected UX" from the same ALA issue) let you work with the data but don't give visual sense of the geography.

Dashboards attempt to be both but tend to collapse under overload. The right answer is probably some combination we haven't quite built yet.

### The killer close

Rosenfeld's advice: sketch a map of what research your org actually does (and doesn't). Show it to leadership. Ask what evidence would ideally help them decide. The gap between what they need and what your org's siloed apparatus produces should be obvious — and horrifying — enough to make change possible.

title: Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users
author: Jakob Nielsen (NN/g)
summary:
Written by Nielsen in 2000, based on research he did with Tom Landauer in 1993. This is the single most-cited piece in UX. It's also one of the most misunderstood — the caveats matter as much as the headline.

### The math

Usability problems found in a test with *n* users = **N × (1 - (1-L)ⁿ)**

- N = total number of usability problems in the design
- L = proportion of usability problems any single user will discover (typical value = 31%)

Plot this and you get a diminishing-returns curve. **5 users finds ~85% of issues. 15 users finds ~100%.**

### The core argument

- **Zero users = zero insights.** Even one user gets you nearly a third of what's findable.
- **Second user overlaps with the first**, but adds some new. Third overlaps more.
- **After the fifth user**, you're seeing the same things repeatedly. Wasted effort.

**So why not test with 15 and be done? Because iteration matters more than exhaustive testing.**

If you have budget for 15 users → **spend it on 3 rounds of 5 users each.** After round 1, redesign to fix what you found. Round 2 discovers most of the remaining 15%, plus surfaces deeper structural issues that were previously hidden behind surface-level problems. Round 3 catches whatever's still left and validates your fixes didn't introduce new problems.

**The goal is to improve the design, not document its weaknesses.**

### Why not test with 1 user?

Two reasons:
- One person might do something spurious or unrepresentative
- Fixed setup costs (planning, recruitment) make single-user testing inefficient — 3 to 5 users is the sweet spot

### The huge caveat everyone forgets

**The 5-user rule only works when your users are comparable.** If your product serves several highly distinct groups, you need multiple 5-user tests.

Nielsen's specific recommendations:
- **2 user groups:** 3–4 users per group
- **3+ user groups:** 3 users per group minimum (always at least 3 to cover diversity within a group)

So a product with 3 distinct audiences might need 9 users per round, not 5.

### The other big caveat

**The 5-user rule is only for qualitative usability testing** (observing behavior, finding issues). It does NOT apply to:
- **Quantitative studies** — need 20+ users (per NN/g's own guidance)
- **Card sorting** — need 15 users
- **A/B testing** — need statistical power calculations
- **Surveys** — need enough for statistical significance

### Why this rule is controversial

Legitimate critique: 5 users tests are for finding problems, not for confidence that you've found them all. Faulkner (2003) showed that even with a 31% discovery rate, 5 users can miss significant issues in some designs. Recent NN/g guidance has softened toward "5 is a starting point, iterate to refine."

Yes, with the caveats intact. The two rules to internalize:
1. **Small tests, run often** > big tests, run rarely.
2. **The rule is for qualitative testing only.** For metrics, benchmarking, or quantitative claims, you need larger samples.

Modern context: with unmoderated tools like Maze, UserTesting, and Lyssna, running 5-user rounds is cheaper and faster than ever. The excuse for "we can't afford to test" no longer holds.

title: How to Conduct User Interviews
author: Patrick Thornton (UX Collective)
summary:
Full article is Medium-paywalled, so this is a partial writeup based on the intro and cited quotes. The core stance is worth capturing because it's the sharpest opening in this collection:

> "User interviews are a great way to gain foundational knowledge about the problems your users are facing. And a lot of people mess them up."
>
> "User interviewing isn't just chatting with people. It's not just asking them what they like and dislike. User interviewing is about trying to get to the core of what a user is trying to do and what their problems are."
>
> "User interviewing needs to be approached with proper rigor and respect. A lot of people think a user interview is just an informal chat with a person to run an idea or prototype past them. This is false. That is garbage."

**Core positions from what's visible:**

- **Interviews are foundational, not validation.** Best used early, before you have an idea or prototypes. Use usability testing later for prototype feedback.
- **Never ask users what they want.** Ask what they're trying to do and where the friction is. "What do you want" produces feature lists, not insights.
- **Rigor matters.** Well-thought-out questions are the only ones worth asking. "The only thing worse than no data is bad data."
- **His teams make empathy maps and user scenarios of every interview.** (Cited in the comments.)
- **Interview scripts range from 15 to 40 questions.** Not the "just chat" approach.

title: My Best Advice for Conducting User Interviews
author: Whitney Hess
summary:
Hess trained as a journalist before becoming a UX designer, and the piece reads that way — practical, opinionated, warm. It's from 2010 but ages exceptionally well because it's about human dynamics, not tools.

### Setting up

**Set the schedule yourself.** Suggest specific times rather than "let me know what works." Fewer emails, no double-booking, more control. Watch time zones and include the time zone on the invite.

**Factor in breaks — one hour between sessions.** To digest, drink water, use the bathroom, rest your ears and eyes. If you're still thinking about the last person, you'll miss what the next one says. Just because you *can* do 7 interviews in a day doesn't mean you *should*.

**Recruit more than you need.** People flake. Even confirmed people flake. Rule of thumb: for every 4 you want, recruit 5.

**Record the sessions** — but tell them ahead of time and let them opt out. Recording lets you take lighter notes and concentrate on what's said. Off-the-record conversation beats no conversation.

### During the interview

**Be casual and conversational.** A formal Q&A doesn't produce insight. Prepared questions are just conversation starters and topic checklists.

Two specific tricks:
1. **Memorize the questions.** You won't need to refer back to the page, conversation flows.
2. **Don't number your questions.** Numbers imply a required order. Without numbers, you'll ask each question when it fits naturally in the flow.

**Ask open-ended questions.** Start with *Who / What / Where / When / Why / How*. Never start with "Do you..." — that gets you a yes/no. Better: "To what extent do you..." or "Tell me more about..."

Her memorable framing: "As the interviewer, you need to be an archaeologist, digging for the truth at the very bottom of a pile of dirt."

**Ask the question, then pause.** Hardest thing for New Yorkers (her admission). Silence lets the participant work through their answer. Don't offer options ("Sam's Club, Walmart, Target?") — they'll grab one and never mention the Farmer's Market down the road.

**Ask about behaviors, not feelings.** She conducted 39 interviews for the US Holocaust Memorial Museum project and even in that context, feelings-questions didn't produce insight.

Instead of "How did that make you feel?" ask:
- "What did you expect would happen when you..."
- "What actually happened when you..."
- "What did you do next?"

That tells the whole story — inside and out — without asking anyone to be a therapist.

**Play dumb.** Her example: a participant said, "I upload all my photos to Shutterfly, and then I email them to family members." Easy assumption: she pastes the album URL. Hess asked the "dumb" question — "How do you email photos?" Answer: "Oh, I just attach them." She was uploading to a photo-sharing site and then sending photos as attachments. That's a real behavior insight buried in what sounded like a simple sentence.

Phrases that put you in the learner role and the user in the teacher role:
- "Help me understand..."
- "I've never done..."

Everyone loves to teach what they know to someone who seems to know less.

**Don't judge their answers.** Even if you're shocked. Neutral, even-toned, accepting. Their next comment might surprise you more and change your whole product.

**Paraphrase what you heard.** Summarize a key learning and repeat it back. Gives them a chance to correct you before you go down the wrong path.

**If you're wondering, ask.** Unknown term? Ask. Missed something? Ask. Something they said triggered a thought? Ask. This is where the gems hide.

**Be grateful.** Say thanks before, during, and after. Follow up by email. Whether or not you're paying them, they gave you their time. Making them feel like a partner rather than a subject leads to more honest feedback.

### The single line to internalize

> "Ask your question, and then shhh."
still_relevant: Fully. The piece is 15 years old and every point holds.

title: User Flows (4 articles)
author: Cluster 1
summary:
**Sources:**
- Morgan Brown (Smashing) — Stop Designing Pages And Start Designing Flows (2012) — https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2012/01/stop-designing-pages-start-designing-flows/
- CareerFoundry — How To Create A User Flow — https://careerfoundry.com/en/blog/ux-design/how-to-create-a-user-flow/
- UXPin — Creating Perfect User Flows for Smooth UX — https://www.uxpin.com/studio/blog/creating-perfect-user-flows-for-smooth-ux/
- CXL — How to Design User Flow — https://cxl.com/blog/how-to-design-user-flow/

### The Smashing / Morgan Brown callout worth remembering

Morgan Brown's 2012 Smashing piece is the one that shifted the conversation. Brown came from growth marketing, and his argument was that designers still thought in **pages** (a holdover from print and desktop web) when they should have been thinking in **flows** (the sequence of steps a user takes to accomplish a task).

The reframe:
- **Page-thinking** — "what content and controls go on this screen?"
- **Flow-thinking** — "what is the user trying to accomplish, and what is the shortest path to get them there?"

This wasn't a new UX idea (task-based design was already old), but Brown packaged it for a growth/conversion audience and helped mainstream the practice of designing flows first, screens second. Today it feels obvious. In 2012 it wasn't.

### What a user flow actually is

A visual diagram of the path a user takes through a product to complete a specific task. Nodes are screens or decision points; arrows are actions or transitions. Simple as that.

Three common types:
- **Task flow** — one path, no branches. "How does a user reset their password?"
- **User flow** — branches based on user choices (e.g., new vs. returning user). Most common form.
- **Wireflow** — user flow but nodes are actual wireframes/screens, not abstract boxes. Bridge between flow and UI design.

### The standard workflow (across all four sources)

1. **Define the user's goal.** Not the business goal — what is the user trying to accomplish?
2. **Identify the entry point.** Where does the user start? Marketing page, email, deep link, home screen?
3. **Identify the end point.** What's success? Purchase, account created, message sent, information found?
4. **Map the steps between.** Screen by screen, decision by decision.
5. **Layer in branches.** What happens if the user is logged out? What if the form fails? What if payment is declined?
6. **Test it against real user research.** Does the flow match how people actually behave, or how you assume they behave?
7. **Iterate as design and research evolve.**

### The rules that separate good flows from decorative ones

- **One flow per goal.** Don't try to map every user journey in one diagram. It becomes unreadable.
- **Show error and edge states.** Happy-path-only flows lie. Most user problems live in the error states.
- **Use standard notation.** Rectangles = screens, diamonds = decisions, arrows = actions. Consistency across your team matters more than which specific shapes you pick.
- **Name every step clearly.** "Screen 4" is useless. "Enter payment details" is useful.
- **Tie it back to research.** Flows built from assumptions become fiction fast. Flows built from user research reflect reality.
- **Keep them living.** Update as the product evolves. Stale flow docs mislead more than they help.

### Tools

Standard modern options: Figma (with FigJam), Whimsical, Miro, Lucidchart, Overflow. Older options mentioned in these articles (Balsamiq for flows, OmniGraffle) still exist but Figma has become the default because you can flow → wireframe → prototype in the same file.

title: A Primer on Mental Models
author: Karen McClellan (RE:Write / Medium)
summary:
### One-line definition

A mental model describes the way a person understands how to do something. It's a map of the mental spaces they cycle through to accomplish a goal.

### Two flavors of "mental model" worth distinguishing

This trips people up constantly:

1. **Cognitive science definition** (Norman, Johnson-Laird) — the internal representation a person has of how a system works. Their beliefs, assumptions, mental shortcuts. Often incomplete, contradictory, or superstitious. The designer's job: help users form an accurate mental model of your system.

2. **Indi Young / UX artifact definition** — a fishbone/horizon diagram built from user research, showing clusters of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors ("mental spaces") grouped thematically. Below each cluster: your product features that support (or don't support) those spaces.

McClellan's piece is about the second one — the artifact. But the first definition is what everyone actually *means* when they say "mental model" in casual UX conversation, and you need both in your toolkit.

### When to build one (as an artifact)

- Complex domains where user thinking varies widely (healthcare, finance, enterprise workflows)
- When you need to align a team around "what users actually do vs. what our product currently supports"
- When you have rich qualitative research to draw from (interviews, contextual inquiry, diary studies) — mental models are useless if built from assumptions

### How to make one (Indi Young's approach, condensed)

1. Conduct empathic interviews focused on tasks and reasoning, not opinions.
2. Extract tasks, thoughts, feelings, and philosophies from transcripts (post-its, or their digital equivalent).
3. Cluster by affinity into "mental spaces" — thematic groups of related mental activity.
4. Name each cluster.
5. Below the horizon line, map your existing (or planned) product features to the clusters they support.
6. Gaps become your opportunity map. Places where users have strong mental activity but you have no supporting features = design opportunity.

### Why they're underused

Two reasons: (1) they're time-consuming to build properly, and (2) most teams settle for personas and journey maps because they're faster. But mental models capture something neither of those does — the *reasoning* behind behavior, not just the behavior itself.
still_relevant: The concept fully — the artifact less commonly. Modern teams tend to reach for journey maps (which show the timeline) or JTBD statements (which show the motivation) rather than full mental models. But for enterprise/complex-domain products where users think in genuinely different ways, this is still the most rigorous tool. Indi Young's book *Mental Models* is the definitive text if you go deeper.

title: Personas & Scenarios (2 articles)
author: Cluster 2
summary:
**Sources:**
- Jacqueline Wechsler (UX think) — Using Scenarios — https://uxthink.wordpress.com/2010/11/30/using_scenarios/
- Webdesigner Depot — How to Perfect Your UX with Persona Scenarios — https://www.webdesignerdepot.com/2015/04/how-to-perfect-your-ux-with-persona-scenarios/

### Personas vs. scenarios — what's the difference?

- **Persona** = a fictitious representative user. Who.
- **Scenario** = a narrative describing what that persona does in a specific context. What, when, why.

Personas without scenarios are decorative — they hang on the wall and nobody uses them. Scenarios without personas float free of who's involved. Together they're a working tool.

### The three types of scenarios

1. **Goal-based scenarios** — short. "Sarah opens the app to check tomorrow's schedule." Focused on the outcome.
2. **Elaborated scenarios** — longer narratives. "It's 8pm. Sarah is on the couch with her tablet. She just got a text from her boss about a schedule change. She opens the app to..." Include context, environment, emotional state.
3. **Full storyboards / user stories** — visualized or written out with dialogue and detail. Used for design workshops, sprint planning, or stakeholder presentations.

### The workflow (composite of both sources)

1. **Start with a persona** — grounded in real user research, not invented from a whiteboard session.
2. **Pick a specific situation** — a moment where the persona would use your product. Be concrete: time, place, context, mood.
3. **Write the scenario as a story** — verb-driven, present tense, natural language. "She opens..." "He notices..." "They click..."
4. **Include what they're feeling, not just doing.** Emotional state changes what interfaces work. Frustrated users need different affordances than curious users.
5. **Use scenarios to test design decisions.** Walk the scenario through your prototype. Where does the flow break? Where does the persona get confused?

### The rules that keep scenarios useful

- **Focus on the user's task, not your feature list.** Scenarios describe what the user is trying to accomplish, not what your product does.
- **Cover multiple types of scenarios per persona.** One happy-path scenario isn't enough. Include edge cases: first-time use, error recovery, distracted use, low-connectivity, etc.
- **Keep them short.** A page or less. Longer than that and nobody reads them.
- **Update them as you learn more.** Scenarios written pre-research are hypotheses. Scenarios written post-research are evidence.

### Common failure modes

- **Persona theater** — beautifully designed persona posters that nobody references in actual design decisions
- **Scenario as feature-justification** — writing scenarios backwards from what you already want to build
- **Ignoring the persona's constraints** — scenarios that assume ideal conditions (fast internet, focused attention, tech literacy) when the actual user rarely has all three
