Same idea, tighter format. Both are valid. Traditional personas + scenarios still work well for design walkthrough and stakeholder alignment.

title: Storyboarding in the Software Design Process
author: UX Magazine
summary:
Storyboards borrow directly from filmmaking: a sequence of sketched panels showing the user's experience over time. Not the same as user flows (which are abstract diagrams) — storyboards are grounded in real-world context.

### Why storyboards work

They force you to include things user flows leave out:
- The **physical environment** (kitchen, subway, office desk)
- The **emotional context** (rushed, bored, anxious, curious)
- The **surrounding people and objects** (a phone ringing, a coworker interrupting, a screaming toddler)
- **What happens before and after** the product interaction (why they picked it up, what they do next)

That surrounding context often reveals design constraints you'd otherwise miss. A voice interface designed for a quiet office fails in a noisy commute. A mobile flow that assumes focused attention fails when the user is holding a baby.

### The workflow

1. **Start with a scenario.** (See previous cluster.)
2. **Sketch 4–8 panels** covering the arc of the interaction. Rough is fine — this is not visual design.
3. **Include a caption per panel** describing what's happening and what the persona is feeling.
4. **Present it as a story**, not a spec. Walk stakeholders through it as a narrative.

### The rule that keeps them useful

**Storyboard the whole experience, not just the app.** If you only sketch what happens on the screen, you might as well have made a wireflow. The value is in showing the real-world context around the product.

### When to use them

- Early in design when you're establishing direction and empathy
- Presenting to stakeholders who don't read specs
- Testing concepts before you build (participants react to storyboards, giving you feedback before you invest in prototypes)
- Workshop settings where you need to align a team on user experience
key_points: What happens before and after — the product interaction (why they picked it up, what they do next)
still_relevant: Yes, though underused. Modern equivalent: video prototypes, animated Figma mockups, or "day in the life" videos. But hand-sketched storyboards still have a place — they're fast, cheap, and their intentional roughness invites feedback that polished mockups don't. Something worth doing occasionally to break out of screen-only thinking.

title: Journey Maps & Service Blueprints (3 articles)
author: Cluster 3
summary:
**Sources:**
- Uxeria — 10 Most Interesting Examples of Customer Journey Maps — https://blog.uxeria.com/10-most-interesting-examples-of-customer-journey-maps/
- Sailthru — Customer Journey Mapping: How to Map a Customer Journey — https://www.sailthru.com/marketing-blog/written-customer-journey-mapping-need-to-know/
- Zbignev Gecis (UX Collective) — The Many Ways of Mapping the Customer Journey — https://uxdesign.cc/customer-journey-map-service-blueprinting-f06750312150

### The stage metaphor that makes the whole topic click (Gecis)

Gecis borrows from theater to explain the difference between journey maps and service blueprints:

- **Front stage** — what the audience (customer) sees. The performance itself. This is what a **customer journey map** shows.
- **Back stage** — what happens behind the curtain to make the performance possible. Lights, sets, crew. This is what a **service blueprint** adds.
- **Behind-the-scenes** — everything the organization has to do to make front + back stage possible. Internal processes, systems, employee support.

Journey maps show the customer's front-stage experience. Service blueprints show the whole production.

### The Steve Jobs quote worth stealing

*"You've got to start with the customer experience and work back toward the technology."*

Journey maps and service blueprints are how you actually do that. Everything else is guessing.

### Customer Journey Maps — the 5 components

A journey map captures what the user does, thinks, and feels over time as they interact with a service. Five components (Gecis's version, which is a good synthesis of standard practice):

1. **Goal** — what specific experience are you mapping? Onboarding? First purchase? Support interaction? A "to-be" future experience?
2. **Actor** — who's this journey about? Grounded in personas from real research.
3. **Stages** — the phases of the experience. Gecis uses the **5Es framework**:
 - **Entice** — how does the user become aware?
 - **Enter** — how do they begin?
 - **Engage** — what's the core of the experience?
 - **Exit** — how do they complete/finish?
 - **Extend** — what happens after?
4. **Touchpoints, emotions, thoughts** — narrative of what the actor does, thinks, and feels at each stage. Emotions plotted as a single line across the map (the "emotional curve") showing ups and downs.
5. **Opportunities** — insights from the map. What needs to happen next? Who owns each change? Where are the biggest opportunities? How will improvements be measured?

### Service Blueprints — the extra dimensions

A service blueprint extends a journey map by exposing the back stage. Five swim lanes:

1. **Customer actions** — from the journey map
2. **Front stage** — what happens in each touchpoint that's visible to the customer (employee interactions, app interactions)
3. **Back stage** — invisible-to-customer actions that support the front stage (kitchen prep, back-office processing)
4. **Support processes** — internal systems and interactions that support employees
5. **Evidence** — tangible elements the customer sees (uniforms, delivery vans, receipts, notification emails)

Plus three lines that separate the layers:
- **Line of interaction** — direct customer/organization interactions
- **Line of visibility** — visible vs. invisible activity
- **Line of internal interaction** — customer-facing employees vs. back office

### The Uxeria examples piece — what to take from it

Uxeria's article is a gallery of 10 real-world journey maps from various companies. Not much analytical content, but useful for:
- **Visual vocabulary** — seeing how different teams visualize the same idea
- **Format inspiration** — what to include, what to leave out, how to lay it out
- **Realistic complexity** — real journey maps are messier than tutorial examples

Standout example types you'll see: LEGO's "Adventures in Experience Land" (very story-driven), Adaptive Path's Rail Europe journey (detailed and analytical), Starbucks (playful and brand-heavy). The pattern: no single "correct" format — pick the visual style that fits your organization and audience.

### The Sailthru piece — marketing-flavored version of the same

Sailthru's article covers the same territory (define stages, capture touchpoints, identify emotions, spot opportunities) with a marketing lens rather than a UX one. Similar output, slightly different vocabulary (they talk about "conversion" more than "delight"). Nothing here that Gecis doesn't cover more thoroughly.

Two useful marketing-flavored additions from Sailthru:
- **Cross-channel emphasis** — journey maps should span email, web, mobile, in-store, support — not just your app
- **Data-driven vs. assumption-driven maps** — if it's not built on real behavioral data, it's a hypothesis map, not a journey map

### The rules that keep journey maps useful

- **One persona, one journey per map.** Trying to fit everyone on one map = unreadable.
- **Ground it in research.** Same rule as personas, scenarios, empathy maps, mental models. Assumption-based maps are just team wishful thinking with nice graphics.
- **Include emotion.** The emotional curve is often where the design opportunity is loudest. A functional-but-frustrating step deserves as much attention as a broken one.
- **Make opportunities actionable.** Every low point should map to a specific opportunity, owner, and metric — otherwise the map is decoration.
- **Update as the product changes.** Journey maps age fast. Living document or dead artifact.

### When to use which

| Situation | Tool |
|---|---|
| Understanding customer experience end-to-end | Journey map |
| Understanding a specific task or flow | User flow (see Cluster 1) |
| Exposing internal operational gaps behind the experience | Service blueprint |
| Understanding the *reasoning* behind behavior | Mental model |
| Aligning stakeholders around who you're designing for | Personas + scenarios |
key_points: Front stage — what the audience (customer) sees

title: Mobile First Is NOT Mobile Only
summary:
NN/g's corrective to mobile-first orthodoxy, backed by a 179-participant study run with WhatUsersDo across six sites (BBC, Bloomberg, Slate, Business Insider UK, 7digital, Supermarket HQ) on both desktop and smartphone.

**The surprising finding:** navigation was used significantly *more* on mobile than on desktop (77% vs 54% on navigation-required tasks). That sounds like mobile navigation had been solved. It hadn't. The correct reading is the inverse: there was *less* navigation use on desktop, because those desktop sites had been ported from mobile designs and were worse as a result.

This is the whole argument. Mobile-first as a *design process* is sound. Mobile-first as a *shipped artifact on every screen* degrades the larger platform.

**Mobile patterns that break on desktop:**
- Hidden nav / hamburger menus (the biggest offender — vague labels like "Menu" carry low information scent, and users forget the menu exists even after using it once in a session)
- Navigation repeated at page bottom
- Sticky top navigation
- Navigation in the top-right corner (standard on mobile, disorienting on desktop)
- Search icon instead of a search box (users complain about hunting for a tiny icon on a large screen)

**The historical pattern they close on** is the part worth remembering. Porting a UI across platforms has failed the same way every decade:
- 1980s: DOS → Windows
- 1990s: Windows → Macintosh
- 2000s: print brochure → website; print → PDF blob
- Late 2000s: desktop web → mobile
- 2010: magazine → iPad
- Late 2010s: mobile → desktop (this article)
- Next: mobile app → watch

Content and feature parity across devices is the right goal. Identical UI across devices is not.

title: Mobile First Helps with Big Issues
summary:
Wroblewski coined "mobile first" and this 2010 post (written after a Big Web Show conversation with Jeffrey Zeldman and Dan Benjamin) is one of the clearest short statements of *why* it works. His book **Mobile First** followed in 2011 from A Book Apart.

**The core mechanism: constraint as a forcing function.** Designing at 320x480 removes about 80% of the screen space you had at 1024x768. So 80% of the content, navigation, promotions and interactions has to go. That's not a limitation, it's the value.

**Two chronic problems mobile-first solves:**

1. **The kitchen sink problem.** Stakeholders each want their thing on the page and nobody has grounds to say no. Mobile-first supplies the grounds. When you design for the small screen first, "what matters most" stops being a matter of opinion and becomes a matter of physics. You create agreement on priority because the constraint forces it.

2. **The "same in every browser" problem.** Designing mobile-first establishes up front that how you present key actions and information will differ by platform, rather than treating pixel-identical rendering as the default expectation and every deviation as a defect.

**The sequencing rule that came out of his wider work:** *content first, navigation second*. Give people what they came for; don't make them wade through your org chart to reach it.

title: Themes — iOS Human Interface Guidelines
summary:
Apple's statement of the three principles underpinning iOS design. The saved URL points at the pre-2022 structure and now redirects, but the principles themselves are stable and worth knowing verbatim because they come up in interviews and in platform arguments.

**The three themes:**
1. **Clarity** — legible text at every size, precise icons, subtle and appropriate adornment, sharpened focus on functionality. Negative space, colour, fonts and graphics highlight what matters.
2. **Deference** — fluid motion and a crisp interface help people understand content without competing with it. Content fills the screen; translucency and blur hint at more. Minimal bezels, gradients and drop shadows keep the UI light.
3. **Depth** — distinct visual layers and realistic motion convey hierarchy and position. Touch and discoverability heighten delight and enable access to functionality without losing context.

**Why this matters beyond iOS:** it's the clearest short articulation of a platform having an opinion. Designing "for iOS" means adopting these priorities, not just using SF Pro and rounded rectangles. The same logic applies to Material Design on Android — platform conventions exist so users don't relearn interaction models per app.

title: A Hands-On Guide to Mobile-First Design
summary:
Practical how-to companion to the LukeW and NN/g pieces. Covers the mechanics rather than the argument.

**The process it describes:**
1. Inventory content and features, then rank by importance to the user's primary task
2. Sketch the smallest viable screen first — usually 320px
3. Establish the content hierarchy at that size; whatever doesn't fit gets cut or deferred, not shrunk
4. Progressively enhance upward through breakpoints, adding rather than subtracting
5. Design for touch from the start: minimum ~44x44pt targets, thumb-reachable primary actions, no hover-dependent interactions

**The distinction it's clearest on:** mobile-first is not the same as responsive design. Responsive is the technical implementation (fluid grids, flexible media, media queries). Mobile-first is the design sequence. You can build responsive sites desktop-first, and plenty of bad ones are.

**Progressive enhancement vs graceful degradation** — mobile-first is the progressive enhancement position applied to layout. Start with the baseline that works everywhere, then add capability where the platform supports it.

title: The Role of Enhancement in Web Design
summary:
Early Nielsen piece arguing for progressive enhancement: build the baseline experience so it works for everyone, then layer capability on top for environments that support it. Never make the enhanced layer a prerequisite for the core function.

**The principle, stated plainly:** an enhancement should improve the experience for users who can receive it and be invisible to users who can't. The moment your site *requires* the enhanced layer to function, it isn't an enhancement, it's a dependency.

Written in the era of Flash, Java applets and browser-sniffing, so the specific technologies are archaeology. The principle became one of the foundations of web standards practice and it's the direct ancestor of the mobile-first argument elsewhere in this sub-module.

title: How to conduct an effective UX audit
summary:
A UX audit is a structured evaluation of an existing product against usability principles, business goals and user data. It's the diagnostic you run before a redesign, and it's one of the most common freelance and consulting deliverables.

**What goes into one:**
- **Business and user goals** — what is this product supposed to achieve, and for whom? Without this the audit has no scoring criteria.
- **Analytics review** — where do users drop off, which pages underperform, what are the actual journeys vs the intended ones
- **Heuristic evaluation** — walk the product against Nielsen's 10 heuristics (or a custom set) and log every violation
- **Content audit** — inventory every page/screen, catalogue what exists, flag what's redundant, outdated or trivial (the ROT framework: Redundant, Outdated, Trivial)
- **Accessibility check** — contrast, keyboard navigation, screen reader behaviour, target sizes
- **User feedback** — support tickets, reviews, NPS comments, session recordings

**The output that makes it useful:** findings prioritised by severity and effort, not an undifferentiated list. A 40-page audit with no prioritisation gets shelved. Rank each issue by impact on the user, impact on the business, and cost to fix, then lead with the high-impact/low-effort items so there's something the team can ship immediately.

**The content audit specifically:** a spreadsheet inventory of every piece of content with URL, title, owner, last updated, traffic, and a keep/revise/delete/merge decision. Tedious, unglamorous, and usually where the biggest quick wins hide.

author: Nishant Panchal

still_relevant: Fully, and directly useful. The app critique round is still standard at product-design-mature companies. Contemporary addition: expect to be asked about AI features specifically — how a product surfaces AI capability, handles uncertainty in AI output, and sets expectations. Having an opinion on a well-designed and a badly-designed AI feature is close to table stakes now.
title: App critique framework for product design interviews
summary:
The app critique is a standard product design interview round: "pick an app you use and critique it." It looks casual and it isn't. It's testing whether you can reason about design decisions systematically rather than react aesthetically.

**The framework, in order:**

1. **State the product's purpose and target user.** Who is this for and what job does it do? Everything downstream is judged against this, so don't skip it to get to the opinions.
2. **Identify the primary user goal** you're going to critique against. One goal. Not the whole app.
3. **Walk the flow** for that goal, step by step, out loud.
4. **Evaluate against criteria** — usability heuristics, information hierarchy, visual design, accessibility, emotional response, business alignment. Name the criterion you're applying.
5. **Separate what works from what doesn't.** Start with what works. Interviewers are watching whether you can recognise good decisions, not just find faults.
6. **Propose improvements with reasoning and tradeoffs.** Every suggestion should name what it costs.
7. **Prioritise** your suggestions. Which would you ship first and why?

**What interviewers are actually assessing:** structured thinking, vocabulary, whether you consider business constraints, whether you can hold a user's perspective that isn't your own, and whether you're pleasant to disagree with.

**The most common failure:** launching straight into "I don't like this button." Unanchored aesthetic reaction with no stated user, goal or criterion reads as junior regardless of how good your taste is.

**Preparation tactic:** have two or three apps you've critiqued in advance, ideally in the domain of the company you're interviewing with. Not memorised scripts, but enough familiarity that you're not discovering the flow live.

title: 100 example UX problems
summary:
A list of 100 design prompts for practice, portfolio filler or whiteboard-challenge rehearsal. Value is in the list itself rather than in analysis.

**Prompt shapes it covers:** redesign an everyday object's digital equivalent, design for a constrained user group, design for an unusual context (one-handed, eyes-free, offline, high-stress), improve a known-bad flow, design a feature for an existing product.

**How to actually use it:** pick prompts that resemble the domain you're targeting rather than working through sequentially. Time-box them — 45 minutes, sketch only. The value is in reps at framing and structuring, not in producing finished artefacts. Two or three of these done properly and written up beat twenty half-finished ones.

**Portfolio caution:** self-generated challenges are visibly self-generated. They work as evidence of process when you have few real projects, but hiring managers weight real constrained work far more heavily. Use them to practise, not to pad.

title: Whiteboard Challenges — 100 Days of Product Design
summary:
Practice resource for the live whiteboard round. The round itself: you're given a vague prompt ("design a parking app for a city") and 30-45 minutes to work it through out loud with an interviewer watching.

**The structure that works, in order:**
1. **Clarify the prompt.** Ask questions. Who's the user? What's the business context? What platform? What's in and out of scope? Interviewers plant ambiguity deliberately and staying silent about it is the failure.
2. **Define the user and their goal.** Narrow explicitly. "I'm going to design for commuters rather than tourists, because..."
3. **Map the problem space** before any UI. Pain points, constraints, context of use.
4. **Diverge.** Sketch 2-3 distinct directions, not one. Show range.
5. **Converge** on one with stated reasoning.
6. **Sketch the core flow** at low fidelity. Boxes and arrows.
7. **Name tradeoffs and what you'd test.** Close by saying what you don't know and how you'd find out.

**What's being assessed:** how you handle ambiguity, whether you ask before assuming, whether you can think out loud coherently, and whether you're collaborative rather than defensive when challenged. The design output is almost secondary.

**The most common failures:** jumping straight to UI, designing for yourself, going silent while thinking, and defending a first idea instead of exploring alternatives.

title: 42 Common UX Designer Interview Questions
summary:
Question bank covering the standard UX interview rounds. Grouped by what's actually being tested, which is the useful way to hold them.

**Process questions** — "walk me through your design process", "how do you decide which research method to use", "how do you know a design is done". Testing whether you have a repeatable process or improvise. Answer with a real project, not an abstract framework diagram.

**Collaboration and conflict** — "tell me about a time you disagreed with a PM/engineer", "how do you handle stakeholder feedback you disagree with", "how do you work with developers". Testing whether you're workable with. Use STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) and always include the result.

**Research questions** — "how do you recruit participants", "how do you handle research that contradicts stakeholder assumptions", "what do you do when you have no budget for research". Testing pragmatism as much as knowledge.

**Craft and critique** — "what's a design you admire and why", "how do you approach accessibility", "how do you handle design systems". Testing vocabulary and taste.

**Failure questions** — "tell me about a project that failed", "what's a design decision you got wrong". Testing self-awareness. Have a real one prepared with a genuine lesson. Fake-humble answers ("I care too much about detail") read as evasion.

**Motivation** — "why this company", "why design", "where do you see yourself". Testing whether you researched them.

**The preparation that matters most:** three to four projects you can tell at varying lengths — a two-minute version, a ten-minute version, and a deep-dive with artefacts. Most interview failures are structure failures, not knowledge failures.

Worth reading the Polar Bear Book properly if you ever want to go deep.
title: Why IA Matters for UX — A Brief History of Information Architecture
summary:
Two overlapping history-of-IA pieces, clustered. The history matters more than it sounds, because IA keeps getting rediscovered under new names and knowing the lineage stops you reinventing it badly.

**The lineage:**
- **1976** — Richard Saul Wurman coins "information architect" at the AIA national conference, arguing that information needs structuring the way buildings do. His framing: the problem isn't information scarcity, it's information anxiety.
- **1990s** — the web explodes and suddenly everyone has a structure problem. Library and information science practitioners move into web work.
- **1998** — Rosenfeld and Morville publish *Information Architecture for the World Wide Web* (the Polar Bear Book). This is the founding text and it's still in print, now in its 4th edition.
- **2000s** — IA becomes a standalone job title, with its own conferences (the IA Summit) and professional identity.
- **2010s onward** — the title largely dissolves into UX design and content strategy. The work didn't go away; it got absorbed.

**The four systems of IA** (Rosenfeld & Morville, the part worth actually memorising):
1. **Organisation systems** — how content is grouped and categorised (hierarchical, sequential, matrix)
2. **Labeling systems** — how content is named and represented
3. **Navigation systems** — how users move through content
4. **Search systems** — how users look for content

**Wurman's LATCH framework** for organising any set of information — there are only five ways:
- **L**ocation
- **A**lphabet
- **T**ime
- **C**ategory
- **H**ierarchy

LATCH is genuinely useful and underused. Next time you're stuck on how to organise a list, run it through the five and see which fits the user's actual mental model.

**Why IA matters for UX:** structure is invisible when it works and infuriating when it doesn't. Bad IA can't be fixed by good visual design, but good IA survives mediocre visual design.

Remote also makes larger samples trivially achievable, which matters given the 15-participant threshold. Do a tree test (Treejack or equivalent) afterwards or you've only done half the job.
title: Card Sorting (clustered: Smashing beginner's guide, IBM Design, IxDF pros and cons)
summary:
Three sources on the same method. Croft's Smashing piece is the best of them and the most cited; the IBM and IxDF pieces add practitioner texture and a balanced critique respectively.

**What it is:** participants group content items (on cards, physical or digital) into categories that make sense to them. You learn how users actually think your content should be organised, rather than how your org chart says it should be.

**The problem it solves**, put bluntly by Croft: IA usually gets decided by whoever in the room is most senior and most confident, not by evidence. Card sorting replaces assertion with data.

**Two types:**

| | Open sort | Closed sort |
|---|---|---|
| Categories | Participants create and name their own | You supply fixed categories |
| Tells you | How users group things, and what they'd call the groups | Whether your existing structure works |
| Use when | Building new IA from scratch | Validating or refining existing IA |

There's also the **hybrid sort** — supplied categories plus the option to create new ones. Useful when you have a partial structure you want to stress-test.

**Running a session:**
- **Inventory first.** Card sorting sorts content that exists. Audit before you sort.
- **Card count: 30 to 60.** Fewer than 30 and you learn little; more than 80 and participants fatigue and start sorting carelessly.
- **One concept per card**, with a short clarifying description. Card labels shouldn't lead — avoid embedding your intended category in the item name.
- **Provide blank cards and a pen** for open sorts so participants can add items or categories you missed.
- **Ask them to think aloud.** The reasoning matters more than the final grouping. "I put these together because they all feel like things I'd do before I buy" is the insight; the grouping is just the artefact.
- **Participants: 15 or so** for quantitative confidence. This is one of the methods where the 5-user rule does *not* apply — you need enough to see agreement patterns statistically.
- **Don't intervene.** No hints, no "are you sure?". Let them put things in the wrong place.

**Analysis:** look for items that consistently group together (high agreement — trust these), items that land everywhere (low agreement — these labels are ambiguous and need rewriting, not re-filing), and category names participants invent (often better than yours).

**The IxDF critique, worth holding onto:**
- Card sorting tells you how people *categorise*, not how they'd *search* or *navigate* under task pressure. It's a mental-model tool, not a behaviour tool.
- Results can be shallow — participants sort by surface similarity rather than by how they'd actually look for something.
- It doesn't validate the final structure. **Pair it with tree testing**, which does: card sorting builds the structure, tree testing checks whether people can find things in it. Running one without the other is the most common mistake.

author: Raluca Budiu
key_points: Discoverable, accessible, space-efficient — pick two, at best
Tab bars cap out at 5 options before touch targets degrade
Hamburger menus: users forget they exist even after using them in the same session
Navigation hubs work for task-oriented sites, waste the homepage for content sites
Prioritise content over chrome
There's no winning pattern, only the least damaging tradeoff for your users' tasks
still_relevant: Yes. The main shift since: bottom navigation has largely won on mobile web as well as in apps, on thumb-reach grounds (Fitts's Law beats convention here). Gesture-based navigation became a fourth pattern after iOS removed the home button, with its own discoverability problem — gestures are invisible and undiscoverable without onboarding. Pair with 'Mobile First Is NOT Mobile Only' earlier in this archive
title: Basic Patterns for Mobile Navigation: A Primer
summary:
The reference piece on mobile navigation patterns and their tradeoffs. Budiu's framing is that there is no good solution, only a choice about which downside hurts your users least.

**The central tension:** mobile navigation must be *discoverable*, *accessible*, and *take little screen space*. You cannot maximise all three. Meanwhile one of the basic tenets of mobile usability is to prioritise content over chrome. Every pattern below sacrifices something.

**The patterns:**

**Top navigation bar** — inherited from desktop. Visible by default, so discoverable. But it consumes vertical space and usually scrolls out of view after the first screenful, at which point it's neither visible nor accessible.

**Tab bar** — the app-specific relative of the nav bar, anchored at the bottom on iOS. Persistent, so always accessible, and it sits in the thumb zone. Hard limit: **more than 5 options and you can't maintain adequate touch-target size.**

**Hamburger / hidden navigation** — accommodates many options in almost no space. The cost is severe: low discoverability, vague labels ("Menu", "Browse") with poor information scent, and users demonstrably forget the menu exists even after using it once in the same session. NN/g's own study found hidden navigation measurably hurts UX metrics.

**Navigation hub (homepage-as-menu)** — the homepage is devoted entirely to navigation options. Highly discoverable, but you sacrifice the homepage as content real estate and add a round-trip step for every navigation action. Works well for **task-oriented** sites where users arrive knowing what they want to do.

**The selection rule:** pick the pattern where the inevitable downside hurts your users least, given the tasks they're most likely to perform. Content-consumption sites, task-oriented tools and e-commerce all land differently.

title: UI Patterns — Design Pattern Library
summary:
Reference library, not an article, and one of the genuinely durable resources in this whole archive. Toxboe has maintained it since 2007.

**What a design pattern is:** a reusable solution to a recurring design problem, described in terms of the problem it solves and the context where it applies. Borrowed from Christopher Alexander's architectural pattern languages via the software world's Gang of Four.

**Why patterns matter more than component libraries:** a component library tells you what a dropdown looks like in your system. A pattern library tells you *when a dropdown is the right answer* and what it costs. The first is implementation, the second is judgment.

**The structure each pattern follows** on the site, which is also a decent template for documenting your own:
- **Problem** — what the user is trying to do
- **Usage** — when this pattern applies and when it doesn't
- **Solution** — how it works
- **Rationale** — why it works, often with the psychology behind it
- **Examples** — real implementations in the wild

**Jakob's Law is the underlying argument for patterns:** users spend most of their time on other sites, so they expect yours to work like the ones they already know. Deviating from an established pattern costs the user learning effort, and you need a real reason to spend it.

**The counter-argument worth holding simultaneously:** patterns encode the status quo, including its mistakes. The hamburger menu is a pattern. Infinite scroll is a pattern. Dark patterns are patterns. Knowing the pattern is step one; deciding whether it's the right answer here is step two, and a pattern library can't do that part for you.

**Related from the same author:** Toxboe also maintains a persuasive-patterns collection covering behavioural-psychology-driven design. Use with care — the line between persuasion and manipulation is exactly where dark patterns live, and regulators have started policing it.

title: The Habit Loop
summary:
Wiki page explaining the habit loop, which underpins most engagement and retention design. The model comes from Charles Duhigg's *The Power of Habit* (2012), with roots in behavioural psychology.

**The loop, three parts:**
1. **Cue** — the trigger that starts the behaviour. External (notification, email, time of day) or internal (boredom, anxiety, loneliness).
2. **Routine** — the behaviour itself.
3. **Reward** — what the user gets, which reinforces the loop and makes the cue more salient next time.

**Nir Eyal's Hooked model** extends this into the version most product teams actually use: Trigger → Action → **Variable Reward** → **Investment**. Two additions matter:
- **Variable reward** — unpredictable rewards are far more compelling than predictable ones. This is the slot-machine mechanic, and it's why pull-to-refresh and social feeds work the way they do.
- **Investment** — the user puts something in (data, content, social connections, configuration), which increases the value of returning and raises switching costs.

**The ethics, which this wiki page doesn't cover and you should:** these mechanics are effective regardless of whether the underlying product is good for the user. Variable reward plus investment is how you build a genuinely useful habit and also how you build a compulsion loop. The technique is neutral; the application isn't. Eyal himself later wrote *Indistractable* partly in response to how *Hooked* was being used.

**The honest test:** would the user, if fully informed about the mechanic, still be glad it's there? Habitica passes — it's explicitly a habit-building tool and users opt into the gamification. An infinite feed with variable-reward notifications generally doesn't.

title: Usability Heuristics & Heuristic Evaluation (clustered: CareerFoundry, IxDF, Muzli)
summary:
Three sources on Nielsen's heuristics and how to evaluate against them. Clustered because they substantially overlap.

**Nielsen's 10 Usability Heuristics** (1994, refined from a 1990 factor analysis with Rolf Molich). These are the most-cited principles in the field and you should know them well enough to apply without looking them up:

1. **Visibility of system status** — always keep users informed about what's going on, through timely feedback
2. **Match between system and the real world** — speak the users' language, follow real-world conventions
3. **User control and freedom** — provide a clearly marked emergency exit; support undo and redo
4. **Consistency and standards** — don't make users wonder whether different words or actions mean the same thing; follow platform conventions
5. **Error prevention** — better than good error messages is a design that prevents the problem occurring
6. **Recognition rather than recall** — minimise memory load; make options visible
7. **Flexibility and efficiency of use** — accelerators for experts, invisible to novices
8. **Aesthetic and minimalist design** — no irrelevant or rarely needed information competing with the relevant
9. **Help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors** — plain language, precise problem, constructive solution
10. **Help and documentation** — ideally unnecessary, but provide it, searchable and task-focused

*(The CareerFoundry version lists 11, splitting or adding one — the canonical NN/g set is 10.)*

**Running a heuristic evaluation:**
- **Use 3 to 5 evaluators.** A single evaluator finds roughly 35% of usability problems; five find around 75%. Different evaluators find different problems, so the aggregation is the point.
- **Evaluate independently first, then combine.** Discussing before you've each formed a view produces groupthink and loses coverage.
- **Go through the interface at least twice.** First pass for flow and feel, second pass for specific elements.
- **Log each issue against a specific heuristic.** "This is bad" isn't a finding. "Violates #1, visibility of system status: no loading indicator during the 4-second save" is.
- **Rate severity.** NN/g's scale: 0 = not a problem, 1 = cosmetic, 2 = minor, 3 = major, 4 = catastrophe. Severity combines frequency, impact and persistence.
- **Evaluators should know the domain**, or you'll log false positives against conventions that are correct for that field.

**The critical limitation, which every source should state and most don't:** a heuristic evaluation is an **expert inspection, not user research**. It predicts problems; it doesn't observe them. It's cheap and fast and catches a lot, and it also generates false positives and misses domain-specific problems that only real users hit. It complements usability testing. It does not replace it.

title: Complete Beginner's Guide to Interaction Design
summary:
Primer on interaction design as a discipline distinct from visual design and from UX broadly. IxD is concerned with the dialogue between user and product: what the user can do, what the system does in response, and how that exchange is communicated.

**Gillian Crampton Smith's four dimensions of IxD**, later extended to five by Kevin Silver:
1. **Words** — text and labels, which must be meaningful and not over-explain
2. **Visual representations** — typography, icons, diagrams; everything graphical the user interacts with
3. **Physical objects or space** — what the user manipulates the product with (mouse, finger, stylus) and where they are when doing it
4. **Time** — media that change with time: animation, video, sound; also how the user's interaction progresses
5. **Behaviour** (Silver's addition) — how the previous four combine into action and reaction: what users do and how the system responds

**The five questions IxD asks of any interface:**
- What can the user do, directly or indirectly?
- What does the user know about the system's state and options?
- Is there feedback, and is it timely?
- Are there constraints preventing error?
- Does the interface follow conventions the user already knows?

**Key concepts it introduces:** affordances (what an object suggests it can do), signifiers (the visible cues indicating an affordance — Norman's later refinement, because a pure affordance can be invisible), mapping (the relationship between control and effect), and feedback loops.

title: Low-Fidelity & Rapid Prototyping (clustered: Marvel POP paper prototyping, IxDF rapid prototyping)
summary:
Two pieces on the cheapest end of prototyping.

**Why paper still earns its place**, and this is the durable argument:
- **Speed.** You can sketch six alternatives in the time it takes to build one in Figma.
- **Disposability.** Cheap things are easy to throw away. Expensive things get defended, and sunk cost makes designers argue for ideas they'd otherwise abandon.
- **It invites criticism.** Something visibly unfinished signals that feedback is wanted. A polished mockup signals that a decision has been made, and people soften their criticism accordingly. This is the single strongest argument for low fidelity and it's a social effect, not a technical one.
- **Anyone can participate.** No tool literacy required, so PMs, engineers and users can all sketch. Enormously useful in co-design workshops.

**Testing with paper prototypes** — the mechanics are odd but they work. One person plays the "computer", swapping screens in response to the participant's taps. It feels ridiculous for about ninety seconds and then people genuinely engage with it. You learn flow and comprehension problems immediately.

**Marvel POP** (Prototyping On Paper) — photograph your sketches, add tap hotspots, get a clickable prototype on a phone. Bridges paper and digital.

**Rapid prototyping as a cycle** (the IxDF piece's framing): **Prototype → Review → Refine**, repeated. The prototype's job is to answer a question and then die. Fidelity is dictated by the question, and the most common mistake is building more prototype than the question needs.

**The horizontal/vertical distinction, worth knowing:**
- **Horizontal prototype** — broad, shallow. Many screens, little functional depth. For testing navigation and overall flow.
- **Vertical prototype** — narrow, deep. One flow fully functional. For testing a specific complex interaction.

Decide which you need before you start, or you'll build a wide shallow thing and then discover you needed depth.

title: Mobile Onboarding (clustered: Smashing beginner's guide, Babich 'Interact Don't Tell', Tapadoo patterns, Apple HIG)
summary:
Four sources on first-run experience. Babich's "Interact, Don't Tell" carries the central argument.

**The problem onboarding solves:** roughly a quarter of apps are used exactly once. The first session determines whether there's a second. Onboarding has to get the user to their first moment of value before they decide it isn't worth the effort.

**The central principle — interact, don't tell.** Carousel tutorials explaining features before the user has any context are the default and they're mostly ineffective. People swipe through them to get to the app and retain almost nothing. Instead, teach in context, at the moment the feature becomes relevant. Progressive disclosure beats a front-loaded lecture.

**The main patterns:**

| Pattern | What it is | Works when |
|---|---|---|
| **Benefits-oriented** | A few screens on value, not features | The value proposition isn't obvious |
| **Function-oriented / coach marks** | Contextual tips overlaid at point of use | Interactions are genuinely non-obvious (especially gestures) |
| **Progressive** | Teach each feature the first time it's encountered | Complex apps with many features |
| **Do-it-yourself / empty states** | No tutorial; the interface teaches itself through good empty states and defaults | The app is simple or conventions are strong |
| **Account-deferred** | Let people use the app before forcing signup | Almost always — forced signup before value is a major drop-off point |

**Apple's HIG position:** get people to the content fast, avoid lengthy tutorials, make onboarding skippable and re-accessible, and if your app needs extensive explanation, reconsider the design rather than the tutorial. That last point is the real one — **onboarding is often a patch over an interface that isn't self-evident.**

**Design rules that hold:**
- Always let people **skip**, and let them find the tutorial again later
- Ask for permissions **in context**, when the need is visible, not in a wall of requests on launch
- **Defer signup** until the user has experienced value
- Use **empty states** as teaching moments; they're the most-wasted real estate in most apps
- **Minimise steps.** Every screen between launch and value costs users.

**The measurement point:** onboarding success isn't completion rate, it's **activation** — the percentage of users who reach a defined first-value moment. Optimising tutorial completion while activation stays flat means you've made the lecture more palatable, not the product more valuable.

title: Wireframes, Mockups & Prototypes: terminology and the fidelity ladder (clustered, 4 sources)
summary:
Four sources arguing about terminology. Clustered because the disagreement between them is itself the useful content — these words are used inconsistently across the industry and knowing that saves you confusion in job interviews and team handovers.

**The distinction that most sources agree on:**

| | Shows | Fidelity | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Wireframe** | Structure, hierarchy, content placement | Low to mid, usually greyscale | Is the layout and hierarchy right? |
| **Mockup** | Visual design — colour, type, imagery | High, static | Does it look right? |
| **Prototype** | Behaviour — clicks, transitions, states | Any fidelity, but interactive | Does it work right? |

The axis everyone conflates: **fidelity** (how finished it looks) and **interactivity** (whether it responds) are independent. You can have a low-fidelity interactive prototype (paper with a human swapping screens) and a high-fidelity static mockup. Keeping these separate in your head makes the terminology arguments evaporate.

**The UX Movement piece's warnings about going high-fidelity**, which are the sharpest content in this cluster:
1. **People critique the wrong layer.** Show a coloured mockup and you'll get feedback on the blue, not the structure. You asked about hierarchy and got an opinion on the brand palette.
2. **Stakeholders think it's finished.** High fidelity reads as "done" to non-designers, which compresses the remaining schedule in their heads and makes structural change feel like a regression.
3. **You get attached.** Hours invested makes you defend the work instead of killing it.
4. **It's slow to change.** The cost of iteration rises sharply with fidelity, so you iterate less, which is exactly backwards.

**The practical conclusion:** the fidelity ladder isn't a sequence you must climb rung by rung. It's a set of options, and you pick the lowest fidelity that answers your current question. Skipping rungs is fine. Climbing too early is expensive.
