**Adhithya's whiteboard framework** adds two things to the structure already captured in 2.9:

**Time-box explicitly and say it out loud.** "I'll spend five minutes on problem framing, fifteen on exploration, ten on the flow, and leave five for questions." This does two jobs: it shows planning, and it stops you spending twenty-five minutes on discovery and then panicking. Interviewers notice.

**Narrate your uncertainty rather than hiding it.** "I'm not sure whether this should be one screen or two — here's the tradeoff, and here's what I'd test to decide." Junior candidates hide uncertainty because it feels like weakness. Senior candidates surface it because it demonstrates judgment about what's actually unresolved.

**Remote-specific mechanics** (the Miro piece, plus what's changed since):
- **Know the tool before the call.** If they send a FigJam or Miro link, open it early and get comfortable. Fumbling with the canvas eats your thinking time and reads as disorganisation.
- **Keep artefacts large and legible.** What's readable on your monitor may be unreadable in a shared screen on a laptop.
- **Narrate more than feels natural.** In person, people read your body language and see where your pen is. On video they see a cursor. Say what you're doing as you do it.
- **Prepare a canvas template in advance** — sections for problem, user, goals, explorations, flow, open questions. Not pre-filled content, just structure. Saves setup time and signals process.
- **Check your setup.** Camera, mic, second screen if you have one. Sharing a Figma file while also seeing the interviewer is much easier with two screens.

**Relevant to applying abroad:** remote interview rounds are what make international applications practical at all. Processes in Japan, for instance, tend to run longer and involve more rounds than European norms, usually including at least one round focused on fit and communication rather than craft.

author: Jeff Sauro (MeasuringU), NN/g, UXmatters
key_points: The screener matters more than the method — wrong participants produce confident wrong conclusions
Screen on behaviour, not demographics
Hide the desired answer in the screener or professional participants will give it to you
Over-recruit: no-show rates run 10-30%. Need 6, book 8.
Your own network is fine for a pilot, dangerous for findings — people who know you are kinder to your design
Existing-customer recruiting never reaches the people who already left
State exact duration in outreach; it converts better than vague brevity
still_relevant: Fully, and research ops has become its own specialism since. Modern tooling: User Interviews, Respondent, Prolific and Askable for panels, Sprig for in-product intercepts, and most large orgs now maintain a consented participant database with re-contact rules. GDPR matters here if you're recruiting in Europe — you need a lawful basis for holding participant data, a retention period, and a deletion process.
title: Recruiting participants (clustered: NN/g report, MeasuringU 7 ways, UXmatters and Medium email templates)
summary:
Recruiting is the part of usability testing that actually kills projects. The method is easy; finding the right eight people who show up is not.

**Where participants come from** (Sauro's list, expanded):
- **Your existing customer list** — cheapest and most representative, but biased toward people who already tolerate your product. You will never hear from the people who bounced.
- **Customer support or sales contacts** — high-quality access, but you're getting the loudest and the most frustrated.
- **In-product intercepts** — a prompt inside the product. Excellent for behavioural targeting, since you can trigger on actual usage. Sprig and similar tools do this now.
- **Panels and recruiting agencies** — fastest, most expensive, and prone to professional participants who have done fifty studies and know what researchers want to hear.
- **Social media and communities** — cheap, good for niche or hard-to-reach groups, self-selecting.
- **Guerrilla / intercept in public** — coffee shops, conferences. Fast and free, and you have almost no control over who you get.
- **Your own network** — fine for a pilot, dangerous for real findings. People who know you are nicer to your design.

**The screener is the whole game.** A study with the wrong participants is worse than no study, because it produces confident wrong conclusions. Screener rules:
- Screen on **behaviour**, not demographics. "Have you booked a flight online in the past three months?" beats "Are you aged 25-40?"
- **Hide what you want.** If the screener reveals the desired answer, professional participants will give it. Ask about several behaviours so the target one isn't obvious.
- Include **disqualifying questions** — people who work in design, marketing or your industry usually shouldn't be in a general-consumer study.
- Keep it **short**. Long screeners have their own drop-off problem.

**Practical numbers:**
- **Over-recruit.** No-show rates run 10-30% depending on channel and incentive. If you need 6, book 8.
- **Confirm twice** — at booking and 24 hours before.
- **Incentives** scale with specialism. General consumers are cheap; doctors, developers and enterprise decision-makers are expensive and may not be motivated by money at all (donations to charity, early access, or a findings summary sometimes work better).

**On email outreach:** keep it short, lead with what's in it for them, state the time commitment precisely, and make scheduling one click. The single most effective change is specifying duration up front — "30 minutes" converts far better than "a short session".

author: David Travis (Userfocus), UX Booth, US HHS
key_points: Four components of consent: disclosure, comprehension, voluntariness, competence
Right to withdraw at any time, without explanation, without losing the incentive
'We're testing the design, not you' — say it out loud, every session
Recording, sharing, and presenting clips each require separate consent
Anonymise by default; participant IDs not names
Stop if the participant becomes distressed. The study is never more important than the person.
Collect only what you need — ethics and GDPR agree here
still_relevant: More relevant than when written, and legally binding in your context. **GDPR governs any research with EU participants**: you need a lawful basis, a privacy notice, a defined retention period, and a working deletion process. Special-category data (health, biometrics, beliefs) has a much higher bar. Practical consequences: session recordings are personal data, AI transcription tools are processors you need an agreement with, and "we'll keep it forever in case it's useful" is not a retention policy. Worth being able to speak to this in interviews — many teams handle it badly and it's a credibility marker.
title: Research ethics and informed consent (clustered: Userfocus, UX Booth, 45 CFR 46)
summary:
Three sources on the ethical floor of user research. The 45 CFR 46 link is the US federal "Common Rule" governing human-subjects research — dry, but it's the legal bedrock the norms descend from.

**Informed consent has four components** and all four must be present:
1. **Disclosure** — the participant knows what the study involves, how long it takes, what will be recorded, who will see it, and how it will be stored
2. **Comprehension** — they actually understand it. Plain language, not a wall of legal text they scroll past.
3. **Voluntariness** — no coercion. Including subtle coercion: an employee "volunteering" for a study their manager knows about is not freely consenting.
4. **Competence** — they're able to consent. Children need guardian consent plus their own assent; some participants need additional consideration.

**The right to withdraw is absolute and must be stated explicitly.** At any time, without explanation, without losing their incentive. Withholding payment from someone who stops early is coercion.

**The non-negotiables:**
- **Never test the user, test the design.** Say this out loud at the start of every session. Participants blame themselves for usability failures and it distorts both their behaviour and their wellbeing.
- **Recording requires separate, specific consent.** So does sharing recordings outside the immediate team, and so does using clips in a presentation. One blanket tick is not consent for all three.
- **Anonymise by default.** Participant IDs, not names, in every artefact that leaves the research team.
- **Stop if the participant is distressed.** The study is never more important than the person. This matters especially in research touching money, health, bereavement or anything else where the domain itself is stressful.
- **Don't collect data you don't need.** Data minimisation is both an ethical principle and a GDPR requirement.

**The harder ethical questions** these articles raise and don't fully answer, worth having a view on:
- Deception in research design — sometimes methodologically necessary, always requiring debrief
- Researching vulnerable populations, where standard consent processes may be insufficient
- What you owe participants after the study, in terms of feeding back what changed
- Whether your research is being used to build something that harms the people you studied

author: Jakob Nielsen
key_points: Five components: learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors, satisfaction
Usability + utility = usefulness. A usable product can still be pointless.
Usability is a component of UX, not a synonym — know this for interviews
On the web, usability is a survival condition, not a differentiator
The method is three things: representative users, representative tasks, silent observation
still_relevant: Foundational and unchanged. The five components are standard vocabulary and the usability/utility/usefulness distinction is genuinely useful analytically — it's the question to ask when a test goes badly and you're not sure whether the design or the premise failed.
title: Usability 101: Introduction to Usability
summary:
The definitional piece. If you need one source for "what is usability and how is it different from UX", this is it.

**Nielsen's five quality components of usability:**
1. **Learnability** — how easy is it to accomplish basic tasks the first time?
2. **Efficiency** — once learned, how quickly can tasks be performed?
3. **Memorability** — after a period away, how easily is proficiency re-established?
4. **Errors** — how many errors, how severe, how easily recovered?
5. **Satisfaction** — how pleasant is it to use?

**Plus utility, which sits alongside:** does it do what people need at all? **Usability + utility = usefulness.** A product can be perfectly usable and pointless. A product can be useful and unusable. You need both, and confusing the two is a common analytical error — "users didn't complete the task" might be a usability failure or it might be that they never wanted to do the task.

**Why usability matters commercially:** on the web, usability is a survival condition rather than a differentiator. If a site is difficult, people leave. There's no support desk, no training, no sunk investment holding them there. The first law of e-commerce, in Nielsen's framing: if users can't find the product, they can't buy it.

**Usability vs UX:** usability is a quality attribute of the interface. UX is the whole experience of encountering the company, its services and its products. Usability is a component of UX, not a synonym. This distinction comes up constantly in interviews.

**How to improve it:** user testing, iteratively, with three components — get representative users, ask them to perform representative tasks, observe silently. That's it. The simplicity is the point, and Nielsen notes that people routinely overlook the method because they assume it must be more complicated.

author: Jakob Nielsen
key_points: Watch what users do, not what they say. Self-report and prediction are both unreliable.
The qualifier everyone drops: collect preference data AFTER they've used the design, in context
The problem isn't asking — it's asking about hypotheticals and the future
Stated preference and measured performance frequently diverge
Behavioural data says what; you still need qualitative to know why
still_relevant: As relevant as in 2001, and Nielsen himself said so in a later article. Contemporary edge: analytics and session-replay make behavioural data abundant and cheap, which has tilted some teams too far the other way — drowning in what, starving for why. The balanced position is triangulation, not picking a side.
title: First Rule of Usability? Don't Listen to Users
summary:
Deliberately provocative title, and the argument underneath is one of the load-bearing principles of the whole field. Paired here with UX Myths #21, which makes the same point in shorter form.

**The claim:** to design the best UX, pay attention to what users *do*, not what they *say*. Self-reported claims are unreliable and speculation about future behaviour is worse. In Nielsen's phrasing, asked whether users know what they want: no, no, and no. Three times no.

**Why self-report fails:**
- People **rationalise** their behaviour after the fact, constructing reasons that feel coherent but aren't what actually drove the action
- People are **bad at predicting** their own future behaviour, consistently and in measurable directions
- People answer the question they think you're asking, and want to be helpful
- Stated preference and actual performance frequently diverge — people say they prefer the design they perform worse with

**The method that follows:** watch users attempt tasks with the interface. Nielsen's own note is that this is so simple people overlook it, assuming usability testing must involve something more elaborate.

**The crucial qualifier everyone drops when quoting this article.** Nielsen does not say ignore users entirely. He says: *collect preference data only after they have used a design and have a real feeling for how well it supports them.* Post-task, in context, grounded in an actual experience. The problem isn't asking; it's asking about hypotheticals and about the future.

**Where this connects:** it's the same principle as the timeline rule in "Interviewing Users" (past is misremembered, future is speculation, present is valid) and the reason contextual inquiry and diary studies exist at all. It also underpins the Henry Ford "faster horses" cliché, which is probably apocryphal but makes the point.

**The counterweight to hold alongside it:** behavioural data tells you *what* happened and is silent on *why*. You need the qualitative layer to interpret it. "Don't listen to users" is a corrective to over-reliance on self-report, not a licence to stop talking to people.

author: Christine Perfetti (UIE)
key_points: Measures first-impression comprehension and visual hierarchy, nothing else
Good for landing pages, marketing pages, dashboards — anything that must orient quickly
Cheap and quant-ish at 20-50 participants
Cannot tell you anything about task completion or flow — routinely over-claimed
The five seconds is arbitrary and was never validated
still_relevant: Method is alive. The standalone fivesecondtest.com folded into UsabilityHub, which rebranded to **Lyssna** in 2023. Maze and UserTesting offer equivalents.
title: 5-Second Tests (clustered: UIE article, FiveSecondTest tool)
summary:
A quick method for testing whether a page communicates its purpose. Show a participant a design for five seconds, remove it, then ask what they remember and what they think the page is for.

**What it actually measures:** first-impression comprehension and visual hierarchy. Whether the most important thing on the page is the thing people register first.

**Good questions to ask afterward:**
- What is this page about / what does this company do?
- What could you do on this page?
- What do you remember seeing?
- What stood out most?

**What it cannot tell you:** anything about task completion, flow, or usability in any meaningful sense. It's a comprehension check on a static view, nothing more. It gets over-claimed constantly.

**Where it's genuinely useful:** landing pages, marketing pages, dashboards, and any screen whose job is to orient someone quickly. It's cheap, fast, and easy to run remotely with reasonable sample sizes (20-50), which makes it one of the few quant-ish methods available on a small budget.

**A caution about the five seconds:** the duration is arbitrary and was never validated as the right number. Treat it as "brief exposure" rather than a precise threshold.

author: Jeff Sauro
key_points: Five types: explorative, assessment, comparative, validation, plus formative/summative as the cross-cutting axis
Formative = find problems, small n, iterate. Summative = measure, large n, tight script.
The one question: am I finding problems or measuring performance?
Never report percentages from a 5-person formative test
Comparative tests: watch for order and anchoring effects
still_relevant: Fully. This taxonomy is the antidote to the most common usability-testing mistake, which is running the wrong type for the question. Sauro's MeasuringU is the best source in the archive for the quantitative side of UX.
title: 5 Types of Usability Tests
summary:
Sauro's taxonomy, which is the clearest way to think about what kind of test you're actually running. The five types are distinguished by purpose, not by logistics.

**1. Explorative** — early, generative, before much exists. Concepts, sketches, competitor products. Participants react and think aloud. Loose structure, few fixed tasks. You're learning what matters, not measuring anything.

**2. Assessment (summative-ish)** — the standard usability test. Participants attempt realistic tasks on a working design; you observe where they struggle. Mostly qualitative, moderate structure. This is what most people mean by "usability testing".

**3. Comparative** — two or more designs, or your design against a competitor's. Can be within-subjects (same people see both, counterbalanced to control order effects) or between-subjects (different groups). Watch for order and anchoring effects; they're the main threat to validity here.

**4. Validation (summative / benchmark)** — measuring performance against a standard or a previous baseline. Quantitative, tightly scripted, larger samples (20+). Metrics: task success rate, time on task, error rate, satisfaction scores. This is what you run before launch and repeat to show improvement.

**5. Formative vs summative** as the cross-cutting distinction:
- **Formative** — testing to *improve*. Small samples, qualitative, iterative, run often.
- **Summative** — testing to *measure*. Larger samples, quantitative, run at milestones.

**The selection question is simply: am I trying to find problems or to measure performance?** Find problems → formative, 5 users, iterate. Measure → summative, 20+ users, tight script, defined metrics. Confusing the two is where most bad usability testing comes from, in both directions: teams run 5 users and report a "68% success rate" as if it meant something, or they spend weeks on a 30-person benchmark when they just needed to know whether the button was findable.

author: Kara Pernice
key_points: The F pattern is a failure signal, not a design target — it means the content gave people nothing better to do
Layer-cake scanning is the good pattern and what structured content produces
Other patterns: spotted, marking, bypassing, commitment
Front-load the first two words of every heading, link and bullet
Don't start consecutive bullets with the same word — people bypass them
Fix content structure rather than just moving things to the left
still_relevant: Very. The misinterpretation is still widespread, and being able to correct it is a small credibility win. Increasingly relevant for a new reason: content that's structured for layer-cake scanning is also content that AI systems parse and summarise well. Clear headings and front-loaded meaning now serve both human scanners and machine readers.
title: F-Shaped Pattern of Reading on the Web: Misunderstood, But Still Relevant
summary:
The 2017 revisit of NN/g's famous 2006 eyetracking finding, and the revisit matters more than the original because the original got badly misused.

**The original finding:** eyetracking heatmaps of people reading web pages often show an F shape — horizontal sweeps across the top, a shorter horizontal sweep further down, then a vertical scan down the left side.

**What people wrongly concluded:** that users read in an F, that you should design in an F shape, and that content on the right is wasted.

**What it actually means:** the F pattern is what happens **when the content gives people nothing better to do.** It's a symptom of unformatted, undifferentiated text — a failure signal, not a design target. People scan in an F when there are no headings, no bold text, no bullets, no visual hierarchy to guide them. Give them structure and the pattern changes.

**Other scanning patterns NN/g documents:**
- **Layer-cake** — scanning headings and subheadings, dipping into body text selectively. This is the *good* pattern, and it's what well-structured content produces.
- **Spotted** — skipping large chunks, hunting for specific words, links or numbers
- **Marking** — keeping the eye in one place while scrolling, like a finger following a line
- **Bypassing** — deliberately skipping the first words of lines when several lines start identically
- **Commitment** — actually reading nearly everything, which happens when motivation is high

**The design implications that follow:**
- Front-load the most important words in headings, subheadings, links and bullets. The first two words carry disproportionate weight.
- Use **meaningful headings**, not clever ones. Scanners read headings to decide whether to dip in.
- Structure content so the layer-cake pattern is possible — that's the pattern you're designing *for*
- Avoid starting consecutive lines or bullets with the same word, or people bypass them entirely
- Put important content where the eye goes, but fix the content structure first rather than just relocating things leftward

author: NN/g, David Travis (Userfocus), Usability.gov
key_points: Objectives come from your worries: difficult tasks, support complaints, untested team beliefs
Tasks are scenarios with goals, never instructions — and never use interface language
One goal per task; compound tasks hide which part failed
Define success criteria in writing before the session
Let people struggle. The struggle is the finding.
Travis's 1-page dashboard is a summary, not a replacement for the plan
Always pilot. One session saves eight.
still_relevant: Method fully current. **Note: usability.gov was decommissioned** and its content archived — much of it moved to digital.gov. It's cited everywhere so it's worth knowing the source, but link to NN/g or digital.gov in current work.
title: Planning a usability test (clustered: NN/g checklist, Userfocus 1-page plan, usability.gov, avoiding bias)
summary:
Four sources on planning. Travis's one-pager is the most practically useful, NN/g's checklist the most thorough.

**What a test plan contains:**
- **Objectives** — what decisions will this test inform? Travis's prompts for finding them: aspects of the product you're worried about, tasks you suspect are difficult, user groups you're unsure about, complaints and support requests, stakeholder concerns, problems raised by the team, and untested beliefs the team holds about users.
- **Research questions** — specific and answerable, not "is it usable?"
- **Participants** — who, how many, how recruited, screener criteria
- **Tasks** — realistic scenarios, not instructions
- **Metrics** — what you'll measure, if anything
- **Logistics** — where, when, what equipment, who observes, who takes notes
- **Roles** — facilitator, note-taker, observers and their rules of engagement

**Travis's 1-page dashboard** reduces this to a single page for agile contexts. His own caveat is the important bit: it's a dashboard, not a plan. It stands in the same relation to a full test plan as the Business Model Canvas does to a business plan — it covers the highlights and deliberately omits detail. You still need the screener, the consent form, the discussion guide, and the post-test questionnaire as separate artefacts.

**Writing tasks well.** This is where most test plans fail:
- Give a **scenario with a goal**, not a set of instructions. "You want to send €50 to a friend" beats "click Transfer, then enter the amount."
- **Never use interface language** in the task. If the task says "find the Settings menu", you've told them where to look and you're testing nothing.
- Make it **realistic and motivated** — tasks should be things a real user would actually want to do.
- **One goal per task.** Compound tasks make it impossible to tell which part failed.
- Define **success criteria before the session**, in writing. Deciding afterward whether something counted as success is how bias enters.

**Avoiding bias:**
- **Leading questions** — "Was that easy?" gets a yes. "How was that?" gets an answer.
- **Confirmation bias** — you notice the evidence supporting what you already believed. Countermeasure: define what would disconfirm your hypothesis, in advance.
- **Helping too soon.** Silence is uncomfortable and the urge to rescue is strong. Let people struggle; the struggle is the finding. Agree a rule beforehand for when you'll intervene.
- **Social desirability** — participants want to please you and will soften criticism. Emphasise repeatedly that you didn't design it (even if you did) and that criticism is useful.
- **Observer effect** — people behave differently when watched. Can't be eliminated, only reduced by putting people at ease.
- **Order effects** — task sequence affects performance. Counterbalance across participants where it matters.

**Pilot every study.** One session with a colleague or a friendly user. You will find broken tasks, ambiguous wording and timing problems, and it costs one session to avoid wasting eight.

author: Kerry Rodden (Google Ventures), Jakob Nielsen
key_points: HEART: Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task success
Goals → Signals → Metrics is the process; skipping to metrics is the classic mistake
You're not meant to use all five HEART categories — choosing which don't apply is part of the method
Success rate is crude, robust, and comprehensible to everyone. Partial success = 0.5.
SUS is the default satisfaction instrument; SEQ is the fast per-task one; UMUX-Lite is the short version of SUS
If nobody would act differently based on a number, don't track it
still_relevant: HEART is standard vocabulary in product organisations and worth knowing cold — being able to walk through Goals-Signals-Metrics is a strong interview answer to 'how do you measure design impact?'. That question has become near-universal, and it's the one designers most often fumble.
title: UX metrics (clustered: Google HEART framework, NN/g success rate, CXL satisfaction measures)
summary:
Three sources on measuring UX. The HEART framework is the one to internalise — it's widely used in industry and it comes up in interviews constantly.

**Google's HEART framework** (Rodden, Hutchinson and Fu at Google Research). Five categories of user-centred metric:
- **H**appiness — attitudinal satisfaction. Survey-based: satisfaction scores, NPS, perceived ease of use.
- **E**ngagement — depth of involvement. Visits per user per week, sessions, actions per session.
- **A**doption — new users of a product or feature in a given period.
- **R**etention — the rate at which existing users return over time.
- **T**ask success — efficiency, effectiveness and error rate. The classic usability metrics.

**The Goals–Signals–Metrics process, which is the actually useful half** and which people skip:
1. **Goals** — what is success for this feature, for the user and the business? Get the team to agree here first; this is usually where disagreement surfaces.
2. **Signals** — what user behaviours or attitudes would indicate that goal being met or missed? Signals should be things that actually change when the goal is met.
3. **Metrics** — how do you turn those signals into something trackable on a dashboard?

Going straight to metrics without goals and signals is how teams end up optimising numbers that don't mean anything.

**Important caveat on HEART:** you are not supposed to use all five. Pick the categories that fit the product. Engagement is meaningless for a tax-filing tool where less time spent is better. Retention is meaningless for a one-time-use service. Choosing which categories *don't* apply is part of using the framework correctly.

**Success rate** (Nielsen): the simplest usability metric and the most robust. Percentage of tasks completed successfully. Count partial success as 0.5 if you need the nuance. Crude, but it's comprehensible to anyone in the organisation, comparable across studies, and hard to argue with.

**Measuring satisfaction** — the main instruments:
- **SUS (System Usability Scale)** — 10 items, score out of 100, decades of benchmark data behind it. The default choice.
- **SEQ (Single Ease Question)** — one 7-point question after each task. Fast and surprisingly predictive.
- **NPS** — one question, widely used, methodologically criticised (see below)
- **CSAT** — straightforward satisfaction rating
- **UMUX-Lite** — 2 items, correlates well with SUS at a fraction of the length

**The metric selection rule:** every metric should be tied to a decision. If nobody would act differently based on the number, don't track it.

author: Jeff Sauro (MeasuringU) and others
key_points: SEQ: one 7-point question per task. Average is 5.5, so 5.0 is below average.
SUS: 10 items, scored 0-100, average is 68. Not a percentage.
Always follow a rating with 'why did you give it that score?'
NASA-TLX measures cognitive workload across six dimensions — valuable for complex B2B tools
NPS is a loyalty indicator, not a usability metric. Treating it as one is a category error.
Default combination: SEQ per task, SUS at the end
still_relevant: All current. Knowing SUS's benchmark of 68 and SEQ's 5.5 is genuinely useful — it lets you say 'that's below average' rather than 'that seems okay', which changes conversations. NASA-TLX is the one most teams overlook: cognitive load is often the real problem in enterprise and B2B tools, and few teams have any instrument for measuring it.
title: Measurement instruments (clustered: SEQ, SUS, NASA-TLX, ASQ, NPS, magnitude estimation)
summary:
Five standardised instruments. Knowing which to reach for is a genuine differentiator, because most designers only know NPS and NPS is the weakest of them.

**SEQ (Single Ease Question)** — "Overall, how difficult or easy was this task?" on a 7-point scale, asked immediately after each task.
- One question, so almost no participant burden, which means you can use it after every task without fatigue
- Correlates well with task completion and time on task
- Benchmark: average is around **5.5**, so a 5.0 is below average even though it looks like a pass. This is the single most useful fact about SEQ and it stops people over-reading mediocre scores.
- Ask it **immediately** after the task, before any discussion contaminates the impression
- Follow the rating with "why did you give it that score?" — the number is the metric, the answer is the insight

**SUS (System Usability Scale)** — 10 alternating positive/negative items, 5-point scales, scored 0-100 (not a percentage). Decades of benchmark data: **68 is average**, above 80 is good, below 50 is poor. Administered after the whole session, not per task. Free, short, robust across domains. The default whole-product satisfaction instrument.

**ASQ (After-Scenario Questionnaire)** — three items after each scenario, covering ease of completion, time taken, and adequacy of support information. IBM-originated. More granular than SEQ, more burden. Useful when you specifically care about whether help and documentation were adequate.

**NASA-TLX** — measures perceived **workload** across six dimensions: mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, performance, effort and frustration. Originally from aviation human factors. Use it where cognitive load is the actual concern: complex professional tools, safety-critical interfaces, multi-step configuration. Overkill for consumer apps, genuinely valuable for enterprise and B2B work.

**NPS (Net Promoter Score)** — "How likely are you to recommend this to a friend or colleague?" 0-10, then promoters (9-10) minus detractors (0-6). Sauro's assessment is worth carrying:
- It's *fine* as a loyalty indicator and it's not the disaster some critics claim
- But it's **not a usability metric**, and treating it as one is a category error. It measures brand sentiment and overall relationship, not whether people can complete tasks.
- The 0-10 collapse into three buckets throws away information
- It's heavily influenced by factors outside the product entirely — price, support, brand, recent news
- Its dominance in industry is a function of executive familiarity, not psychometric quality

**Magnitude estimation** — participants assign numbers to perceived intensity with no fixed scale, producing ratio-level data. Psychophysics technique, rarely used in practice, but useful to know exists when you need finer discrimination than a 7-point scale allows.

**The practical selection:** SEQ after each task, SUS at the end of the session, NASA-TLX if cognitive load is the question, NPS only if a stakeholder demands it and you've explained what it does and doesn't measure.

author: Steve Krug
key_points: 'Don't make me think' — every unanswered question is a cognitive tax
People scan, satisfice, and muddle through. Design for that, not for the rational reader.
Krug's Law: testing one user is 100% better than testing none
Three users, once a month, forever. Whole team watches. Fix the worst three things.
Instinct is to add a fix; removing or simplifying usually works better
Get rid of half the words, then half of what's left
still_relevant: Permanently. *Don't Make Me Think* is still the book to give a non-designer colleague who needs to understand why usability matters, and Krug's Law is the most effective counter to the no-budget objection you'll encounter. The free downloadable test script and consent forms on his site are still usable as-is.
title: Steve Krug — Usability, mostly (Don't Make Me Think / Rocket Surgery)
summary:
Krug's site, and the home of the free downloadable materials that accompany *Rocket Surgery Made Easy*. Referenced across several modules of this curriculum.

**The two books:**
- ***Don't Make Me Think*** (1st ed 2000, revised 2014) — the most widely read usability book ever written, and deservedly. Short, funny, and its core principle is in the title.
- ***Rocket Surgery Made Easy*** (2010) — the practical companion on running your own tests cheaply.

**Krug's central arguments:**

**"Don't make me think."** Every question a user has to stop and answer — *Is that clickable? Where am I? What does this mean?* — is a small cognitive tax. The cumulative weight of those taxes is what makes a product exhausting. Self-evident beats self-explanatory beats requiring explanation.

**We don't read pages, we scan them.** People satisfice rather than optimise: they pick the first reasonable option rather than the best one. They muddle through rather than figuring out how things work, and they keep muddling through indefinitely because it works well enough. Design for scanning and satisficing, not for the careful rational reader who doesn't exist.

**Krug's Law of usability testing:** *"Testing one user is 100 percent better than testing none."* This is the single most useful sentence in the discount-usability tradition and it's the answer to almost every "we don't have budget for research" objection.

**His prescription** from *Rocket Surgery*:
- **Three users, once a month**, every month, forever. A morning of testing, a debrief over lunch, fix the worst three things.
- **Do it yourself.** Don't wait for a specialist, a lab, or a budget line.
- **Whole team watches.** Live, in the room or on a stream. Watching someone fail with your design does more than any report.
- **Fix the most serious problems first**, and resist the urge to add things. His observation is that teams instinctively want to *add* a feature or a help text to fix a problem, when removing or simplifying usually works better.
- **Take away rather than add.** "Get rid of half the words on each page, then get rid of half of what's left."

**Why Krug still matters:** he made usability testing accessible to people without research training, at a time when it was presented as a specialist lab discipline. The whole guerrilla and discount-usability tradition descends from this.

author: UXPA Magazine, UXmatters, Shawn Lawton Henry (uiAccess)
key_points: The standard usability protocol assumes a non-disabled, working-age, tech-comfortable participant
Older adults: trusted-intermediary recruiting, more time, and actively counter self-blame
Children: guardian consent AND child assent; shorter sessions; observe rather than ask
Disabled participants: their own assistive tech, their own configuration, substantially more time
Recruit across a range of AT expertise — experts and novices find different problems
Accessibility testing belongs in regular rounds, not as a late separate stage
still_relevant: More relevant every year. The **European Accessibility Act came into force in June 2025**, making accessibility a legal requirement for a wide range of digital products and services sold in the EU. Combined with WCAG 2.2 and EN 301 549, accessibility has moved from good practice to compliance. Being able to speak credibly about inclusive research, not just WCAG checklists, is a real differentiator in the European market right now.
title: Testing with specific populations (clustered: older adults, children, accessibility)
summary:
Three sources on adapting usability testing for populations that standard protocols serve badly. This is the part of the course most often skipped and it's disproportionately valuable, because the standard protocol quietly assumes a non-disabled, working-age, tech-comfortable participant.

**Older adults:**
- Recruit through **trusted intermediaries** — community organisations, clubs, existing relationships. Cold recruiting works poorly.
- **Allow more time.** Not because of slower cognition necessarily, but because sessions involve more rapport-building, more context-setting, and less familiarity with the testing format itself.
- **Test in their environment** where possible. Their own device, their own chair, their own lighting, their own glasses.
- Watch for **self-blame**, which is much stronger in this group. "I'm just not good with computers" is a learned response and it suppresses honest feedback. Counter it explicitly and repeatedly.
- **Sensory and motor considerations**: text size, contrast, target size, and no assumptions about fine pointer control or multi-touch gestures.
- Avoid **jargon and metaphors** that assume a particular technology history. "Hamburger menu" means nothing; neither does "drag and drop" to someone who's only used touch.

**Children:**
- **Guardian consent plus the child's own assent.** Both. A child who doesn't want to participate doesn't participate, regardless of what the parent agreed.
- **Sessions must be shorter** — attention spans vary enormously by age and 20-30 minutes is often the ceiling.
- Children are **highly susceptible to social desirability**. They want to please adults and will say what they think you want. Ask fewer opinion questions and observe more.
- **Think-aloud often doesn't work** with younger children. Observation and post-task questions work better.
- Never test a child alone — **a guardian or teacher present**, always. This is a safeguarding requirement, not a methodological preference.
- Age bands matter enormously. A 6-year-old and a 12-year-old are entirely different research populations.

**Participants with disabilities** (the uiAccess material, from Shawn Lawton Henry, who also worked on W3C/WAI guidance):
- **Recruit for a range of disabilities and a range of assistive-technology expertise.** A screen-reader expert and a recent screen-reader user will find completely different problems, and both matter.
- **Let people use their own assistive technology**, configured the way they normally configure it. Testing with your lab's default screen-reader setup tests your setup, not their experience.
- **Allow substantially more time.** Navigating a badly built interface with a screen reader can take many times longer.
- Ask about **accommodation needs before the session**, as a matter of course, and make the venue and format accessible by default.
- **Don't treat accessibility testing as a separate late-stage activity.** Including disabled participants in your regular rounds finds problems earlier and produces better designs for everyone.
- The facilitator needs at least basic familiarity with the assistive tech being used, or they'll misread normal operation as a problem and vice versa.

**The principle underneath all three:** the standard protocol encodes assumptions. Adapting it isn't a special accommodation, it's correcting for a default that was never neutral.

author: Smashing Magazine, ThoughtWorks
key_points: Mobile testing's core problem: capturing screen and hands together without distorting grip
A device in a stand loses the grip and thumb-reach data you probably wanted
Options: overhead camera, DIY sled rig, screen mirroring, or built-in recording plus face camera
Test with realistic interruptions and connection quality, not office wifi and full attention
still_relevant: Logistics have improved a lot. Remote unmoderated mobile testing (Maze, UserTesting, Lookback) handles screen and front-camera capture automatically, and most platforms now show tap locations. The physical rig problem mostly disappears for remote work. The context point — realistic conditions, not lab conditions — is the durable part.
title: Mobile usability testing (clustered: Smashing guide, ThoughtWorks recording setup, mydevice.io)
summary:
Practical logistics for testing on mobile, where the mechanics are genuinely harder than desktop.

**The specific problems mobile creates:**
- You can't see the screen and the participant's hands at once without a rig
- Screen recording on device often doesn't capture touch points, so you lose where they tapped
- Holding position, grip and thumb reach are part of what you're testing, so a device clamped in a stand loses real data
- Context matters more — mobile use happens while walking, in poor light, on bad connections, with interruptions

**The setups, cheapest first:**
- **Overhead camera or phone on an arm** pointed at the device. Cheap, shows hands and screen together, slightly unnatural grip.
- **Sled or harness rig** — a lightweight frame holding a camera above a handheld device. Preserves natural grip. ThoughtWorks' guerrilla approach is essentially a DIY version of this.
- **Screen mirroring** (AirPlay, scrcpy for Android, QuickTime for iOS over cable) — clean screen capture, but you lose the hands unless you also film them.
- **Built-in screen recording** plus a separate camera on the participant's face for expression.

**mydevice.io** — utility that reports the actual capabilities of the device you visit it from: viewport size, pixel ratio, OS, touch support. Useful for confirming what you're actually testing on rather than what you assume.

**The design implications of mobile context**, which matter more than the rig: test with realistic interruptions, on realistic connections, and where possible in realistic settings. A flow that works flawlessly on office wifi with full attention can fail completely on a train.

key_points: First-click testing: first-click accuracy strongly predicts eventual task success
Unmoderated gives you scale and speed; you lose the ability to ask why
Sensible pattern: unmoderated to locate problems, moderated to understand them
still_relevant: UsabilityHub **rebranded to Lyssna in 2023**; the guides moved with it. Competitors: Maze, Optimal Workshop, UserTesting. First-click testing is a genuinely underused method for the cost.
title: UsabilityHub / Lyssna guides and examples
summary:
Vendor guide library covering the unmoderated remote test types: five-second tests, first-click tests, preference tests, navigation tests and design surveys.

**The method worth extracting: first-click testing.** Show a design, give a task, record where they click first. The finding behind it is strong — users who get the first click right succeed at the task far more often than those who don't. It isolates findability and the information scent of your labels, cheaply and at scale.

**What unmoderated remote testing is good for:** large samples, quick turnaround, geographic spread, no scheduling, and quantitative comparison between designs.

**What it's bad for:** understanding *why*. There's no follow-up question, no probing, no noticing that the participant misread the task. You get the what without the why, which is exactly the tradeoff the moderated/unmoderated choice always involves.

**The sensible combination:** unmoderated for breadth and numbers, moderated for depth and explanation. Run unmoderated first to find where the problems are, then moderated to understand them.

author: Jeff Sauro (MeasuringU), Neil Turner (UXM)
key_points: Severity = frequency × impact × persistence. Any one factor alone misleads.
Standard scale 0-4, from 'not a problem' to 'catastrophe'
Multiple independent raters, then reconcile — single-rater severity is noisy
Add effort-to-fix: severity alone isn't a plan. Severity × effort gives you the sequence.
Lead the report with the top three issues, never with methodology
A 20-second clip of a user failing beats any paragraph you could write
'4 of 6 participants' beats 'several users'
still_relevant: Fully. The reporting advice is the part to actually act on — this is where research effort most commonly gets wasted, and 'my findings didn't lead to changes' is a very common frustration. Modern tooling (Dovetail, Condens, Marvin) makes clip-based reporting trivial, which removes the last excuse for text-only reports. AI-assisted tagging of session transcripts is now standard for larger studies.
title: Rating severity and running usability reviews (clustered: MeasuringU, UX for the Masses)
summary:
What to do after the sessions. Severity rating is how findings become decisions, and it's where most junior research work falls down — producing a flat list of thirty problems with no guidance on what to do first.

**The three factors severity combines** (Nielsen's formulation, which Sauro builds on):
1. **Frequency** — how many users hit it? Is it common or rare?
2. **Impact** — how badly does it block them? Annoyance or complete failure?
3. **Persistence** — is it a one-time learning bump, or does it obstruct people every single time?

A problem that's rare but catastrophic and a problem that's universal but trivial both score oddly on any single factor. The combination is what makes the rating meaningful.

**The standard 0-4 scale:**
- **0** — not a usability problem
- **1** — cosmetic; fix if there's spare time
- **2** — minor; low priority
- **3** — major; important to fix, high priority
- **4** — usability catastrophe; imperative to fix before release

**How to rate more reliably** (Sauro's practical points):
- **Multiple independent raters**, then reconcile. A single rater's severity scores are noisy.
- **Combine severity with frequency data** from the sessions rather than rating from memory
- **Add a business-impact dimension** where relevant — a problem in the checkout flow matters more than an equally severe problem in account settings
- **Add effort-to-fix.** Severity alone doesn't produce a plan. Severity × effort gives you the quick wins to ship immediately and the big rocks to schedule.

**On usability reviews (expert review) from the UXM piece:** distinct from heuristic evaluation in being less formal and more holistic — an experienced practitioner walks the product and documents problems, using heuristics as a lens rather than a checklist. Fast, cheap, no recruiting. Same limitation as always: it's expert prediction, not user observation, so it generates false positives and misses domain-specific problems.

**Reporting so findings actually get used:**
- **Lead with the top three issues**, not with methodology. Nobody reads past page two of a research report.
- **Show, don't tell** — a 20-second video clip of a user failing beats three paragraphs describing it, and it's the single most effective tool you have for making findings land
- **Pair every problem with a recommendation** and a severity rating
- **Quantify where you honestly can** — "4 of 6 participants" is more actionable than "several users"
- **Separate findings from recommendations** clearly, so the evidence stands independently of your proposed solution
- Get the team to **watch sessions live**. A report is a poor substitute for having seen it happen.

author: Jonathan Shariat
key_points: Usability failures in safety-critical systems injure and kill people
Tragic Design's categories: design that kills, angers, saddens, excludes
The strongest argument available for why testing isn't optional
Caveat: medical errors are multi-causal; single-cause framing oversimplifies
still_relevant: Yes, and the stakes have widened. AI-driven decision support in healthcare, finance and public services has created a new category of the same problem, where the interface design determines whether a human can meaningfully review an automated recommendation or just clicks through it. Automation bias is the current form of this argument.
title: How Bad UX Killed Jenny
summary:
A case study about a teenage cancer patient who died after a medication error that a badly designed medical software interface contributed to. Shariat later expanded this work into the book *Tragic Design* (O'Reilly, 2017, with Cynthia Savard Saucier).

**The argument:** design decisions have consequences beyond conversion rates and satisfaction scores. In healthcare, aviation, finance, automotive and government systems, usability failures injure and kill people. The case is used to argue that designers bear real professional responsibility, not merely aesthetic preference.

**The categories the book develops:**
- Design that **kills** — safety-critical interface failures
- Design that **angers** — exclusion, alienation, insulting defaults
- Design that **saddens** — insensitive handling of grief, loss, and difficult life events
- Design that **excludes** — inaccessibility and unconsidered assumptions about users

**Why it belongs in a usability testing module:** it's the strongest available argument for why testing is not optional. The stakes framing changes the conversation with stakeholders who treat research as a nice-to-have.

**A caution on the specific case:** medical errors are almost always multi-causal — staffing, training, process, fatigue and interface design compound. Presenting a single interface as the cause of a death oversimplifies, and the article has been criticised on those grounds. The broader point about interface design in safety-critical systems is sound and well-documented elsewhere (the Therac-25 radiation overdoses being the classic case study).

author: Eric Ries, Toyota, Jeff Gothelf
key_points: Lean UX descends from the Toyota Production System via Lean Startup
Overproduction is the designer's waste: more design, more detail, earlier than needed
MVP means the smallest thing that lets you learn — an experiment, not a stripped-down v1
Outcomes over outputs. The deliverable isn't the point; the behaviour change is.
Hypothesis format: We believe [X] for [Y] will achieve [Z]; we'll know when we see [signal]
Shared understanding beats documentation — teams that watched the research need fewer reports
Weakest for zero-to-one work and regulated domains where you can't iterate publicly
still_relevant: Core vocabulary in product organisations. 'Outcomes over outputs' and the hypothesis format are both worth being able to deploy naturally in interviews — they signal that you think in terms of impact rather than deliverables, which is the main thing separating mid from senior in most rubrics. Gothelf and Seiden's later *Sense and Respond* and *Outcomes Over Output* develop the argument further.
title: Lean UX and its lineage (clustered: Lean Startup, Toyota Production System, Jeff Gothelf)
summary:
Three sources tracing where Lean UX came from. The Toyota link is the genuinely interesting inclusion, because most designers use Lean vocabulary without knowing it descends from 1950s manufacturing.

**Toyota Production System** — the origin. Two pillars:
- **Just-in-Time** — produce only what's needed, when it's needed, in the amount needed. Inventory is waste because it hides problems.
- **Jidoka** — "automation with a human touch". Machines stop themselves when a defect occurs, so problems surface immediately rather than propagating downstream. The andon cord that any worker can pull to halt the line comes from this.

Plus the **seven wastes** (muda), of which the design-relevant ones are overproduction, waiting, and defects. **Overproduction is the one that matters most for designers**: producing more design than is needed, in more detail than is needed, before it's needed. Every fully-specified screen for a feature that gets cut is inventory.

**The Lean Startup** (Eric Ries, 2011) applied this to product:
- **Build-Measure-Learn** as the core loop, optimised for cycle time
- **MVP** — the smallest thing that lets you learn, *not* the smallest shippable product. This is the most widely misunderstood term in product work. An MVP is an experiment, not a stripped-down v1.
- **Validated learning** — progress measured in what you've learned, not in what you've built
- **Pivot or persevere** — decide explicitly and on evidence, at intervals

**Lean UX** (Jeff Gothelf with Josh Seiden, 2013) brought this to design practice:
- **Outcomes over outputs.** The deliverable isn't the point; the change in user behaviour is. This is the single most useful idea in the book and the one most worth carrying into interviews.
- **Assumptions made explicit.** State what you believe, rank by risk, test the riskiest first. A design is a set of bets.
- **Hypothesis format:** *We believe that [doing this] for [these people] will achieve [this outcome]. We'll know we're right when we see [this signal].*
- **Shared understanding over documentation.** A team that watched the research together needs less documentation than one that receives a report.
- **Cross-functional collaboration** replaces designers producing specs and throwing them over the wall.
- **Reduce waste** — if a deliverable doesn't advance learning or shared understanding, don't make it.

**The honest criticisms**, worth holding:
- "MVP" has been widely abused as cover for shipping unfinished, bad products
- Speed pressure can crowd out the slower generative research that produces genuinely new directions
- Lean works best with existing products and measurable behaviour; it's weaker for zero-to-one work and for domains where you can't iterate publicly (medical devices, regulated finance)
- "Outcomes over outputs" is easy to say and hard to practise in organisations that fund and measure teams by output

author: Smashing, Dotmocracy, Christina Wodtke (Eleganthack), IxDF
key_points: Frame research plans around stakeholder questions and decisions, not around your methods
Their untested beliefs make excellent research questions — and involving them creates ownership
Getting a skeptic to observe one session converts better than any report
Dot voting: vote silently and simultaneously or the first voter anchors everyone
Dot voting favours safe familiar options — discuss the outliers, don't just take the winner
Findings presented as narrative stick; findings presented as lists don't
Guerrilla research is unrepresentative by design — fine for directional questions, not for investment decisions
still_relevant: The stakeholder and facilitation skills are what separate designers who get things shipped from designers who produce good work nobody acts on. Worth weighting heavily. Remote workshop facilitation in FigJam or Miro is now the default, and dot voting is built into both. Guerrilla research has partly been displaced by cheap unmoderated remote testing, which gives you better sampling for similar cost and effort.
title: Stakeholders and workshops (clustered: Smashing UX research plan, dot voting, presenting with story, guerrilla research)
summary:
Four sources on the political and facilitative side of research — getting it funded, getting decisions made, and getting findings acted on.

**Writing a research plan stakeholders actually support** (Smashing):
- **Frame around their questions, not your methods.** Stakeholders don't care that you'll run a diary study; they care whether the new onboarding will reduce churn. Lead with the decision the research informs.
- **State what decisions the research will enable.** If you can't name one, question whether to run it.
- **Involve them early** — ask what they want to learn, and what they believe is true. Their untested beliefs make excellent research questions and involving them creates ownership.
- **Be explicit about cost, time and what you need from them** (access to customers, a room, their attendance at a session)
- **Invite them to observe.** The single most effective conversion tool for research skeptics is watching one user struggle with something they were sure was obvious.

**Dot voting** (Dotmocracy) — group prioritisation. Each participant gets N dots to place on options; highest total wins. Cheap, fast, visible, and gets quiet people's views counted.
- Rough guide: dots ≈ options ÷ 3
- **Vote silently and simultaneously**, or the first voter anchors everyone else. This is the rule people break most.
- Allow stacking multiple dots on one option to express intensity, or forbid it to force spread — decide deliberately
- **It's an input, not a decision.** Popularity isn't correctness, and dot voting systematically favours safe familiar options over good unfamiliar ones. Use it to surface the group's view, then discuss the outliers, which are often where the interesting ideas are.

**Presenting with story** (Christina Wodtke) — research findings presented as a list of problems get forgotten. Presented as a narrative about a person trying to do something and being obstructed, they stick. Structure: a character with a goal, an obstacle, consequences, and a change that resolves it. Wodtke's broader point is that persuasion in organisations runs on narrative, and designers who can't tell a story lose arguments to people with worse evidence.

**Guerrilla research** (IxDF) — fast, cheap, informal research: approaching people in public, short sessions, minimal recruiting.
- **Pros:** very cheap, very fast, needs no budget approval, breaks the "we have no research" deadlock, good for early directional questions
- **Cons:** unrepresentative samples (you get whoever is in that coffee shop), short sessions limit depth, no context of use, ethically thinner if consent is handled casually, and results are easy for skeptics to dismiss
- **When it's right:** early-stage directional questions, testing comprehension of a concept or label, when the alternative is genuinely no research at all
- **When it isn't:** specialist or B2B audiences (your users are not in the coffee shop), anything requiring domain expertise, anything you'll base a major investment on
- **Handle consent properly even when informal.** Brief verbal consent is still consent; skipping it isn't made acceptable by the setting.

author: CXL, Smashing Magazine, VWO
key_points: Peeking and stopping early is the most common and most damaging error — fix sample size and duration in advance
Statistical significance ≠ business significance. Do the arithmetic on whether the lift is worth the cost.
p < 0.05 does not mean a 95% chance the variant is better
Calculate sample size up front from baseline rate, minimum detectable effect, and power
Run full business cycles; weekday and weekend traffic differ
Watch for novelty effects — segment new vs returning users
Most tests are inconclusive. Published case studies are survivorship-biased marketing.
A/B testing is a local optimiser: it walks you uphill, it can't tell you you're on the wrong hill
Usability testing gives you why with 5 users; A/B gives you which with thousands
still_relevant: Statistics are permanent; tooling has changed. VWO and Optimizely still exist, but experimentation has largely moved in-house at larger companies with feature-flag platforms (LaunchDarkly, Statsig, GrowthBook) running it. Bayesian approaches have gained ground over frequentist for commercial testing partly because they handle the peeking problem more gracefully. Worth knowing the term if it comes up. Regulated industries — finance, health, insurance — are a special case: what you're permitted to experiment on is often legally constrained, which is its own interesting design problem.
title: A/B testing (clustered: Smashing ultimate guide, CXL statistics, VWO case studies, KlientBoost)
summary:
Four sources on split testing. CXL's statistics piece is the one that matters — most A/B testing content teaches the mechanics and skips the statistics, which is exactly backwards, because the statistics are where people go wrong.

**What A/B testing is:** randomly split traffic between two or more variants, measure a defined conversion metric, determine whether the difference is real or noise.

**What it's good for:** optimising within a known design direction, settling disagreements with evidence, and measuring real behaviour at scale rather than stated preference.

**What it's bad for:** anything requiring a large change, anything with low traffic, and understanding *why* a variant won. A/B testing is a local optimiser — it walks you uphill from where you are, and it cannot tell you that you're on the wrong hill.

**The statistics people get wrong, which is most of it:**

- **Peeking.** Checking results repeatedly and stopping when significance appears massively inflates false positives. If you check daily and stop at the first p < 0.05, your actual error rate is far above 5%. **Decide the sample size and duration in advance and don't stop early.** This is the single most common and most damaging error in commercial A/B testing.
- **Statistical significance is not business significance.** A statistically significant 0.2% lift may not be worth the engineering cost. Run the arithmetic.
- **p < 0.05 does not mean 95% chance the variant is better.** It means: if there were truly no difference, you'd see a result this extreme less than 5% of the time. Different claim, and the misreading leads to overconfidence.
- **Sample size must be calculated up front**, from your baseline conversion rate, the minimum effect you care about detecting, and your desired power (usually 80%). Small effects need very large samples — detecting a 1% relative lift takes enormous traffic.
- **Run for full business cycles**, minimum one to two weeks. Weekday and weekend traffic behave differently, as do paydays and campaign periods. Stopping mid-cycle biases the result.
- **Multiple comparisons.** Testing many variants or many metrics at once inflates false positives. Correct for it, or pre-register your primary metric and treat the rest as exploratory.
- **The novelty effect.** Returning users react to change as change. Early results can reverse as the novelty fades. Segment new vs returning users.
- **Most tests are inconclusive**, and that's normal. Published case studies are heavily survivorship-biased — you see the 30% lifts, not the hundreds of flat results.

**On VWO's case studies specifically:** vendor-published success stories are marketing. They're useful for pattern inspiration and useless as evidence — the methodology is rarely disclosed, failures are never published, and the incentive to report favourable results is obvious. The "do human photos increase conversions?" piece is a good example: sometimes yes, sometimes no, entirely dependent on context, and a single case study tells you nothing generalisable.

**The relationship to usability testing:** they answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other. **Usability testing tells you why something fails, with 5 users. A/B testing tells you which variant wins, with thousands.** Qualitative to generate the hypothesis, quantitative to test it. Running A/B tests without qualitative input means testing arbitrary guesses.

author: UsabilityHub, Jeff Sauro
key_points: Preference testing measures appeal, not usability. Never conflate them.
People frequently prefer the design they perform worse with
The forced choice is the metric; 'why did you choose that?' is the insight
With n=20, a 60/40 split is not distinguishable from chance — use a binomial test
Detecting a modest preference reliably needs well over 100 responses
still_relevant: Method current, tool rebranded to Lyssna. The statistical point about under-powered preference tests is the thing worth carrying — declaring a winner from a 60/40 split at n=20 is extremely common and simply wrong.
title: Preference and concept testing (clustered: UsabilityHub guides, MeasuringU on preference data)
summary:
Show people two or more designs, ask which they prefer and why. Simple, cheap, and easy to over-interpret.

**What it's actually good for:** visual direction, brand perception, first-impression appeal, and settling internal aesthetic arguments with something better than seniority.

**What it can't tell you:** whether people can *use* it. Stated preference and measured performance diverge routinely — people frequently prefer the design they perform worse with. This is the same say/do gap as everywhere else. Never treat preference data as a usability finding.

**Always ask why.** The forced choice is the metric; the explanation is the insight. A 60/40 split tells you very little on its own, and the reasons behind it often reveal that both options fail in the same way.

**Sauro's statistical point**, which is the useful part: preference data is binary and you can test it properly. For a two-option preference test, a **binomial test** tells you whether a split is distinguishable from chance. The practical implication is sobering — with 20 participants, a 60/40 split is **not** statistically distinguishable from a coin flip. You need substantially larger samples than people assume to make confident claims from preference data, and teams routinely declare winners from splits that are pure noise.

**Sample size guidance:** small samples (under ~30) can only detect large preferences. If you want to detect a modest preference reliably, you need well over 100 responses. Cheap remote tools make this achievable, so there's little excuse for under-powering it.

Define the success metric early — it's the most reliable differentiator and almost nobody does it
Assessed on problem-framing, business awareness, prioritisation, communication and collaborativeness

title: Product Design Exercises We Use At WeWork Interviews
summary:
Written by a designer who ran hiring at WeWork, later expanded into the book *Solving Product Design Exercises* — one of the more useful interview-prep books for product design roles.

**The exercise format:** a broad prompt ("design a solution to help people find a new apartment"), 30-60 minutes, worked through with the interviewer.

**The structure he recommends:**
1. **Clarify scope and constraints.** Ask questions. Narrow the problem explicitly.
2. **Identify the user and their goal.** Pick one segment and say why.
3. **Define success** — what metric would tell you this worked? Naming this early separates strong candidates from the rest, and almost nobody does it unprompted.
4. **Explore multiple solutions.** Breadth before depth.
5. **Choose one and justify it** against the constraints and the success metric.
6. **Sketch the key flow.**
7. **Name tradeoffs and next steps** — what you'd validate, and how.

**What's being assessed** (his framing as the person on the other side of the table):
- Can you turn a vague prompt into a defined problem?
- Do you consider business goals, not only user needs?
- Can you prioritise and say no to things?
- Do you communicate clearly under mild pressure?
- Are you pleasant to work through a problem with?

**His most useful specific advice:** **define the success metric early.** Most candidates jump to solutions. Naming how you'd know it worked demonstrates product thinking rather than craft alone, and it's the most reliable single differentiator in these exercises.

**Common failure modes he names:** designing for yourself, ignoring business context, solving the whole world instead of one problem, and going quiet while thinking.

title: Gestalt principles and the principles of design (clustered, 6 sources)
summary:
Six overlapping sources. Clustered hard because they all cover the same ground, and the underlying material is genuinely foundational.

**Gestalt psychology** came out of 1920s Berlin (Wertheimer, Köhler, Koffka) and describes how human perception organises visual information into wholes rather than parts. The core claim: *the whole is other than the sum of its parts* — usually misquoted as "greater than". These aren't style rules, they're descriptions of how perception works, which is why they hold across cultures and eras.

**The principles that matter for UI:**

- **Proximity** — things placed near each other are perceived as related. The single most powerful and most underused tool in interface design. Most layout problems are proximity problems: a label sitting equidistant between two fields, a caption closer to the wrong image, form sections with uniform gaps. Fix spacing before you reach for borders, boxes or colour.
- **Similarity** — things that look alike are perceived as belonging to the same group. Shared colour, shape, size, or type treatment implies shared function. The corollary matters more: if two things look the same, users expect them to behave the same. Inconsistent styling of clickable vs non-clickable elements is a similarity violation.
- **Common region** — elements inside a shared boundary are grouped. Cards, panels, fieldsets. Stronger than proximity, which is why cards became ubiquitous.
- **Closure** — we complete incomplete shapes. Lets you imply structure without drawing every line. Why a table works without full gridlines.
- **Continuity** — the eye follows lines and curves, and prefers continuous paths. Underpins alignment: things on a shared axis read as a sequence.
- **Figure/ground** — we separate an object from its background. Determines what reads as foreground content vs surface. Modals, overlays and elevation all depend on it.
- **Common fate** — things moving together are perceived as related. The motion principle, and increasingly relevant as interfaces animate.
- **Prägnanz (simplicity / good figure)** — we interpret ambiguous images in the simplest way available. The reason overly complex layouts feel effortful.

**Symmetry and asymmetry** (the Sympli piece): symmetry reads as stable, formal and calm; asymmetry reads as dynamic and creates tension that directs attention. Neither is better. Symmetrical layouts risk being static and unremarkable; asymmetrical ones need deliberate balance or they read as mistakes. The useful concept is **visual weight** — size, colour, contrast and density all contribute, and balance is about weight rather than mirroring.

**The classic elements and principles of design** (Canva and 99designs versions) — the art-school inheritance:
- **Elements** (the raw material): line, shape, colour, texture, space, form, value, type
- **Principles** (how you arrange them): balance, contrast, emphasis/hierarchy, movement, pattern/repetition, rhythm, proportion/scale, unity, white space

**The one principle to take most seriously: contrast creates hierarchy.** If everything is emphasised, nothing is. Most weak interface designs fail here first — insufficient differentiation between levels — and the fix is usually to weaken the secondary elements rather than strengthen the primary ones.

**And the honest note about white space:** it isn't empty, it's structural. It's also the first thing stakeholders ask you to fill. Having the Gestalt vocabulary lets you defend it as function rather than taste, which is a practical negotiating advantage.

still_relevant: The scepticism is the durable content. Accessibility requirements have hardened considerably — the European Accessibility Act (in force June 2025) makes contrast compliance a legal matter for many products in the EU, and WCAG 2.2 added requirements around focus appearance. title: Colour and emotion (clustered: Creative Bloq, Daily Infographic, Plutchik's wheel, Plutchik's postulates)
summary:
Four sources on colour and emotion. Worth reading with scepticism, and the scepticism is the most useful thing to take away.

**The standard claims** you'll see in every colour psychology infographic: red is urgent and appetite-stimulating, blue is trustworthy and calm, green is natural and financial, yellow is optimistic and attention-grabbing, black is luxurious, white is clean, purple is premium or spiritual.

**Why to treat this carefully:**

- **Colour associations are heavily culture-dependent.** White signals purity and weddings in much of Europe and North America, and mourning in parts of East Asia. Red is danger in Western contexts and luck and prosperity in China. If you're designing for markets beyond your own, the Western infographic is actively misleading.
- **Most popular colour psychology is under-evidenced.** It circulates as infographics citing other infographics. The rigorous research that exists shows much weaker and more context-dependent effects than the pop versions claim.
- **Context dominates hue.** The same blue reads differently in a banking app, a children's toy, and a horror game. Saturation, brightness, surrounding colours and the object itself all matter more than the hue in isolation.
- **Brand familiarity overrides association.** People don't think "green means growth" when they see Spotify; they think Spotify.

**What is actually reliable about colour:**
- **Contrast and legibility.** WCAG contrast ratios are measurable, testable and legally relevant. 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and UI components, at AA.
- **Never use colour as the only carrier of meaning.** Around 8% of men and 0.5% of women have some form of colour vision deficiency. Error states need icons or text, not just red. Chart series need patterns or labels, not just colour.
- **Consistency within a system** teaches meaning far more effectively than any innate association. If red consistently means destructive in your product, users learn it regardless of cultural baggage.
- **Colour creates hierarchy and grouping** — this is the Gestalt similarity principle, and it's the actually load-bearing use of colour in interfaces.

**Plutchik's wheel of emotions** — a genuine psychological model, distinct from the colour-psychology material it's filed next to. Eight primary emotions arranged as four opposing pairs: joy/sadness, trust/disgust, fear/anger, surprise/anticipation. Intensity varies radially (annoyance → anger → rage), and adjacent emotions combine into dyads (joy + trust = love). Plutchik's ten postulates frame emotions as evolved adaptive responses common across species. Useful as **vocabulary** for specifying a target emotional response more precisely than "delightful", which is what emotional design work usually needs. The colour assignments on the wheel are illustrative, not a colour-psychology claim.

The levels can conflict — naming which one a problem sits at sharpens critique

title: Emotional Design (Don Norman)
summary:
Book page for Norman's *Emotional Design: Why We Love (or Hate) Everyday Things* (2004), plus the companion TED talk. This is Norman's partial correction to his own earlier work — *The Design of Everyday Things* was about usability, and he later concluded he'd underweighted the role of emotion and aesthetics.

**The three levels of processing**, which is the framework worth knowing:

1. **Visceral** — immediate, pre-conscious, automatic. Appearance, first impressions, gut reaction. Operates before thought. Influenced by colour, form, texture, material, sound. This is where "beautiful" happens.
2. **Behavioural** — the experience of use. Function, performance, usability. Mostly not conscious either. This is where classic usability lives.
3. **Reflective** — conscious, considered, retrospective. Meaning, self-image, memory, the story you tell about the product. "What does owning this say about me?" Brand lives here, and so does most long-term attachment.

Good design has to work at all three levels, and they can conflict — a product can be beautiful and frustrating (visceral wins, behavioural fails), or functional and unloved (behavioural wins, reflective fails). Being able to name which level a problem sits at is genuinely useful in critique.

**Norman's central and counterintuitive claim: attractive things work better.** Positive affect broadens thinking, increases tolerance for minor difficulties, and makes people more creative at problem-solving. Negative affect narrows focus — useful for detail work and dangerous situations, unhelpful for exploration. So an attractive design doesn't merely feel nicer; it measurably changes how well people cope when things go slightly wrong.

**This is also the source of the "aesthetic-usability effect"** — users perceive attractive designs as more usable, and report fewer problems with them, even when measured performance is identical. The uncomfortable implication for researchers: aesthetics can mask usability problems in testing.

**Why it matters in this module specifically:** this is the theoretical justification for why "refining design" isn't decoration. Visual refinement does work, and Norman gives you the argument for it in terms a sceptical stakeholder can follow.
