title: Designers and code (clustered: W3Schools HTML formatting, 'The Unicorn' hybrid designer-developer, Toptal on how much to know)
summary:
The perennial "should designers code?" argument, plus a basic HTML reference.

**The honest answer, which these sources circle around:** you don't need to *write production code*, you need to *understand the medium you're designing for*. Those are different claims and conflating them fuels a decade-old argument that keeps going nowhere.

**What's genuinely worth understanding:**
- **The box model** — content, padding, border, margin. Explains most of what happens to your spacing in implementation.
- **Flexbox and Grid** — how modern layout actually works. If you understand these, your designs become buildable and your handoff conversations get shorter.
- **Responsive behaviour** — how things reflow, what breakpoints cost, why fixed heights cause problems
- **States** — hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error. Every interactive element has them and designers routinely deliver only the default.
- **Semantic HTML and the accessibility tree** — why heading order matters, why a div with a click handler isn't a button, what a screen reader actually announces. This is where the biggest accessibility failures originate, and it's the most valuable thing on this list.
- **Performance implications** — what a large image, a custom font, or a heavy animation costs

**What you don't need:** to build production components, manage state, write tests, or argue about frameworks.

**The "unicorn" framing** (Martinez's piece) — the designer-developer hybrid as a mythical, highly-sought creature. Worth treating with some suspicion. It's often used in job ads to ask for two salaries' worth of work at one salary, and being a mediocre generalist is usually a weaker position than being genuinely strong at one thing with fluency in the adjacent one. The valuable version is depth in design plus enough technical literacy to collaborate well.

**Why it matters more now:** design systems put designers and engineers in the same vocabulary — tokens, components, variants, states. Figma's variables map conceptually onto CSS custom properties. Dev Mode made handoff a shared surface rather than a throw-over-the-wall. And AI code generation means a designer with technical literacy can now produce a working prototype without an engineer, which shifts what "understanding the medium" is worth.

**W3Schools note:** fine for a quick syntax lookup, weaker on accessibility and modern best practice. **MDN Web Docs** is the better reference and it's free.

title: Layout grids and the 8-point system (clustered, 7 sources)
summary:
Seven sources on grids and spacing. Clustered because they converge on the same system, and it's a system worth knowing precisely because it's the practical foundation of every design system you'll work in.

**Why grids exist:** consistency, alignment, faster decisions, and buildability. A grid removes the need to make a fresh spacing judgment on every element. The time saved is real, but the bigger win is that arbitrary spacing is the single most common thing separating amateur from professional layout work.

**Grid anatomy:**
- **Columns** — the content areas. 12 is the web default because it divides cleanly by 2, 3, 4 and 6.
- **Gutters** — the space between columns
- **Margins** — the space outside the outermost columns
- **Rows and baseline grid** — vertical rhythm, mostly inherited from print and less rigidly applied on the web

**Grid types:**
- **Column grid** — the standard for web and app layout
- **Modular grid** — columns plus rows, forming modules. Good for dense, card-based or dashboard layouts.
- **Baseline grid** — horizontal lines at consistent intervals for text alignment. Powerful in print, awkward on the web because line heights and dynamic content fight it.
- **Hierarchical grid** — irregular, content-driven. Editorial work.

**The 8-point grid system** — the dominant convention in digital product design:
- All spacing and sizing values are multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64
- **4 is used as a half-step** for tight cases — icon padding, small gaps, type adjustments
- **Why 8:** most common screen dimensions divide by 8, it scales cleanly across density multipliers (@1x, @1.5x, @2x, @3x), and it dramatically reduces the decision space. Instead of choosing between 13px and 14px, you choose between 8 and 16.
- **The practical benefit is decision elimination.** You stop debating spacing and start noticing when something is actually wrong.

**Applying it well:**
- Use it for **padding, margins, gaps, and component dimensions**
- **Type is the common exception** — line heights and font sizes often follow their own modular scale rather than strict multiples of 8, and forcing them into it produces bad typography
- **Don't be dogmatic.** A 1px border or a 2px focus ring doesn't break the system. Optical alignment sometimes beats mathematical alignment — icons in particular often need nudging off-grid to *look* centred.
- **Spacing should be proportional to relationship** — this is Gestalt proximity in numeric form. Related elements get 8, related groups get 16, distinct sections get 32 or 48. Uniform spacing everywhere destroys hierarchy just as effectively as random spacing.

**Desktop vs mobile:** the "only rule" pieces reduce to content priority and touch targets. Mobile needs larger tap targets (44pt iOS / 48dp Android minimum), fewer columns (typically 4), tighter margins, and a single-column reading flow. Desktop can support denser information, hover states, and multi-column scanning.

**Responsive grids:** column count changes at breakpoints (commonly 4 mobile / 8 tablet / 12 desktop) while gutters and margins scale. The important habit is designing the *system* rather than three fixed layouts.

title: The Secret Law of Page Harmony
summary:
The most unusual piece in this module and the one most worth reading in full. It's about how medieval and Renaissance bookmakers positioned the text block on the page, and it turns out they were using a geometric system that predates printing, standard measurement units, and any of the tools we now consider essential.

**The Van de Graaf canon** — Dutch book designer J. A. van de Graaf published this in 1946 as a reconstruction of the method he believed medieval scribes used, derived by studying 15th-century manuscripts and incunabula. It's constructed with nothing but a straight edge, using a series of diagonals across the page spread.

**What it produces:** regardless of page proportion, the canon places the top-left corner of the text block **one-ninth from the top and one-ninth from the inner margin**. The text block ends up with the same proportions as the page itself, and sits in whole-unit relationships to it.

**Jan Tschichold** — the modernist typographer, and one of the most important figures in 20th-century book design — picked this up and refined it, calling his version with a 2:3 page ratio "the Golden Canon of book page construction as it was used during late Gothic times by the finest of scribes." He described the method as producing not a good book but *the perfect book*.

**The two things worth taking from it:**

1. **Margins are not wasted space; they're the structure.** The reason old books have those generous, apparently excessive margins is that the proportional relationship between text block and page is what creates the sense of harmony. When you crowd a layout to the edges to fit more in, you're not being efficient, you're removing the thing that made it feel composed.

2. **The relationship between container and content is what produces harmony**, not any absolute measurement. The canon works at any page size and any proportion, because it's about ratio. That's directly transferable to responsive design, where you also can't rely on absolute dimensions.

**The connection to modern practice:** this is the same idea as a modular scale, the same idea as proportional spacing systems, and the same idea as designing with ratios rather than fixed values. Understanding the print lineage makes the digital versions feel less arbitrary.

**Related:** the Villard de Honnecourt diagram (13th century, divides the page into twelfths) reaches an equivalent result by a different route, and Raúl Rosarivo's ninths-based method turns out to be mathematically the same as Van de Graaf's.

title: Responsive Design Best Practices
summary:
Babich's practical responsive checklist. Overlaps with the Toptal piece earlier in this archive, so treat as reinforcement.

**The practices that hold up:**
- Content priority first — decide what matters most, then let layout serve that across sizes
- Breakpoints driven by content, not by device models (which change constantly)
- Touch targets sized for fingers, not cursors
- Readable line length: roughly 45-75 characters regardless of viewport
- Images that scale and, ideally, are served at appropriate resolutions
- Navigation that adapts rather than just shrinks
- Test on real devices, not just resized browser windows

author: various
key_points: Bootstrap and Foundation solved a real problem: responsive grids were hard before flexbox and grid
Framework defaults produce homogeneous design — the Bootstrap-site look was a real phenomenon
Material Design is a full design language, not a CSS framework — and it's the Android platform convention
Modern CSS made the frameworks' core value proposition obsolete
Tailwind and utility-first largely displaced component frameworks; design systems replaced them for product work
Foundation is effectively discontinued; Bootstrap survives in enterprise and internal tools

still_relevant: Mostly historical. The durable lesson is about inherited design decisions, which applies equally to today's component libraries and to AI-generated UI — both produce competent, homogeneous output unless you intervene deliberately. That's arguably a sharper problem now than it was in the Bootstrap era. Material Design is the one thing in this cluster to actually keep current with.
title: CSS frameworks and responsive examples (clustered: Bootstrap, Foundation, Material, W3Schools RWD, showcases)
summary:
Seven sources on CSS frameworks and responsive showcases. This cluster has aged more than anything else earlier in this archive, so it's mostly worth understanding as context rather than as guidance.

**What these frameworks were for:** in the early 2010s, building a responsive grid from scratch was genuinely hard. Bootstrap (Twitter, 2011) and Foundation (ZURB, 2011) provided a ready-made 12-column responsive grid plus a component library. They solved a real problem and they solved it well.

**Bootstrap vs Foundation, the comparison of the era:** Bootstrap had the larger community and faster setup; Foundation was more flexible, more semantic, and more customisable. Bootstrap won decisively on adoption.

**The criticism that mattered and still matters:** framework defaults produce homogeneous design. There was a well-known period where an enormous number of sites were visibly Bootstrap sites — same navbar, same card, same button, same jumbotron. Using a framework without customising it means your product inherits someone else's design decisions wholesale.

**Material Design** is a different thing and shouldn't be lumped in. It's a full **design language** from Google (2014), not just a CSS framework — with a documented philosophy (material as a metaphor, bold graphic intentional, motion provides meaning), an extensive component spec, and platform implementations. It's now on Material 3 / Material You, with dynamic colour extracted from user wallpaper. Worth knowing well because it's the Android platform convention and comes up constantly in cross-platform work.

**What happened since:**
- **Utility-first CSS** (Tailwind, from 2017) largely displaced component frameworks for new work — composition from small utilities rather than pre-built components
- **Modern CSS made the frameworks' core value proposition obsolete.** Flexbox and Grid are native, well-supported, and better than any framework grid. Container queries went further.
- **Design systems replaced generic frameworks** for serious product work. Organisations build their own component libraries rather than adapting someone else's.
- **Headless component libraries** (Radix, Headless UI, React Aria) separated behaviour and accessibility from visual styling, which is closer to what designers actually wanted
- **Bootstrap still exists and is still widely used**, particularly in enterprise and internal tools where speed matters more than distinctiveness. Foundation was effectively discontinued — ZURB stopped active development.

**What's actually transferable:** the responsive showcases are dated as inspiration, but the underlying point holds. A framework is a set of design decisions someone else made. Adopt them deliberately or you'll ship their product's personality instead of yours.

title: Style guides and pattern libraries (clustered: Boagworld, Figma component library, Creative Bloq examples, Adobe XD template, UI-Patterns)
summary:
Five sources on documenting design decisions. The terminology here is used loosely across the industry, so getting the distinctions straight is worth doing.

**The vocabulary, from narrowest to broadest:**

| | Contains | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| **Style guide** | Colours, type, logo, spacing, tone of voice | What should things look and sound like? |
| **Pattern library** | Reusable interface patterns with usage guidance | When do I use which solution? |
| **Component library** | The actual built components, in code and/or in Figma | What do I assemble this from? |
| **Design system** | All of the above plus principles, governance, contribution process, and the team that maintains it | How do we work? |

The common mistake is calling a component library a design system. A Figma file full of components with no principles, no usage guidance, no governance and nobody maintaining it is a component library that will rot within a year.

**Boag's argument for why you should bother:**
- **Consistency at scale** — beyond a certain product size, consistency cannot be maintained by memory and goodwill
- **Speed** — you stop redesigning the same button
- **Shared vocabulary** — designers, engineers and PMs can name the same thing, which removes a surprising amount of friction
- **Onboarding** — new team members become productive faster
- **It surfaces inconsistency you didn't know you had.** The audit that precedes building one routinely finds twenty shades of grey and eleven button variants. That audit is often more valuable than the library.

**What makes one actually get used:**
- **Usage guidance, not just specimens.** "Here is the button" is less useful than "use the primary button for the single main action per screen; never two on one screen."
- **Include the don'ts.** Anti-examples prevent more misuse than examples prevent.
- **Keep it current** or it becomes actively harmful — people build from stale documentation and then have to redo it.
- **Name a maintainer.** Unowned systems decay. This is the most common failure mode and it's organisational, not technical.
- **Make contribution possible.** If adding a component requires going through one bottleneck person, people will work around the system instead.

**Building one in Figma** (the Prototypr piece, now substantially dated on mechanics): the modern approach is styles and variables for tokens, components with variants and properties, auto layout throughout, and a published library other files consume. Figma's variables and modes (2023) added real theming and made the token layer properly first-class.

**UI-Patterns.com** appears here for the second time in the course — full writeup is earlier in this archive. The distinction worth restating: a pattern library tells you *when* and *why*; a component library tells you *what it looks like*. Most organisations build the second and skip the first, which is why they end up with beautifully consistent interfaces that make the wrong choices consistently.

title: Design languages in practice (clustered: Airbnb visual language and Airshots, IBM Design Language, Atlassian Design System)
summary:
Three organisations' published design languages, plus one workflow piece. These are primary sources — the actual systems, not articles about systems — which makes them more useful than most commentary.

**Airbnb's "Building a Visual Language"** documents the creation of their Design Language System (DLS) around 2016, and it's the most instructive of the three because it explains the reasoning.

Their stated problems before the DLS: designs were inconsistent across platforms, the team was growing faster than shared understanding, and every new feature meant redesigning existing elements.

Their principles for the system:
- **Unified** — each piece is part of a greater whole and contributes positively at scale. No exceptions that only make sense locally.
- **Universal** — Airbnb is used globally, so the system must work across cultures, languages and contexts
- **Iconic** — bold and clear where focus matters
- **Conversational** — motion and interaction express a personality

The insight worth extracting: **they designed components as a system rather than designing screens and extracting components afterward.** That inversion is the actual shift, and it's the thing most teams get wrong when they "start a design system" by tidying up what they already shipped.

Airbnb also went further than most into **cross-platform component parity** — the same component defined once, implemented natively on each platform. That work led toward their later explorations in design-to-code tooling.

**Airshots** — a smaller piece about building a workflow for generating app store screenshots at scale across locales and devices. Niche, but a good example of the kind of unglamorous production problem that eats design team time, and of treating tooling as a design deliverable.

**IBM Design Language** — the most philosophically ambitious of the three. Rooted explicitly in IBM's design heritage (Paul Rand, Eliot Noyes, Charles and Ray Eames), it covers not just UI but typography, colour, iconography, motion, photography and even three-dimensional and physical expression. **IBM Plex**, their open-source typeface family, came out of it. The Carbon Design System is the code implementation.

Worth knowing because it demonstrates that a design language is broader than a component library — it's an articulated position on what the organisation's work should feel like, from which components are derived.

**Atlassian Design System** — the most practically useful of the three to actually study, because it's exhaustively documented, publicly accessible, and covers the boring-but-essential parts most systems skip: content guidelines, writing style, accessibility requirements per component, and clear usage/anti-usage guidance. If you want a model for how to document a system well, this is the one to read.

**What to take from all three:** read them as examples of *documentation quality* and *reasoning*, not as things to copy. Every good design system is specific to its organisation's product, values and constraints. Copying Airbnb's DLS into a B2B analytics tool produces something incoherent.

title: Exporting Image Assets for Different Screen Resolutions (@2x, @3x)
summary:
Practical piece on exporting raster assets at multiple densities for different screen resolutions.

**The underlying concept:** screens differ in pixel density. A point (iOS) or density-independent pixel (Android) is a logical unit; the physical pixels per logical unit varies by device. So a 24pt icon needs a 24px asset at @1x, 48px at @2x, 72px at @3x. Android uses the same idea with named buckets: mdpi, hdpi, xhdpi, xxhdpi, xxxhdpi.

**The practical rules:**
- **Design at @1x** and export at multiples, so your source dimensions stay simple
- **Keep dimensions divisible** so the multiples land on whole pixels — a 25px asset at @1.5x gives you 37.5px and a blurry result. This is one reason the 8-point grid helps.
- **Name exports by the platform's convention** — `icon@2x.png` for iOS, density-bucket folders for Android
- **Use vectors wherever possible.** SVG for web, PDF or SF Symbols for iOS, vector drawables for Android. Vectors sidestep the whole problem.
- **Raster is only genuinely necessary for photography and complex texture**

**Why this still matters despite vectors:** photography, illustration with gradients or texture, and app store assets all still need raster exports at multiple densities. It's unglamorous production work that's easy to get subtly wrong.

title: Giving and receiving design feedback (clustered, 4 sources)
summary:
Four sources on critique. This is one of the highest-value clusters in the whole archive, because feedback handling is a skill that visibly separates experience levels and it's almost never taught.

**Giving feedback well:**

- **Ask what kind of feedback is wanted** before giving any. Early exploration needs different input than pre-handoff polish. "Where are you with this and what would be most useful?" prevents most bad critique.
- **Critique against stated goals**, not against your taste. "Does this achieve the goal of X?" beats "I'd have done it differently."
- **Describe what you observe before you prescribe.** "My eye goes to the illustration before the headline" is information. "Make the headline bigger" is a solution that skips the diagnosis and may be the wrong fix.
- **Ask questions rather than issuing verdicts.** "What led you to the two-column layout?" often reveals a constraint you didn't know about, and sometimes reveals to the designer that there wasn't a reason.
- **Be specific and prioritise.** Twenty equally-weighted comments are unusable. Name the two or three that matter.
- **Say what's working**, and mean it specifically. Not politeness — if you don't name what works, it gets changed in the next iteration.
- **Avoid the compliment sandwich.** People discount the praise and hear only the criticism, so you lose both.

**Receiving feedback well:**

- **Separate yourself from the work.** Easy to say. The practical technique is to present the work in third person — "this layout" rather than "my layout" — which genuinely changes how criticism lands.
- **Don't defend immediately.** Listen fully, ask clarifying questions, then respond. The impulse to explain why they're wrong is strong and almost always counterproductive.
- **Listen for the problem behind the proposed solution.** This is the most important skill in the cluster. When someone says "make the logo bigger", the underlying observation might be "I couldn't tell whose site this was." The solution is theirs to propose and usually wrong; the observation is theirs to have and usually valid.
- **You don't have to act on everything.** You do have to acknowledge it and be able to explain your reasoning if you don't.
- **Ask for the reasoning** when feedback is vague. "Can you say more about what feels off?"
- **Write it down** and follow up on what you changed and why. This builds trust and stops the same feedback recurring.

**Feedback from non-designers specifically** (Christian Beck's piece, the most practically useful of the four):
- Non-designers often lack vocabulary, so they reach for solutions instead of descriptions. That's a translation problem, not a competence problem.
- **Set context before showing.** What stage this is at, what you want input on, what's deliberately unresolved. Most bad stakeholder feedback comes from unset expectations.
- **Give them a frame.** "Does this clearly communicate X?" produces better input than "what do you think?"
- **Beware the highest-paid person's opinion (HiPPO).** Research and stated goals are the counterweight. This is what the evidence is *for*.
- Aesthetic preferences dressed as requirements are the common failure. Redirect to the goal: "the brand guidelines specify this palette — is there a specific reason this feels wrong for this screen?"

**The structural point nobody says directly:** most design work fails not because the design was bad but because the designer couldn't navigate the feedback and get it shipped. Craft gets you to a good design; this skill gets it built.

still_relevant:
This has moved from best practice to law across the EU. The **European Accessibility Act came into force in June 2025**, applying to a broad range of digital products and services sold in the EU — e-commerce, banking, e-books, transport, telecoms. **EN 301 549** is the European standard and it references WCAG. Combined with WCAG 2.2 (2023, which added focus appearance, target size and dragging-alternative criteria), accessibility is now a compliance requirement with real consequences.

In hiring, European employers are actively looking for designers who can speak to this credibly, and most candidates can't get past reciting contrast ratios. Being able to discuss the social model, situational disability, and how to build accessibility into a process rather than audit it at the end is a genuine differentiator.

Two of these six links are dead: the InVision microcopy piece (site shut down Dec 2024) and the Adobe XD Ideas article (XD on maintenance-only).
title: Accessibility in UX (clustered: IxDF social needs, Berryhill on framing, UsabilityGeek visual principles, Forbes, Adobe XD, InVision microcopy)
summary:
Six sources on accessibility. Berryhill's framing piece carries the most weight, and the framing is the thing most teams get wrong.

**The central argument: communicate accessibility as needs to be met, not rules to be followed.** When accessibility arrives as a compliance checklist, teams treat it as a tax — done late, done minimally, resented. When it arrives as a description of real people with real needs, it becomes a design problem, which is the thing designers are actually good at. Same requirements, completely different engagement.

**The social model of disability** (the IxDF piece's foundation, and worth understanding precisely because it changes what you think you're fixing):
- The **medical model** locates disability in the person — something wrong with them, to be treated or accommodated
- The **social model** locates disability in the environment — a person using a wheelchair isn't disabled by their legs, they're disabled by stairs

For design, that means **the interface is the disabling factor**, not the user. A blind person isn't disabled from using your app; your unlabelled buttons disable them. That reframing puts responsibility where it belongs and makes the work feel like design rather than charity.

**The categories to design for** — and note that most are situational or temporary, not permanent:
- **Visual** — blindness, low vision, colour vision deficiency. Also: bright sunlight, a cracked screen, forgotten glasses.
- **Auditory** — deafness, hard of hearing. Also: a noisy train, a sleeping baby, no headphones.
- **Motor** — tremor, paralysis, limited dexterity. Also: a broken arm, holding a child, a bumpy bus.
- **Cognitive** — dyslexia, ADHD, memory conditions, learning differences. Also: stress, exhaustion, distraction, operating in a second language.

Microsoft's **permanent / temporary / situational** framing is the clearest version of this. Designing for one-armed use serves the person with an amputation, the person with a broken arm, and the person holding a baby. Accessibility work has a much wider beneficiary set than people assume.

**The visual accessibility principles** (UsabilityGeek's six, condensed):
1. **Sufficient contrast** — 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text and UI components at WCAG AA
2. **Never rely on colour alone** — pair it with icons, text, patterns or position
3. **Readable type** — adequate size, sensible line height, no all-caps for long text, avoid ultra-light weights
4. **Clear focus indicators** — keyboard users need to see where they are. WCAG 2.2 strengthened this.
5. **Adequate target size** — 24×24 CSS px minimum at WCAG 2.2 AA, with larger recommended
6. **Respect user settings** — text resizing, reduced motion, dark mode, system font size

**Accessible microcopy** (the InVision piece, now a dead link — the site shut down at the end of 2024): plain language, descriptive link text (never "click here"), meaningful alt text, error messages that say what's wrong and how to fix it, and labels that stay visible rather than disappearing placeholders.

**WCAG in practice:** Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust (POUR) are the four principles. Levels A, AA, AAA — **AA is the standard target** and the level most legislation references.

still_relevant:
Both sides more relevant now. Cheap experimentation and AI-assisted rapid iteration make it easier than ever to optimise locally and never question the direction. The critique is the less-heard half and therefore the more useful one to be able to articulate — 'when is iteration the wrong tool?' is a strong thing to have an answer to in a senior interview.

title: Iterative design and its critics (clustered: NN/g, IxDF, Pidoco, and 'Iteration is not design')
summary:
Three sources arguing for iteration and one arguing against it. The disagreement is the valuable part, and it's rare for a curriculum to include the counter-argument.

**The case for iteration** (Nielsen's 1993 study is the empirical backbone):
Nielsen tracked usability across design iterations on real projects and found **measured usability improved by around 38% on average per iteration**, with cumulative improvement across four iterations often exceeding 150%. The improvements didn't plateau quickly — later iterations kept delivering.

The mechanism: each round of testing surfaces problems, fixing them surfaces the *next* layer of problems that were previously hidden behind the first. You cannot see the second-order problems until the first-order ones are gone. This is the argument for three rounds of five users rather than one round of fifteen.

The standard loop: **design → prototype → test → analyse → refine → repeat.**

**The counter-argument** (Gavin Lau, "Iteration is not design — debunking design Darwinism"). His term for the failure mode is **design Darwinism**: the belief that great design emerges from enough iterations, A/B tests and incremental improvements. His claims:

- **Iteration cannot innovate.** User feedback in an iteration cycle mainly identifies *problems with the current design*. It cannot tell you that a fundamentally different design would be better. You can iterate your way to a locally excellent version of the wrong thing.
- **Iteration cannot create delight.** Incremental refinement removes friction; it doesn't produce the leap that makes something remarkable.
- **His example is Google** — vast resources, engineering-led product management, extensive experimentation, and a long list of failed products. His reading is that they expected iteration to substitute for design vision. Whether or not you accept the Google diagnosis, the structural point stands.
- **To mistake the design tool of iteration for design itself is a grave error.**

**The synthesis, which is where you should actually land:** iteration is a refinement mechanism, not a generative one. It is extremely good at making a chosen direction work well and completely incapable of choosing the direction. The direction comes from research, insight, synthesis and judgment — the whole first half of this curriculum.

This is the same thing as the A/B testing point earlier in this archive: **a local optimiser walks you uphill and cannot tell you you're on the wrong hill.** Iteration without periodic step-back is how products get incrementally better and strategically stuck.

**Practical reconciliation:** iterate tightly within a direction, and separately maintain a slower cycle of generative research and divergent exploration that can propose a different hill entirely. Teams that only do the first get polished mediocrity. Teams that only do the second never ship.

still_relevant:
Directly actionable, and the advice has sharpened since. Current additions worth knowing:

**AI has changed the bar.** Polished visual output is now cheap, which makes reasoning, constraints and outcomes the differentiating content — exactly what the Shopify 'rough work' argument was already pointing at. Expect to be asked to talk through your process live, partly because portfolios can be AI-assisted.

**Case study length has come down.** Long scrolling case studies are frequently skimmed. A short summary at the top with expandable detail below works better.

**For applications abroad**, state your work authorisation situation somewhere findable, note language levels honestly, and consider whether the strongest case studies read clearly to someone reading in a second language. Shorter sentences and clearer structure help more than you'd expect. Site builders like Framer and Webflow handle the summary-then-detail structure well without custom development.
title: UX portfolios (clustered: Indeed hiring managers, Lisefski 'Person before portfolio', Shopify on rough work, Dribbble guide)
summary:
Four sources on portfolios, including two written by people who actually do the hiring. Directly applicable rather than archival.

**What hiring managers say they look for** (Indeed Design, collated from hiring managers):
- **Process over polish.** Beautiful final screens with no visible reasoning are the most common weakness. They want to see how you think.
- **Your specific contribution.** Team projects are fine, but state exactly what you did. Vague "we" language reads as hiding.
- **Problem framing.** What was the actual problem, how did you determine that, and how did you know it was the right problem?
- **Constraints and tradeoffs.** Real projects have budget limits, technical constraints, stakeholder disagreements and deadlines. Showing how you navigated them is more convincing than showing an unconstrained ideal.
- **Outcomes.** What happened? Even qualitative outcomes beat none. "Reduced support tickets about X" or "the team adopted Y" counts.
- **Fewer, deeper case studies.** Three strong ones beat eight thin ones, consistently.

**Martin Sitar's Shopify piece — show your rough work.** The most useful specific advice in the cluster. Sketches, discarded directions, whiteboard photos, the ugly middle. Polished final screens prove you can use Figma. Rough work proves you can think, and it's the part most portfolios omit precisely because it feels unimpressive. It's also what distinguishes a real project from a redesign concept.

**Benek Lisefski's "Person before portfolio"** — argues the portfolio is over-weighted in how designers approach job hunting. What actually converts is relationships, reputation and how you communicate. The portfolio gets you considered; the conversation gets you hired. His practical implication: time spent on network, writing, and being visible in a community often returns more than another week of portfolio polish.

**Structuring a case study** — the reliable shape:
1. **Context** — company, product, your role, timeline, team
2. **Problem** — what was wrong, and how you knew
3. **Research** — what you did, what you found, what surprised you
4. **Process** — explorations, including the ones you rejected and why
5. **Solution** — what you shipped, with the reasoning
6. **Outcome** — measured if possible, qualitative if not
7. **Reflection** — what you'd do differently. This one is optional and it's the one that most signals seniority.

**Common failures:**
- All output, no reasoning
- No stated problem, so the solution has nothing to be judged against
- Unstated role on team projects
- Too many projects, none deep
- No outcomes
- Unexplained process theatre — a persona and a journey map included because the course said to, with no evidence they informed anything

**On the last point specifically:** including artefacts that didn't change a decision is worse than omitting them, because it signals process-following rather than thinking. Show the artefacts that *changed what you did*, and say what they changed.

title: Module 1 stragglers (Broadcom Rally user stories, UX StackExchange thread, OERu research methods, Wikipedia research question, Pearltrees file)
summary:
Five leftovers from a related section, cleared here. Mostly low-value, with one idea worth keeping.

**The one worth keeping — what makes a good research question** (OERu's research methods module and the Wikipedia entry, which is surprisingly decent on this). A usable research question is:
- **Focused** — narrow enough to actually answer
- **Researchable** — answerable with the methods and access you have
- **Feasible** — within your time, budget and reach
- **Specific** — not "is our app usable?" but "can new users complete first-time setup without assistance?"
- **Open** — not answerable yes/no in a way that closes off learning
- **Relevant** — tied to a decision someone will make

The **FINER** criteria from research methodology are a compact version: Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant.

This connects directly to the test-planning material earlier in this archive — most weak research is weak because the question was never sharpened, and no amount of good method rescues a vague question.

**Broadcom / Rally on user stories** — vendor documentation for a specific agile tool. Superseded entirely by the Pichler, Cohn and Atlassian material already covered earlier in this archive Rally itself changed hands repeatedly (Rally → CA Technologies → Broadcom) and the URL is unstable.

**UX StackExchange thread on where UX stories go in an agile process** — forum discussion, no authoritative answer, and the question is genuinely contested. The short version of the answer that emerged in practice: UX work generally happens a sprint ahead of development (dual-track agile), with discovery and delivery running as parallel tracks rather than UX being a phase inside a sprint. Marty Cagan's dual-track framing is the reference worth knowing instead.

**Pearltrees file** — dead link, expired signature, titled only "Fichier". Unrecoverable.

title: History of UX and the UX Wheel (clustered: CareerFoundry, UX Booth, Uxeria, UX Wheel)
summary:
Three overlapping histories plus the UX Wheel diagram. The history is worth knowing mainly because it stops you thinking UX was invented alongside the iPhone.

**The lineage:**
- **~1900s — Frederick Winslow Taylor and scientific management.** Studying the efficiency of human interaction with tools. Ethically dubious in application, methodologically the ancestor of task analysis.
- **1940s — Toyota's human-centred production**, where workers' input shaped the system. (Same lineage that later produced Lean.)
- **1948 — Henry Dreyfuss**, industrial designer, publishes *Designing for People*: "when the point of contact between the product and the people becomes a point of friction, then the designer has failed."
- **1955 — Dreyfuss's anthropometric work** (*The Measure of Man*) systematised designing around real human bodies.
- **WWII and after — human factors and ergonomics** as a formal discipline, driven by aviation. Cockpit design errors were killing pilots, and the research showed the problem was the interface, not the pilots. The famous case: B-17 "pilot error" crashes traced to identical adjacent controls for flaps and landing gear.
- **1966 — Walt Disney** and the opening of Disney World, often cited as experience design before the term existed.
- **1970s — Xerox PARC.** The GUI, the mouse, WYSIWYG. Also where Don Norman later worked.
- **1988 — Don Norman publishes *The Psychology of Everyday Things*** (later retitled *The Design of Everyday Things*). Affordances, signifiers, mapping, feedback.
- **~1993 — Norman joins Apple and coins the title "User Experience Architect"**, explicitly because "human interface" and "usability" were too narrow for what he wanted to cover — the whole experience of the company, its products and its services.
- **1998 onward** — the web forces the discipline to scale; Nielsen and Rosenfeld/Morville define usability and IA as professional practices.

**The UX Wheel** (Magnus Revang, 2007) — an early attempt at mapping the whole field onto one diagram: the disciplines, deliverables, processes and considerations that make up UX. Historically interesting as a snapshot of how sprawling the field already felt in 2007. Superseded by cleaner models like Morville's honeycomb (covered earlier in this archive) and Garrett's five planes.

**Why the history matters practically:** the argument that UX is a young, trendy, dispensable discipline comes up in organisations that want to cut it. Knowing that the human factors work is 80 years old and came out of people dying in aircraft is a better response than enthusiasm.

**One dead link** in this cluster — a Pearltrees image capture of the wheel, expired signature.

title: Intro-level research (clustered: IxDF design thinking overview, CareerFoundry how-to, Helsinki Design Lab ethnography fieldguide)
summary:
Two of these three duplicate material already covered at greater depth earlier in this archive (design thinking frameworks, research methods overview). Cross-referenced rather than repeated.

**The one genuinely worth keeping is the Helsinki Design Lab ethnography fieldguide.** HDL was Sitra's strategic design unit (the Finnish Innovation Fund), and it produced unusually good, practical public-sector design material before closing in 2013.

**What it adds beyond the standard research-methods coverage:** it's written for ethnographic fieldwork in a *service and systems* context rather than a product one — studying how people move through public services, institutions and physical environments. The emphasis is on studying the system as experienced, not the interface.

Practical points that don't appear in the product-focused sources:
- **Go where the thing happens**, and stay longer than feels necessary. The interesting behaviour appears after people stop performing for you.
- **Record the environment, not just the person** — signage, queues, paperwork, physical layout, who else is present
- **Note what's absent** as carefully as what's present. Missing signage, missing staff, missing information.
- **Follow the artefact** — forms, receipts, tickets, letters. Paper trails reveal the system's actual structure, which frequently differs from its official one.
- **Write field notes the same day**, in two columns: observation on one side, interpretation on the other, kept visibly separate.

That last one is a discipline worth adopting generally. Conflating observation and interpretation in notes is how weak insights get laundered into findings.

**Note:** Helsinki Design Lab closed in 2013 and the site is a static archive. Still accessible, no longer maintained.

Being visibly rigorous about defining the problem first is a strong differentiator. The personas critique is useful for portfolio hygiene too: if you include a persona, be able to say what it changed.
title: Personas, their alternatives, and problem framing (clustered: 17 alternatives, HBR, problem statements, quick guide)
summary:
The two genuinely valuable pieces here are the personas critique and the HBR problem-framing article. Both add something the main curriculum doesn't.

**"Ditch your personas — 17 alternatives"** — the critique of personas that the rest of the course lacks.

The case against traditional personas:
- Often **built from assumption** rather than research, then treated as evidence
- **Demographic detail is usually irrelevant** and sometimes actively misleading. Knowing "Sarah, 34, marketing manager, loves yoga" tells you almost nothing about how she'll use your product.
- They **average people into fictions** nobody actually resembles
- They **go stale** and sit on walls unread
- They can **encode and launder bias** — stock photos and invented lifestyle details smuggle in assumptions

The alternatives worth knowing:
- **Jobs to be Done statements** — "When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome]." Focuses on the job, not the person.
- **Behavioural archetypes** — grouped by what people *do*, not who they are
- **Mindsets** — grouped by attitude and approach to the task
- **Proto-personas** — explicitly labelled as assumption-based, to be validated. Honest about their status.
- **Empathy maps**, **user scenarios**, **journey maps** — already covered earlier in this archive
- **Anti-personas** — who this is explicitly *not* for. Surprisingly clarifying.
- **Real named users** — for small B2B products, just use actual customers
- **Capability or context grids** — segment by access, expertise or constraint rather than identity

**The useful synthesis:** the problem isn't personas as a concept, it's personas built on demographics rather than behaviour, and personas built on assumption rather than research. A behaviour-based persona grounded in real interviews is fine. A stock photo with an invented biography is decoration.

**"Are You Solving the Right Problem?"** (Dwayne Spradlin, HBR 2012) — the strongest piece in the intro course, and it's about problem framing rather than design specifically.

Spradlin's argument: organisations routinely invest heavily in solving problems they never properly defined, and problem definition is a skill that can be made rigorous. His four-step framework:
1. **Establish the need for a solution.** What's the desired outcome, who benefits, what's the business case for solving it at all?
2. **Justify the need.** Is this consistent with strategy? What happens if we don't solve it?
3. **Contextualise the problem.** What's been tried before, internally and elsewhere? Why did it fail? What constraints are real and which are assumed?
4. **Write the problem statement.** Independent of any solution, with clear success criteria and a defined scope.

**The key discipline: state the problem without embedding a solution.** "We need a mobile app" is a solution disguised as a problem. "Field staff cannot record inspection results until they return to the office, which delays reporting by an average of two days" is a problem — and it might be solved by an app, or a form redesign, or a process change, or a phone call.

**Problem statements** (Lavoie's piece) — the practical format:
> [User] needs a way to [need] because [insight], and we'll know it works when [measurable outcome].

The "because" is the load-bearing part. If you can't articulate why, you haven't done the research.

kill_reason: Marketing-funnel buyer personas, which are a different artefact from UX personas despite the shared name — they segment for targeting and messaging, not for design decisions. Content-marketing pieces with lead-gen intent. Conflating the two is a common confusion and worth avoiding rather than reinforcing.

title: IA and flows at intro level (clustered: NN/g mental models, UX Booth IA guide, task vs user flows, flowchart notation, Journal of IA)
summary:
Six sources, three of which add something beyond what a related section and 3 already cover.

**NN/g on mental models** (Nielsen, 2010) — the canonical short statement, complementing the McClellan piece earlier in this archive

The definition: **a mental model is what the user believes about the system, not what the system actually is.** Built from prior experience with other systems, assumptions, and partial information. It is frequently wrong and it governs behaviour anyway.

The practical consequence: **you are designing against the user's existing mental model whether you acknowledge it or not.** If your system works differently from what they expect, they will make errors that look inexplicable to you and perfectly logical to them.

Two ways to close the gap:
1. **Change the design to match the mental model** — usually the better option, and the reason conventions exist
2. **Change the mental model through the design** — possible, but expensive. Requires teaching, and people resist. Only worth it when your model is genuinely better and the benefit is large.

Nielsen's warning to designers: **you have a different mental model from your users** because you know how the system works internally. That knowledge is unrecoverable — you cannot un-know it — which is why you cannot assess your own design's learnability.

**Task flows vs user flows, demonstrated by pancakes** (Erika Harano) — a clean distinction, memorably explained:
- **Task flow** — one path, no branches, the same for everyone. Making pancakes: mix, pour, flip, serve.
- **User flow** — branches by user type, decision or entry point. One person uses a mix, another makes batter from scratch, another has a waffle iron.

Use task flows when the process is identical for all users and you want to examine one sequence closely. Use user flows when different users take different routes and you need to see the branching. Most people conflate the terms; being precise is a small, easy credibility marker.

**Flowchart notation** (Lucidchart and RFF references): oval = start/end, rectangle = process or screen, diamond = decision, parallelogram = input/output, arrow = flow direction. Standard notation matters less than internal consistency, but using the conventions means your diagram is legible to engineers and PMs without a key.

**Journal of Information Architecture** (Resmini) — peer-reviewed academic IA. Worth knowing it exists. Resmini's work on **pervasive information architecture** — IA across channels and physical/digital boundaries rather than within a single website — is the most interesting thread there and it prefigured a lot of current cross-channel service thinking.

**UX Booth's IA beginner guide** overlaps with the IA history material earlier in this archive; cross-referenced.

author: Jakob Nielsen
key_points: 0-4 scale from 'not a problem' to 'catastrophe'

still_relevant: Standard practice, unchanged. The separate-pass recommendation is the detail most people skip and it meaningfully improves rating quality.
title: Severity Ratings for Usability Problems
summary:
The primary source for the 0-4 severity scale used throughout usability practice. The method is covered in full earlier in this archive; this is the original.

**The scale:**
- **0** — Not a usability problem at all
- **1** — Cosmetic only; need not be fixed unless extra time is available
- **2** — Minor usability problem; low priority
- **3** — Major usability problem; important to fix, high priority
- **4** — Usability catastrophe; imperative to fix before release

**The three factors** severity combines: frequency (how common), impact (how hard to overcome), and persistence (one-time bump vs repeated obstruction).

**Nielsen's methodological point, which is the reason to read the original:** severity ratings from a single evaluator are unreliable. His data showed you need **around three evaluators** to get a reasonably reliable severity estimate, and more for high-stakes decisions. Rate independently, then average — don't discuss first.

He also recommends collecting severity ratings **as a separate pass after the evaluation**, sending evaluators the aggregated problem list and having them rate everything, rather than rating as they go. Rating in the moment is biased by recency and by how frustrating the problem felt to *you*.

author: Cindy Alvarez
key_points: Interview the stakeholder before you design the test — that's the first research interview

still_relevant: Permanently, and directly useful in interviews. 'How do you get stakeholders to act on research?' is a common question and most answers are vague. Alvarez gives you four specific tactics and a memorable line.
title: 5 Ways to Ensure Usability Testing Results Aren't Ignored
summary:
Alvarez was UX Director at Yammer and later at Microsoft, and wrote *Lean Customer Development*. This is a short piece on the problem nobody teaches: research that gets done and then ignored.

**Her five:**

**1. Understand the purpose of the thing you're testing.** Why are we building this? How does it benefit the company when it succeeds? What do end users get? If you can't answer these, your test will measure the wrong things.

**2. Find out what questions the testing needs to answer — by interviewing the stakeholder first.** Her framing is sharp: *the first user research interview you should be doing is on the stakeholder of the testing.* Task-based usability testing frequently feels conceived in a vacuum because nobody asked what decision it was meant to inform. If the real question is "will people pay for premium features", testing the mechanics of the checkout flow won't answer it.

**3. Get people to watch.** *"When people don't watch the results, they don't act on the results."* Reading a report engages a different part of the brain than watching a real person fail. Live viewing, a stream, a recording played in a team meeting — anything beats a document.

**4. Recommend changes based on the results. Take a stand.** Her point: how can you expect stakeholders to make changes based on research if you aren't willing to suggest them? Two supporting observations:
 - "Pure usability" rarely wins in a business context; it's always a tradeoff, so frame recommendations in those terms
 - Stakeholders won't necessarily follow your recommendation, but **a strong stance gives them something to bounce ideas off.** A neutral findings dump gives them nothing to react to and the conversation dies.

**5. Tell a SHORT story with the results — quotes, numbers, screenshots.** You have about 15 seconds to capture attention. Lead with that. The five hours of video can be a link at the bottom.

**Why this is the most useful piece in the intro course:** everything else teaches how to do research. This is about whether the research changes anything, which is the failure mode most likely to make a research practice look worthless inside an organisation. Pairs directly with the reporting guidance earlier in this archive and the stakeholder material in 4.7.

title: Storytelling for UX (clustered: UX Knowledge Base, Nessler's 6 principles, Pixar's Story Spine, Pixar's 22 Rules)
summary:
The best-kept section of the intro course and the one thing in it not covered anywhere else in the course. Storytelling shows up in UX in two distinct ways and these sources cover both.

**Two uses of narrative in UX:**
1. **Designing the product as a narrative** — the user is the protagonist, the product is a tool or helper, and the experience has an arc
2. **Presenting your work as a narrative** — persuading a room, which is covered in the next cluster

**The Story Spine** (Kenn Adams, popularised through Pixar and Emma Coats's rule #4) — the most practically useful storytelling structure for designers because it's short enough to actually use:

> Once upon a time there was ___.
> Every day, ___.
> One day ___.
> Because of that, ___.
> Because of that, ___.
> Until finally ___.

Map it onto a user narrative: *Once upon a time there was a freelance designer. Every day she tracked invoices in a spreadsheet. One day a client disputed a payment she had no record of. Because of that she lost three days reconstructing it. Because of that she started turning down clients she didn't trust. Until finally she needed a system that made the record automatic.*

That's a user story, a problem statement and a pitch, in six lines. It works for research findings, for case studies, and for explaining to stakeholders why a problem matters.

**Pixar's 22 Rules of Storytelling** (Emma Coats, then a Pixar storyboard artist, tweeted these in 2011). The ones that transfer directly to design work:
- **#2: Keep in mind what's interesting to the audience, not what's fun to do as a writer.** The design equivalent: what's interesting to the user, not what's fun to design.
- **#4: The story spine** (above)
- **#5: Simplify. Focus. Combine characters. Hop over detours.** It'll feel like you're losing valuable things; you're freeing the story up. This is a direct statement of design reduction.
- **#9: When you're stuck, make a list of what WOULDN'T happen next.** Excellent ideation unsticking technique.
- **#11: Getting it out of your head lets you start fixing it.** Argument for sketching and rough prototypes.
- **#14: Why must you tell THIS story?** The belief burning inside you is the story's heart. For design: why does this problem matter enough to solve?
- **#19: Coincidences to get characters into trouble are great; coincidences to get them out of it are cheating.** For design: don't resolve a user's problem with a lucky assumption.

**Nessler's six storytelling principles for UX** — condensed: know your audience, have a clear protagonist (the user, not the product), establish conflict (the problem), show change, keep it concrete with specifics rather than abstractions, and end with a resolution that implies action.

**Why this matters more than it sounds:** organisations run on narrative. The design decision that gets funded is frequently not the best-evidenced one but the best-told one. Designers who can't narrate lose to people with weaker cases and better stories. Learning the structure is a small investment with a large return.

still_relevant: Fully, and it maps directly onto portfolio presentation rounds. The structure above — problem, constraints, process with rejected directions, solution with reasoning, self-surfaced tradeoffs — is essentially the case study format interviewers are hoping for. Rehearsing the 2-minute, 10-minute and deep-dive versions of each project against this structure is among the highest-leverage interview prep available.
title: Presenting design work (clustered: InVision art of presenting, Shopify on communication, UXM 10 ways, Kawasaki 10/20/30, Forbes on PowerPoint, Visage tips, conference tips)
summary:
Seven sources on presenting. The Shopify piece is the most valuable because it argues the skill is not peripheral.

**Cattapan's argument (Shopify): describing your work is a critical design skill, not a soft add-on.** Design work that can't be explained doesn't get built. The ability to articulate *why* is what separates a designer whose work ships from one whose work sits in Figma. It's also, uncomfortably, a large part of what gets people promoted.

**Structuring a design presentation:**
1. **Restate the problem and the goal.** Never open with the solution. The audience needs the criteria before they can evaluate anything.
2. **Recap the constraints** — technical, business, timeline. This pre-empts half the objections.
3. **Show the process briefly**, including rejected directions. It demonstrates that the choice was made rather than stumbled into.
4. **Present the solution with reasoning attached**, decision by decision
5. **Name the open questions and tradeoffs yourself.** If you don't surface them, someone else will and it'll look like you missed them.
6. **Ask for specific feedback**, not general reactions

**The rules from the presentation-craft sources:**

**Kawasaki's 10/20/30 rule** — 10 slides, 20 minutes, 30-point minimum font size. Originally for pitch decks and widely applicable. The font size rule is the sneaky-good one: forcing 30pt means you cannot fit paragraphs, which means you have to know what you're saying rather than reading it.

**Gallo (Forbes) on the 10-minute wall** — attention measurably drops around the ten-minute mark. His prescription: build in a deliberate change every ten minutes. A demo, a video clip, a question to the room, a shift in speaker, a story. Not new information — a change in *mode*.

**The recurring practical advice** across these sources:
- **Know your audience and what they care about.** Executives want outcomes and risk. Engineers want constraints and edge cases. Designers want reasoning. Same work, different emphasis.
- **One idea per slide.** If it needs a paragraph, it needs to be a document instead.
- **Don't read your slides.** The slide supports you; it isn't the script.
- **Show real work, not decoration.** Actual screens beat stock imagery.
- **Rehearse out loud.** Reading it in your head hides every awkward sentence.
- **Land the ending.** Say the one thing you want remembered, last.

**On the Visage and conference-tips pieces:** standard presentation-design advice — contrast, hierarchy, limited type, generous space. Most designers know this already; the failure mode is applying it to client work and forgetting it for your own decks.

**Two dead links** in this cluster: both InVision pieces (site shut down December 2024).

still_relevant: All three durable. The skill-shape exercise is worth doing during any active job search — it turns 'which roles should I target' into a concrete question rather than a vague one, and it surfaces which adjacent skill is worth developing next. *Universal Methods of Design* is the best desk reference in the field.
title: Career next steps (clustered: Simon Pan on portfolio stories, Jason Mesut on skill shapes, UX methods and deliverables, books, Berlin UXD meetup)
summary:
Career and next-steps material. Three things here are worth keeping.

**Simon Pan — "Great Design Portfolios Are Great Stories."** Pan's Uber case study was one of the most-copied portfolio pieces of its era, for good reason. His argument extends the storytelling material above into the portfolio specifically.

The structure he advocates is narrative, not documentary:
- **Set the scene** — context, stakes, what was at risk
- **Establish the conflict** — the problem, and why it was hard
- **Show the struggle** — the attempts, the dead ends, the constraint that forced a rethink
- **Resolve** — what you shipped and what changed

The key distinction: **a documentary portfolio lists what you did; a narrative portfolio makes the reader care whether it worked.** Same content, different ordering and emphasis. The struggle section is the one most people cut and it's the one that creates investment.

**Jason Mesut — "Understanding your shape."** Mesut runs a well-known framework for mapping design skills, and this is more useful than the usual T-shaped/generalist discussion.

Rather than a single T, he has designers plot themselves across many skill dimensions — research, interaction, visual, prototyping, strategy, facilitation, writing, technical, management — at their actual level in each, producing a **shape** rather than a label. The value:
- It shows what you're genuinely deep in, rather than what you'd like to claim
- It reveals which adjacent skill would most improve your shape
- It's useful for team composition — you want complementary shapes, not identical ones
- **It's useful for job hunting**: you can match your shape against a role's shape rather than against a job title, which is far more informative given how inconsistently design titles are used

Worth actually doing rather than reading about. An hour with this produces a clearer picture of what roles to target than another week of portfolio tweaking.

**The two books** — both worth owning:
- **Norman, *The Design of Everyday Things*** (revised edition). The foundational text. Affordances, signifiers, mapping, feedback, the gulfs of execution and evaluation, human error as a design failure.
- **Martin & Hanington, *Universal Methods of Design*** (expanded and revised, 125 methods). A reference rather than a read-through — one method per spread with when to use it, how, and what it produces. Genuinely useful as a desk reference and the single best answer to "what method should I use here?" after Rohrer's framework.

**Berlin UXD meetup** — community. Worth noting this one is still active and Berlin has one of the larger European UX communities. Relevant if you're job hunting in Germany: community presence converts better than applications, and it's exactly what Lisefski's "person before portfolio" argument points at.

**Two dead:** usability.gov's methods index (site decommissioned; the *Universal Methods of Design* book covers the same ground better anyway), and the CareerFoundry sign-in page, which was the portal itself. It isn't listed below, since nothing is left behind it, but it is the whole reason this archive exists.
